Module 2 — Complete Unit Compendium

All 15 units of I/O Interfacing Techniques, with the deck's own diagrams, every numerical worked, 90+ solved coding scenarios, and both CAT-1 questions answered in the official key format.

Source BCSE305L Module 2 deck, 138 slides Diagrams reproduced from the deck PYQ CAT-1 Aug 2026, D1+TD1

How to use this

Every unit follows the same five-part shape, so you always know where you are:

PartWhat it gives you
SlidesThe deck's own diagrams, so you never have to switch to the PDF
ConceptWhat the slides say, plus what they leave out
Key pointsYellow boxes — the facts that earn or lose marks
NumericalsEvery calculable variation, worked in full
QuestionsSix or more coding scenarios per unit, at CAT difficulty, with complete solutions
Work it in this order

Read the concept → cover the solution and attempt the question on paper → simulate it in Tinkercad or Wokwi → open the solution and compare. Solutions are collapsed deliberately; opening one before attempting it teaches you nothing.

The exam pattern this is built for

CAT-1 is 90 minutes, 50 marks, five compulsory questions of ten marks each — 18 minutes per question including the diagram. Module 2 supplies two of those five.

TypeLooks likeAnswer skeleton
P — Program"Write an Arduino program to…"Aim → Components → Circuit → Working → Flowchart → Program → Result
D — Design"Design a system using X sensor and Y actuator…"Same as P, with a fuller component table
T — Theory"Explain ADC / UART / timer with a neat diagram"Intro → Diagram → Block explanation → Features → Applications
N — NumericalADC count, resolution, duty cycle, timer preloadFormula → substitution → answer with unit
The habit that guarantees structure marks

Before writing any content, put the skeleton headings down the page — empty. Two minutes. A rushed answer with headings still scores; an unstructured wall does not. The flowchart is the most commonly dropped section and always carries a mark.

UNIT 01

The Board and the Chip

Slides 4–7  ·  Question types: T, N  ·  Weight: medium

Annotate slide 6 mentally every time you look at it: the six ~ pins are PWM-only; A0–A5 are the only analogRead pins; pins 0 and 1 belong to Serial and must not be used for I/O.

The distinction that costs marks

Arduino Uno ≠ ATmega328. The ATmega328 is the microcontroller — the black chip. The Uno is a board built around it, adding a USB-to-serial converter, a 5 V regulator, a 16 MHz crystal, headers and a reset button.

That is why the deck gives two spec lists. A question saying "features of Arduino Uno" wants slide 4; "architecture of ATmega328" wants slide 7.

Port mapping — the bridge between the two lists

Chip portChip pinsArduino nameNotes
Port DPD0–PD7Digital 0–7PD0 = RX, PD1 = TX
Port BPB0–PB5Digital 8–13PB6, PB7 → crystal, unavailable
Port CPC0–PC5Analog A0–A5PC6 = RESET, unavailable

14 digital + 6 analog = 20 usable pins out of 24 port bits. The missing four went to the crystal and reset — that is the complete answer to "why 14 and 6?"

Key points — each number is a wall you will hit
  • 8-bit data bus → the ALU handles 8 bits per operation. An int is 16 bits (two operations); a float is far slower.
  • 16-bit address bus → 216 = 65,536 locations. This is where 65535 in the timer preload formula comes from, and why the deck's SPI EEPROM is exactly 65,536 bytes.
  • 32 KB Flash / 2 KB SRAM / 1 KB EEPROM → three different memories. Flash holds the program and survives power-off; SRAM holds variables and is lost on power-off; EEPROM holds data you want kept. This table is the entire justification for CAT Q3.
  • 40 mA per pin → one LED (≈20 mA) is fine. A motor or servo needs hundreds of mA, so it can never be driven directly. This single number justifies every transistor and relay in every design answer.
  • 16 MHz → one clock tick = 62.5 ns. Every timer calculation starts here.
  • 32 general-purpose registers → RISC design: arithmetic cannot be done on memory directly, operands must be loaded into a register first.

Numericals

N1.1 — The Uno runs at 16 MHz. Find (i) the clock period, (ii) cycles in 1 ms, (iii) the longest interval a 16-bit timer can measure with no prescaling.

(i) T = 1/f = 1/(16 × 10^6) = 62.5 ns (ii) 1 ms / 62.5 ns = (1 × 10^-3)/(62.5 × 10^-9) = 16,000 cycles (iii) 65536 × 62.5 ns = 4.096 ms → this is exactly why a prescaler is needed

N1.2 — An LED draws 20 mA at 2 V forward voltage from a 5 V pin. Find the series resistor, and the maximum LEDs one pin can drive.

R = (Vsupply − Vf)/I = (5 − 2)/0.020 = 150 Ω (220 Ω is used in practice for margin) Max per pin = 40 mA / 20 mA = 2 LEDs, and even that is at the absolute limit Practical answer: one LED per pin

N1.3 — A program declares int buffer[400];. What percentage of SRAM does it consume, and will it fit?

An int on AVR = 2 bytes → 400 × 2 = 800 bytes SRAM = 2 KB = 2048 bytes Usage = 800/2048 × 100 = 39% It fits, but leaves little room for the stack — a classic cause of random crashes

N1.4 — How many bytes of Flash are available to your sketch, and why is it not 32 KB?

Flash = 32 KB = 32768 bytes Bootloader occupies 0.5 KB = 512 bytes Available = 32768 − 512 = 32,256 bytes The bootloader is what lets you program over USB instead of needing an ICSP programmer

Coding scenarios

Q1.1   Type P  ·  basic I/O

Blink with a serial counter

Blink the onboard LED on pin 13 at 500 ms intervals and print a running blink count to the serial monitor on each cycle.

Solution Q1.1
const int LED = 13;
unsigned long blinkCount = 0;

void setup() {
  pinMode(LED, OUTPUT);
  Serial.begin(9600);
  Serial.println("System ready");
}

void loop() {
  digitalWrite(LED, HIGH);
  delay(500);
  digitalWrite(LED, LOW);
  delay(500);

  blinkCount++;
  Serial.print("Blink count = ");
  Serial.println(blinkCount);
}

Why unsigned long: a 16-bit int overflows at 32,767 and goes negative after about nine hours of blinking. On an 8-bit chip, integer width is a real design decision.

Q1.2   Type P  ·  ports B/C/D

Direct port manipulation

Turn digital pins 8 to 13 on and off together using direct port manipulation on Port B rather than six separate digitalWrite calls. Explain why this is faster.

Solution Q1.2
void setup() {
  DDRB = DDRB | B00111111;   // PB0..PB5 = pins 8..13 as OUTPUT
}

void loop() {
  PORTB = PORTB | B00111111;   // all six HIGH in ONE instruction
  delay(500);
  PORTB = PORTB & B11000000;   // all six LOW  in ONE instruction
  delay(500);
}

The three port registers — this is the register model from Unit 2 applied to I/O:

RegisterRole
DDRxData Direction Register — 1 = output, 0 = input
PORTxOutput data register — 1 = HIGH, 0 = LOW
PINxInput register — read the actual pin state

Why faster: digitalWrite performs a pin-number lookup, a timer check and a bit calculation each call — roughly 50 clock cycles. A direct port write is a single instruction, about 2 cycles. Six pins therefore change in 2 cycles instead of ~300, and they change simultaneously rather than one after another.

Why PB6 and PB7 are masked off: they carry the 16 MHz crystal. Writing to them would stop the clock.

Q1.3   Type P  ·  memory

Measure free SRAM at run time

Write a program that reports the number of free SRAM bytes, then allocates a 400-element integer array and reports it again. Explain the difference.

Solution Q1.3
int freeRam() {
  extern int __heap_start, *__brkval;
  int v;
  // distance between the top of the stack and the top of the heap
  return (int) &v - (__brkval == 0 ? (int) &__heap_start : (int) __brkval);
}

int bigBuffer[400];        // 400 x 2 bytes = 800 bytes of SRAM

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  Serial.print("Free SRAM = ");
  Serial.print(freeRam());
  Serial.println(" bytes");

  for (int i = 0; i < 400; i++) bigBuffer[i] = i;   // touch it so it is not optimised away

  Serial.print("Still free    = ");
  Serial.print(freeRam());
  Serial.println(" bytes");
}

void loop() {}

What you observe: total SRAM is 2048 bytes. A global array of 800 bytes is allocated at compile time, so free memory starts around 1200 bytes rather than 2048. Globals are reserved before your program even runs.

Exam point: this is why the deck's SPI EEPROM example uses a 128-byte buffer and not a 1024-byte one — 1024 bytes would be half of all available SRAM.

Q1.4   Type P  ·  PWM pins

Prove which pins support PWM

Write a program that fades an LED on pin 9 and simultaneously attempts to fade an LED on pin 8. Describe and explain the difference in behaviour.

Solution Q1.4
const int pwmPin    = 9;    // marked ~ on the board
const int nonPwmPin = 8;    // NOT marked ~

void setup() {
  pinMode(pwmPin,    OUTPUT);
  pinMode(nonPwmPin, OUTPUT);
  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
  for (int v = 0; v <= 255; v += 5) {
    analogWrite(pwmPin,    v);    // fades smoothly
    analogWrite(nonPwmPin, v);    // only switches at v = 128
    Serial.println(v);
    delay(30);
  }
}
The observation, and why

Pin 9 fades smoothly. Pin 8 stays dark until the value reaches 128, then snaps fully on. analogWrite on a non-PWM pin does not raise an error — it silently degrades into digitalWrite, going LOW below 128 and HIGH at 128 and above.

PWM pins are 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11. There are six, because the ATmega328 has six PWM output compare channels across its three timers.

Q1.5   Type P  ·  pins 0 and 1

Demonstrate the serial pin conflict

Write a program that reads a switch on pin 2 and echoes its state over serial. Then modify it to use pin 0 instead and explain what breaks.

Solution Q1.5
const int SWITCH = 2;      // safe

void setup() {
  pinMode(SWITCH, INPUT_PULLUP);
  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
  Serial.println(digitalRead(SWITCH) == LOW ? "PRESSED" : "released");
  delay(300);
}

Moving the switch to pin 0 breaks the program. Pin 0 is RX and pin 1 is TX — the hardware UART owns them, and the onboard USB-to-serial converter is wired to them. Using them as I/O produces corrupted serial output and phantom pin readings, and can prevent the board from being programmed.

Deck wording to quote: "It communicates on digital pins 0 (RX) and 1 (TX) as well as with the computer via USB. Thus, if you use these functions, you cannot also use pins 0 and 1 for digital input or output."

Q1.6   Type D  ·  current budget

LED chase with a current budget

Design a six-LED running-light (chase) display on pins 8–13. State the resistor value and verify that the design stays within the ATmega328's total current limit.

Solution Q1.6
const int LEDS[6] = {8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13};

void setup() {
  for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) pinMode(LEDS[i], OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) {            // forward
    digitalWrite(LEDS[i], HIGH);
    delay(120);
    digitalWrite(LEDS[i], LOW);
  }
  for (int i = 4; i > 0; i--) {            // reverse, skipping the ends
    digitalWrite(LEDS[i], HIGH);
    delay(120);
    digitalWrite(LEDS[i], LOW);
  }
}

Resistor: R = (5 − 2)/0.015 = 200 Ω → use the standard 220 Ω, giving about 13.6 mA per LED.

Current budget: only one LED is lit at a time in a chase, so the instantaneous draw is 13.6 mA — well inside the 40 mA per-pin limit. Even if all six were lit together the total would be 82 mA, still inside the ATmega328's 200 mA total port limit, though four simultaneous LEDs is the sensible ceiling.

The sentence examiners want

Per-pin limit 40 mA, whole-chip limit 200 mA. Anything larger must be switched through a transistor or relay, not driven directly.

UNIT 02

The I/O Programming Model

Slides 8–12  ·  Question types: T, P  ·  Weight: medium-high  ·  The conceptual spine of the module

1 — Digital vs analog devices (slide 8)

  • Information is exchanged through input and output devices; the signal may be digital or analog.
  • Digital signals interface directly to the CPU — a switch is 0 V or 5 V, which the CPU already understands.
  • Analog devices require a converter — an ADC coming in, a DAC going out.
  • "All peripherals cannot always be on-chip."

2 — Internal vs external I/O (slide 9)

InternalExternal
WherePhysically on the silicon dieA separate component
SizeSmallLarge
InterfaceDirectNeeds a bus interface
ExamplesRTC, ADCs, memoryLCD, keypad, MIC

3 — The register model (slide 10)

A CPU never talks to a device. It reads and writes registers.

  • Data register — read and write. Holds the bytes moving in and out.
  • Status register — read only. The device writes it to report busy, done or error. You cannot write it because you do not get to decide whether the device has finished.

4 — Two ways to address registers (slide 11)

Memory-mapped I/OI/O-mapped I/O
Address spaceShared with memorySeparate, dedicated
InstructionsOrdinary load/storeSpecial (IN, OUT)
Address decodingSimplerNeeds an extra control line
UsageWidely used — AVRx86
Why memory-mapped wins

No special instructions are needed, so the entire instruction set — arithmetic and bit operations included — works directly on device registers. In C this is why you write TCCR1B = 0x05;: it looks like assigning to a variable, because to the CPU it is one. The cost is that device registers consume part of the memory address range.

Deck example: MOV TMOD, #01H on the 8051 — TMOD is a timer-mode register at a fixed address, written exactly like memory.

5 — Two ways to know a device is done (slide 12)

Busy-wait / polling — loop reading the status register until a bit flips.

AGAIN:  JNB TF0, AGAIN

Read as: Jump if Not Bit — if TF0 (Timer 0 overflow Flag) is not set, jump back to AGAIN. The CPU spins there, useless, until the timer overflows.

Interrupt — the device raises a signal, the CPU drops what it is doing and runs a handler.

MOV IE, #82H

82H = 1000 0010 → bit 7 = EA (enable all interrupts), bit 1 = ET0 (enable Timer 0 interrupt). Decoding that hex into bits is worth a mark.

Busy-wait (polling)Interrupt
CPU during waitWasted, 100% blockedFree for other work
ComplexityTrivialHandler + vector setup
Response timePredictableFaster, but variable
PowerHigher — CPU always activeLower — CPU can sleep
Use whenWait is very shortWait is long or unpredictable
Key points — carry these to Unit 8
  • delay() is busy-wait. That is why a program using it cannot see a button press during the delay — and exactly why millis() exists.
  • The Uno has only two external interrupt pins: 2 (INT0) and 3 (INT1), matching the "26 interrupts (2 Ext.)" line on slide 7.
  • Variables shared between an ISR and loop() must be volatile, or the compiler may cache them in a register and never see the change.
  • Never use delay() inside an ISR — interrupts are disabled there, so millis() stops advancing and delay() hangs forever.
  • Keep an ISR minimal: increment a counter, set a flag, return. Do the slow work in loop().

Arduino interrupt syntax

attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(pin), ISR_name, mode);
// modes: LOW, CHANGE, RISING, FALLING
detachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(pin));

Coding scenarios

Q2.1   Type P  ·  the core comparison

Polling versus interrupt, side by side

Write two programs that count button presses on pin 2 while blinking an LED at 500 ms. The first must poll; the second must use an external interrupt. Explain why the polled version loses presses.

Solution Q2.1

Version A — polling (loses presses)

const int BUTTON = 2, LED = 13;
int count = 0;

void setup() {
  pinMode(BUTTON, INPUT_PULLUP);
  pinMode(LED, OUTPUT);
  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
  digitalWrite(LED, HIGH); delay(500);     // CPU blocked here
  digitalWrite(LED, LOW);  delay(500);     // and here

  if (digitalRead(BUTTON) == LOW) {        // polled ONCE per second
    count++;
    Serial.print("Polled count = "); Serial.println(count);
  }
}

Version B — interrupt (catches every press)

const int BUTTON = 2, LED = 13;
volatile unsigned int count = 0;
volatile bool newPress = false;

void buttonISR() {          // hardware calls this, whatever the CPU is doing
  count++;
  newPress = true;
}

void setup() {
  pinMode(BUTTON, INPUT_PULLUP);
  pinMode(LED, OUTPUT);
  Serial.begin(9600);
  attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(BUTTON), buttonISR, FALLING);
}

void loop() {
  digitalWrite(LED, HIGH); delay(500);
  digitalWrite(LED, LOW);  delay(500);

  if (newPress) {           // ISR only set a flag; slow work happens here
    newPress = false;
    Serial.print("Interrupt count = "); Serial.println(count);
  }
}

Explanation: in version A the CPU spends the whole second inside delay(), which is busy-wait — it cannot execute digitalRead. Any press shorter than one second is missed entirely. In version B the interrupt hardware detects the falling edge and vectors to the ISR regardless of what the CPU is executing, so no press is lost.

Q2.2   Type P  ·  safety-critical

Emergency stop for a conveyor

A conveyor motor runs under PWM control on pin 6. An emergency-stop button on pin 2 must halt the motor immediately, no matter what the main program is doing. Write the program and justify the choice of mechanism.

Solution Q2.2
const int ESTOP = 2;
const int MOTOR = 6;      // PWM pin
const int ALARM = 8;

volatile bool emergency = false;

void estopISR() {
  analogWrite(MOTOR, 0);     // cut the motor inside the ISR - it must be instant
  emergency = true;
}

void setup() {
  pinMode(ESTOP, INPUT_PULLUP);
  pinMode(MOTOR, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(ALARM, OUTPUT);
  Serial.begin(9600);
  attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(ESTOP), estopISR, FALLING);
}

void loop() {
  if (emergency) {
    analogWrite(MOTOR, 0);
    digitalWrite(ALARM, HIGH);
    Serial.println("EMERGENCY STOP - reset required");
    while (true) { }         // latch: only a board reset clears it
  }

  // normal operation - ramp the conveyor up and down
  for (int s = 80; s <= 255 && !emergency; s += 5) { analogWrite(MOTOR, s); delay(50); }
  for (int s = 255; s >= 80 && !emergency; s -= 5) { analogWrite(MOTOR, s); delay(50); }
}
Justification — the marks are here

Why an interrupt and not polling: the main loop contains delay(50) calls, so a polled stop button could go unnoticed for up to 50 ms. On a conveyor that is 50 ms of continued motion after someone hits the button. An interrupt responds within microseconds.

Why the motor is cut inside the ISR: this is the rare case where an action belongs in the handler. Deferring it to loop() would reintroduce the delay you were trying to eliminate.

Why it latches: a safety stop must not self-clear. The while(true) forces a deliberate operator reset.

Q2.3   Type P  ·  two interrupts

Bidirectional people counter

Two IR sensors are placed at a doorway, on pins 2 and 3. Sensor A triggering before sensor B means a person entered; B before A means they left. Maintain and display the occupancy count using both external interrupts.

Solution Q2.3
const int SENSOR_A = 2;    // INT0 - outer
const int SENSOR_B = 3;    // INT1 - inner

volatile int  occupancy = 0;
volatile bool changed   = false;
volatile unsigned long lastA = 0, lastB = 0;

const unsigned long WINDOW = 1000;   // ms allowed between the two beams

void isrA() {
  lastA = millis();
  if (lastB != 0 && lastA - lastB < WINDOW) {   // B fired first -> exit
    occupancy--; lastB = 0; changed = true;
  }
}

void isrB() {
  lastB = millis();
  if (lastA != 0 && lastB - lastA < WINDOW) {   // A fired first -> entry
    occupancy++; lastA = 0; changed = true;
  }
}

void setup() {
  pinMode(SENSOR_A, INPUT_PULLUP);
  pinMode(SENSOR_B, INPUT_PULLUP);
  Serial.begin(9600);
  attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(SENSOR_A), isrA, FALLING);
  attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(SENSOR_B), isrB, FALLING);
  Serial.println("Occupancy counter ready");
}

void loop() {
  if (changed) {
    changed = false;
    if (occupancy < 0) occupancy = 0;
    Serial.print("Occupancy = "); Serial.println(occupancy);
  }
}

Why both pins 2 and 3: these are the only two external interrupt pins on the Uno (INT0 and INT1). A three-sensor version would need pin-change interrupts instead.

Why millis() works inside these ISRs: reading millis() is safe; it is delay() that hangs, because it waits for a counter that interrupts have frozen.

The time window rejects a single sensor triggering twice from noise — a beam pair must complete within one second to count as a crossing.

Q2.4   Type P  ·  debouncing

Interrupt with software debounce

A mechanical switch on pin 2 produces contact bounce, causing one physical press to register several times. Modify an interrupt-based counter to reject bounces, and explain the mechanism.

Solution Q2.4
const int BUTTON = 2;
const unsigned long DEBOUNCE = 50;    // ms - longer than the bounce, shorter than a real press

volatile unsigned int count = 0;
volatile unsigned long lastTrigger = 0;
volatile bool changed = false;

void buttonISR() {
  unsigned long now = millis();
  if (now - lastTrigger > DEBOUNCE) {   // ignore edges inside the window
    count++;
    lastTrigger = now;
    changed = true;
  }
}

void setup() {
  pinMode(BUTTON, INPUT_PULLUP);
  Serial.begin(9600);
  attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(BUTTON), buttonISR, FALLING);
}

void loop() {
  if (changed) { changed = false;
    Serial.print("Debounced count = "); Serial.println(count); }
}
What bounce actually is

A mechanical contact does not close cleanly. Over roughly 1–20 ms the metal springs open and shut several times, generating multiple electrical edges. The interrupt fires on each one.

The fix: record the time of the accepted edge and ignore any further edge within 50 ms. That is long enough to cover the bounce and short enough that no human can press twice inside it.

Hardware alternative: an RC filter or a Schmitt trigger on the input pin.

Q2.5   Type P  ·  status register model

Polling a status flag directly

Without using analogRead(), start an ADC conversion by writing the control register and poll its status flag until the conversion completes. Relate the code to the data/status register model of slide 10.

Solution Q2.5
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);

  ADMUX  = (1 << REFS0);                                  // AVcc reference, channel A0
  ADCSRA = (1 << ADEN) | (1 << ADPS2) | (1 << ADPS1) | (1 << ADPS0);
                                                          // enable ADC, prescaler 128
}

void loop() {
  ADCSRA |= (1 << ADSC);              // CONTROL: start conversion

  while (ADCSRA & (1 << ADSC)) {      // STATUS : busy-wait until the flag clears
    ;                                 // this is JNB TF0, AGAIN in C
  }

  int value = ADC;                    // DATA   : read the result register

  Serial.print("ADC = "); Serial.println(value);
  delay(500);
}
Mapping code to the slide-10 model
Slide 10 conceptATmega328 register
ControlADCSRA, ADMUX — written by the CPU
StatusThe ADSC bit — set by the CPU, cleared by the hardware when done
DataADC — the 10-bit result, read only

The while loop is literally busy-wait: the CPU does nothing but re-read a status bit. This is what analogRead() does internally, and it is why one reading costs about 100 µs of blocked CPU time.

Q2.6   Type T+P  ·  classification

Interface an internal and an external device

Write one program that reads an internal I/O device and drives an external one, printing both. Classify each device per slide 9 and state which needs a bus interface.

Solution Q2.6
#include <LiquidCrystal.h>

// External device: 16x2 LCD needs a 6-wire bus interface
LiquidCrystal lcd(12, 11, 5, 4, 3, 2);

const int tempPin = A0;      // Internal device: the on-chip ADC

void setup() {
  lcd.begin(16, 2);
  Serial.begin(9600);
  lcd.print("Temp monitor");
  delay(1000);
  lcd.clear();
}

void loop() {
  int   adc   = analogRead(tempPin);      // INTERNAL - on-chip ADC, direct access
  float tempC = (adc * 4.88) / 10.0;      // LM35: 10 mV per degree C

  lcd.setCursor(0, 0);                    // EXTERNAL - driven over a parallel bus
  lcd.print("Temp: ");
  lcd.print(tempC, 1);
  lcd.print((char)223);                   // degree symbol
  lcd.print("C  ");

  Serial.println(tempC, 1);
  delay(1000);
}
DeviceClassWhy
ADC (A0)InternalPhysically on the silicon die, small, accessed directly through registers — no bus needed
16×2 LCDExternalLarge, a separate component, requires a bus interface — here six data and control lines

The trade-off to state: the external LCD consumes six of the fourteen digital pins. This is why I2C LCD backpacks exist — they reduce the same display to two wires at the cost of some speed.

UNIT 03

ADC — Theory and Numericals

Slides 14–20  ·  Question types: T, N  ·  Weight: highest

What an ADC is (slide 14)

An ADC is an electronic circuit whose digital output is proportional to its analog input. It "measures" the input voltage and gives a binary output number proportional to its size. The list of possible analog inputs is endless — audio and video, medical or climatic variables. An ADC operating within a larger environment is called a data acquisition system.

How a SAR ADC works

The deck shows the block; here is what the blocks do. The ATmega328 uses successive approximation.

  1. Sample and hold freezes the input so it cannot drift during conversion.
  2. The SAR guesses the most significant bit — is Vin above half of full scale?
  3. The internal DAC converts the guess back to a voltage.
  4. The comparator reports higher or lower.
  5. The SAR keeps or clears the bit and moves to the next. Ten comparisons give ten bits.

Types to name if asked: flash (fastest, most hardware), successive approximation (balanced — used here), dual-slope (slow, very accurate, multimeters), sigma-delta (high resolution, audio and the HX711).

The formula (slide 15) — derive it, do not memorise it

D = ( Vi / Vr ) × 2n Vi input voltage · Vr reference voltage · n output bits · D digital output (integer, 0 to 2n−1)

The derivation is one line: the fraction of full scale your input represents, times the number of available codes. For the Uno, n = 10, so 210 = 1024 values, numbered 0 to 1023. 0 V → 0. 5 V → 1023.

Resolution (slide 16)

Resolution = Vr / 2n = 5 / 1024 = 4.88 mV The smallest voltage change the ADC can detect — the size of one step
BitsCodesResolution at Vr = 5 VWhere you meet it
825619.5 mVPWM output side
1010244.88 mVArduino Uno ADC
1240961.22 mVESP32, STM32
166553676.3 µVInstrumentation
2416,777,2160.3 µVHX711 — the weighing-machine answer

Quantization error is at most ±½ step = ±2.44 mV on the Uno. If your sensor changes by 2 mV, the Arduino sees nothing at all.

The 1023 vs 1024 confusion — settle it now

Slide 16 uses 1024. Slide 18 uses 1023. Both are correct, for different questions:

QuestionUseWhy
"How big is one step?"2n = 10241024 steps span the range
"What voltage does this reading mean?"2n−1 = 10231023 is the maximum reading

In an exam, state which you used and why. Both are accepted; silence is not.

Vi = ( D / 1023 ) × Vr

The three analog functions

FunctionSpecification
analogRead(pin)10-bit resolution · pins A0–A5 only · returns int 0–1023 · ~100 µs per reading · max rate ~10,000/sec · needs no pinMode
analogReference(type)Changes Vr via the AREF pin. DEFAULT = 5 V, INTERNAL = 1.1 V on the Uno, EXTERNAL = AREF pin. INTERNAL1V1 / INTERNAL2V56 are Mega-only. Must be called before analogRead
analogWrite(pin,value)PWM, not DAC. Pins 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11 · value 0–255 (8-bit) · needs no pinMode
Key points
  • Where the 100 µs comes from: the ADC needs a 50–200 kHz clock for full 10-bit accuracy. Arduino sets the prescaler to 128, giving 16 MHz ÷ 128 = 125 kHz. One conversion takes 13 ADC clocks → 13/125,000 = 104 µs.
  • Why lower the reference: a sensor swinging only 0–1 V uses just 205 of 1024 codes — 80% wasted. At 1.1 V reference, resolution becomes 1.07 mV instead of 4.88 mV, about 4.5× finer. The cost: nothing above 1.1 V can be measured.
  • AREF hazard: with EXTERNAL, call analogReference(EXTERNAL) before connecting anything to AREF, or you short the internal reference against the external one and can damage the chip.
  • Input/output asymmetry: input is 10-bit (0–1023), output is 8-bit (0–255). That mismatch is why the motor program divides by 4.
  • Reading five sensors costs 500 µs before any logic runs — relevant when a question asks about sampling rate.

Numericals — every variation

N3.1 — An input of 3.3 V is applied to the Uno's ADC. Find the digital output.

D = (Vi/Vr) × 2^n = (3.3/5) × 1024 = 675.84 → D = 675 Using 2^n − 1: (3.3/5) × 1023 = 675.2 → 675 (same answer; state your convention)

N3.2 — Deck example. An ADC reading of 434 is obtained. Find the input voltage.

434 = (Vi/5) × 1023 Vi = (434 × 5)/1023 = 2.12 V

N3.3 — A 12-bit ADC has Vr = 3.3 V and reads 2048. Find the voltage and the resolution.

Vi = (2048/4095) × 3.3 = 1.65 V Resolution = 3.3/4096 = 0.000806 V = 0.806 mV Check: 2048 is half of 4095, and 1.65 V is half of 3.3 V ✓

N3.4 — By what factor does resolution improve using analogReference(INTERNAL)? State one disadvantage.

Default : 5/1024 = 4.88 mV Internal: 1.1/1024 = 1.07 mV Improvement = 4.88/1.07 = 4.55× Disadvantage: maximum measurable input falls from 5 V to 1.1 V; anything higher saturates at 1023

N3.5 — The ADC takes 100 µs per conversion. How many sensors can be sampled at 200 Hz each?

Period at 200 Hz = 1/200 = 5 ms = 5000 µs Conversions available = 5000/100 = 50 sensors (fewer in practice — the loop must also process and output)

N3.6 — An LM35 is at 40 °C. Find the sensor output voltage and the resulting ADC count.

LM35 gives 10 mV per °C → Vout = 40 × 10 = 400 mV = 0.4 V D = (0.4/5) × 1023 = 82 counts Reverse check: 82 × 4.88 = 400.2 mV → /10 = 40.0 °C ✓

N3.7 — What is the smallest temperature change an LM35 + Uno system can detect, at 5 V and at 1.1 V reference?

At 5 V : one step = 4.88 mV → 4.88/10 = 0.488 °C At 1.1 V: one step = 1.07 mV → 1.07/10 = 0.107 °C This is the quantitative version of "how would you improve accuracy?"

N3.8 — A load cell outputs 2 mV per volt of excitation at 5 V. Show why the internal ADC is unusable and an HX711 is required.

Full-scale output = 2 mV/V × 5 V = 10 mV Uno ADC step = 4.88 mV Counts across the entire range = 10/4.88 = ≈ 2 counts → unusable HX711: 24-bit with a 128× gain amplifier → millions of counts This is the CAT weighing-machine justification.

N3.9 — What is the maximum quantization error of the Uno ADC, in volts and as a percentage of full scale?

Error = ±½ × resolution = ±½ × 4.88 mV = ±2.44 mV As % of full scale = 2.44/5000 × 100 = ±0.049 % (about 0.05 %)

Coding scenarios

Q3.1   Type P  ·  the base pattern

Analog reader with voltage and percentage

Read a potentiometer on A0 and print the raw count, the equivalent voltage to three decimals, and the percentage of full scale, every 200 ms.

Solution Q3.1
const int potPin = A0;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);          // note: no pinMode needed for analog input
}

void loop() {
  int   adc     = analogRead(potPin);          // 0..1023
  float voltage = (adc * 5.0) / 1023.0;        // count -> volts
  float percent = (adc / 1023.0) * 100.0;

  Serial.print("ADC = ");   Serial.print(adc);
  Serial.print("   V = ");  Serial.print(voltage, 3);
  Serial.print(" V   ");    Serial.print(percent, 1);
  Serial.println(" %");

  delay(200);
}
The trap that destroys more lab marks than any other

Write 5.0 and 1023.0, never 5 and 1023. In C, adc * 5 / 1023 is integer arithmetic: an ADC value of 900 gives 4, then 4/1023 = 0. Your voltage prints as 0.00 forever.

Q3.2   Type P  ·  reference switching

Improve resolution with the internal reference

A sensor outputs 0–1 V. Write a program that reads it on the default 5 V reference and again on the internal 1.1 V reference, printing both resolutions and both voltages. Derive the new constant yourself.

Solution Q3.2
const int sensorPin = A0;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);

  // --- Pass 1: default 5 V reference ---
  analogReference(DEFAULT);
  analogRead(sensorPin);                       // discard - let the ADC settle
  int   adc5 = analogRead(sensorPin);
  float mv5  = adc5 * 4.88;                    // 5000 mV / 1023

  Serial.print("DEFAULT  ref: count = "); Serial.print(adc5);
  Serial.print("  V = ");                 Serial.print(mv5 / 1000.0, 4);
  Serial.println(" V   step = 4.88 mV");

  // --- Pass 2: internal 1.1 V reference ---
  analogReference(INTERNAL);                   // MUST precede analogRead
  analogRead(sensorPin);                       // discard the first reading
  int   adc1 = analogRead(sensorPin);
  float mv1  = adc1 * 1.075;                   // 1100 mV / 1023

  Serial.print("INTERNAL ref: count = "); Serial.print(adc1);
  Serial.print("  V = ");                 Serial.print(mv1 / 1000.0, 4);
  Serial.println(" V   step = 1.07 mV");
}

void loop() {}

The derivation to show: resolution = Vr/2n; for the mapping constant use 1100 mV / 1023 = 1.075 mV per count.

What you observe: a 0.8 V signal reads about 164 counts on the 5 V reference but about 744 counts on the 1.1 V reference — 4.5× more counts for the same physical signal, which is 4.5× more precision.

State the trade-off: the ceiling drops from 5 V to 1.1 V.

Q3.3   Type P  ·  noise reduction

Averaging to beat quantization noise

Sensor readings jitter by ±2 counts. Write a program that takes 16 samples, averages them, and prints both the raw and averaged values. Explain the improvement and its cost.

Solution Q3.3
const int sensorPin = A0;
const int SAMPLES   = 16;

int readAveraged() {
  long sum = 0;                       // long, not int - 16 x 1023 = 16368 overflows nothing
  for (int i = 0; i < SAMPLES; i++) {
    sum += analogRead(sensorPin);
    delayMicroseconds(200);           // small gap between conversions
  }
  return sum / SAMPLES;
}

void setup() { Serial.begin(9600); }

void loop() {
  int raw = analogRead(sensorPin);
  int avg = readAveraged();

  Serial.print("raw = "); Serial.print(raw);
  Serial.print("   avg(16) = "); Serial.print(avg);
  Serial.print("   V = "); Serial.println((avg * 5.0) / 1023.0, 3);

  delay(500);
}
The engineering argument

Benefit: averaging N samples reduces random noise by √N. Sixteen samples give a 4× improvement in noise, effectively buying about two extra bits of usable resolution.

Cost: 16 conversions × 100 µs = 1.6 ms per reading plus the delays, so the maximum sampling rate falls from ~10 kHz to a few hundred Hz. Averaging trades speed for precision.

Limitation: averaging only helps against random noise. It cannot remove a systematic offset or a calibration error.

Q3.4   Type P  ·  multi-channel

Four-channel data acquisition system

Build a data acquisition system reading four analog channels A0–A3, printing all four voltages in a single tab-separated line, and reporting the actual achieved sampling rate.

Solution Q3.4
const int CHANNELS = 4;
const int pins[CHANNELS] = {A0, A1, A2, A3};

unsigned long lastReport = 0;
unsigned int  sampleCount = 0;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);                 // faster port - serial is the bottleneck
  Serial.println("CH0\tCH1\tCH2\tCH3\trate");
}

void loop() {
  float v[CHANNELS];

  for (int i = 0; i < CHANNELS; i++) {
    int adc = analogRead(pins[i]);      // ~100 us each -> 400 us for all four
    v[i] = (adc * 5.0) / 1023.0;
  }
  sampleCount++;

  for (int i = 0; i < CHANNELS; i++) { Serial.print(v[i], 3); Serial.print('\t'); }

  unsigned long now = millis();
  if (now - lastReport >= 1000) {
    Serial.print(sampleCount); Serial.println(" Hz");
    sampleCount = 0;
    lastReport  = now;
  } else {
    Serial.println();
  }
}

The deck's term: an ADC operating in this arrangement is a data acquisition system — quote slide 14.

Why 115200 baud: four floats plus tabs is roughly 30 characters. At 9600 baud that costs 30 ms per line, capping the rate at about 33 Hz. The serial link, not the ADC, is the bottleneck. Raising the baud rate to 115200 cuts it to 2.6 ms.

Theoretical ceiling: 4 × 100 µs = 400 µs per sweep → 2500 sweeps/sec if serial were free.

Q3.5   Type P  ·  calibration

Two-point calibration of a sensor

A sensor reads 102 counts at a known 0.5 V and 820 counts at a known 4.0 V, but is not perfectly linear from the origin. Write a program that applies a two-point calibration and reports the corrected voltage.

Solution Q3.5
const int sensorPin = A0;

// Measured calibration points
const int   ADC_LOW  = 102;    const float V_LOW  = 0.50;
const int   ADC_HIGH = 820;    const float V_HIGH = 4.00;

float calibratedVolts(int adc) {
  // straight line through the two measured points: V = m*adc + c
  float m = (V_HIGH - V_LOW) / (float)(ADC_HIGH - ADC_LOW);
  float c = V_LOW - m * ADC_LOW;
  return m * adc + c;
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  Serial.println("adc\tideal\tcalibrated");
}

void loop() {
  int   adc   = analogRead(sensorPin);
  float ideal = (adc * 5.0) / 1023.0;         // uncorrected
  float cal   = calibratedVolts(adc);         // corrected

  Serial.print(adc);        Serial.print('\t');
  Serial.print(ideal, 3);   Serial.print('\t');
  Serial.println(cal, 3);

  delay(500);
}

The slope and intercept: m = (4.00 − 0.50)/(820 − 102) = 3.50/718 = 0.004875 V per count; c = 0.50 − 0.004875 × 102 = 0.0028 V.

Why this matters in a design answer: the ideal formula assumes a perfect 0–5 V span with no offset. Real sensors have gain and offset errors. Two-point calibration corrects both, and the constants belong in EEPROM so they survive power-off — which is exactly what the CAT weighing machine stores.

Q3.6   Type P  ·  measuring the ADC itself

Measure conversion time and prove the 10 kHz limit

Write a program that measures how long analogRead actually takes and calculates the maximum achievable sampling rate. Compare against the deck's claim of 100 µs and 10,000 readings per second.

Solution Q3.6
const int pin = A0;
const int N   = 1000;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);

  unsigned long t0 = micros();
  for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) analogRead(pin);
  unsigned long t1 = micros();

  float perRead = (t1 - t0) / (float)N;

  Serial.print("Average conversion time = ");
  Serial.print(perRead, 1);
  Serial.println(" us");

  Serial.print("Maximum sampling rate  = ");
  Serial.print(1000000.0 / perRead, 0);
  Serial.println(" samples/sec");
}

void loop() {}

Expected output: about 112 µs and roughly 8,900 samples/sec — close to the deck's 100 µs and 10,000/sec.

Where the number comes from — say this in a theory answer

The ADC requires a clock of 50–200 kHz for full 10-bit accuracy. Arduino sets the ADC prescaler to 128, giving 16 MHz ÷ 128 = 125 kHz. A conversion takes 13 ADC clock cycles, so 13 ÷ 125,000 = 104 µs. The extra few microseconds are the function-call overhead.

Speeding it up: reducing the prescaler to 16 gives a 1 MHz ADC clock and roughly 13 µs conversions, at the cost of accuracy in the lowest bits.

UNIT 04

ADC Programming

Slides 21–27  ·  Question types: P, D  ·  Weight: highest  ·  The template for every design question

The universal sensor chain

Every analog-sensor program in this module is the same four-step chain. Learn the chain, not the programs.

SensorOutputRead withConversion
LM3510 mV/°C, no offsetanalogRead(adc*4.88)/10
TMP36 (Tinkercad)10 mV/°C + 500 mV offsetanalogRead(adc*4.88-500)/10
LDRAnalog via divider, non-linearanalogReadThreshold, not a formula
Potentiometer0–5 V linearanalogReadmap()
Soil moistureAnaloganalogReadmap() to %
MQ gas sensorAnaloganalogReadThreshold

Example 1 (slides 22–23) — read and report

int sensorValue = 0;

void setup()
{
  Serial.begin(9600);   //initiating serial communication with 9600 baud rate
}

void loop()
{
  sensorValue = analogRead(A0);   //analog input is read from A0 pin
  Serial.println(sensorValue);    //printing the output in serial port
  delay(100);                     // simple delay of 100ms
}

Example 2 (slides 25–26) — the template for every design question

Read a temperature sensor on A0, display the temperature, and glow an LED when it exceeds 40 °C.

const int lm35_pin = A0;    /* LM35 O/P pin */
const int ledPin = 13;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(ledPin, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  int temp_adc_val;
  float temp_val;

  temp_adc_val = analogRead(lm35_pin);   /* Read Temperature */
  temp_val = (temp_adc_val * 4.88);      /* adc value to equivalent voltage */
  temp_val = (temp_val/10);              /* LM35 gives output of 10mv/degC */

  if (temp_val > 40) { digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH); }   // turn LED on
  else               { digitalWrite(ledPin, LOW);  }   // turn LED off

  Serial.print("Temperature = ");
  Serial.print(temp_val);
  Serial.print(" Degree Celsius\n");
  delay(1000);
}

The two magic numbers, derived: × 4.88 is one ADC step in millivolts (5000 mV ÷ 1023); / 10 is the LM35's datasheet rating of 10 mV per °C.

Key points — the four traps in ADC code
  1. Integer division. adc * 5 / 1023 returns 0. Always write 5.0 and 1023.0.
  2. Multiple thresholds need an ordered else if ladder. Because the first branch catches the top band, later branches need no compound conditions.
  3. No hysteresis = chattering. At exactly the threshold, sensor noise flips the output rapidly. Turn on above 42, off below 38. Saying this earns a mark.
  4. Name your pins with const int at the top — examiners credit it, and changing hardware becomes one edit.

map() — never introduced by the deck but needed constantly: map(value, fromLow, fromHigh, toLow, toHigh) linearly rescales one range onto another. map(adc,0,1023,0,255) equals /4; map(adc,0,1023,0,180) drives a servo.

Coding scenarios

PYQ   Deck slide 150  ·  Type D  ·  10 marks

Petrochemical boiler monitoring system

In a petrochemical industry having a boiler for generating steam, develop a system to monitor the boiler temperature. (i) Temperature > 60 °C — display "Boiler is Overheating!", glow a red LED, and turn on the cooling system. (ii) Temperature < 45 °C (idle) — display "Idle State" and glow a yellow LED. (iii) Between 45 °C and 60 °C — display "Boiler Working" and glow a green LED. Write an Arduino program for an optimal embedded system.

Model answer — full exam format

Aim

To design a temperature monitoring and control system for an industrial boiler that classifies its state into three bands, indicates each with a distinct LED and message, and automatically activates a cooling system on overheating.

Components required

ComponentPurpose
Arduino Uno (ATmega328P)Control unit
LM35 temperature sensorSenses boiler temperature, 10 mV/°C
Red LED + 220 ΩOverheating indication
Yellow LED + 220 ΩIdle-state indication
Green LED + 220 ΩNormal-working indication
Relay moduleSwitches the cooling system

Circuit connections

Arduino pinConnected to
A0LM35 output
D8Red LED
D9Yellow LED
D10Green LED
D11Relay input (cooling system)
5V, GNDSensor and module supply

Working

  1. The LM35 output is connected to A0 and produces 10 mV per °C.
  2. analogRead(A0) returns a 10-bit count between 0 and 1023.
  3. The count is multiplied by 4.88 to obtain millivolts, since one ADC step equals 5000 mV / 1023.
  4. The millivolt value is divided by 10 to obtain temperature in degrees Celsius.
  5. All indicator outputs are first cleared so that exactly one state is displayed at a time.
  6. If the temperature exceeds 60 °C the red LED glows, "Boiler is Overheating!" is displayed and the cooling relay is energised.
  7. If the temperature is below 45 °C the yellow LED glows and "Idle State" is displayed.
  8. Otherwise the temperature lies between 45 °C and 60 °C, so the green LED glows and "Boiler Working" is displayed.
  9. The cycle repeats every second, giving continuous monitoring.

Flowchart

Arduino program

const int lm35_pin  = A0;    // LM35 output
const int redPin    = 8;     // overheating
const int yellowPin = 9;     // idle
const int greenPin  = 10;    // working
const int coolerPin = 11;    // cooling system relay

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(redPin,    OUTPUT);
  pinMode(yellowPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(greenPin,  OUTPUT);
  pinMode(coolerPin, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  int   temp_adc_val = analogRead(lm35_pin);
  float temp_mv      = temp_adc_val * 4.88;   // count -> millivolts
  float temp_val     = temp_mv / 10.0;        // LM35: 10 mV per degree C

  // clear all indicators so only one state is shown
  digitalWrite(redPin,    LOW);
  digitalWrite(yellowPin, LOW);
  digitalWrite(greenPin,  LOW);
  digitalWrite(coolerPin, LOW);

  if (temp_val > 60) {                        // overheating
    digitalWrite(redPin,    HIGH);
    digitalWrite(coolerPin, HIGH);            // turn ON cooling system
    Serial.print("Boiler is Overheating!   ");
  }
  else if (temp_val < 45) {                   // idle
    digitalWrite(yellowPin, HIGH);
    Serial.print("Idle State               ");
  }
  else {                                      // 45 to 60 : normal
    digitalWrite(greenPin, HIGH);
    Serial.print("Boiler Working           ");
  }

  Serial.print("Temperature = ");
  Serial.print(temp_val, 1);
  Serial.println(" Degree Celsius");

  delay(1000);
}

Result

The system continuously monitors boiler temperature, displays the correct status message with the corresponding LED for each of the three bands, and automatically energises the cooling system whenever the temperature exceeds 60 °C.

The five points that make this a 10
  • Derive 4.88 rather than quoting it — 5000 mV ÷ 1023 from the 10-bit resolution and 5 V reference.
  • Explain the ladder ordering — because > 60 is caught first, the second test needs only < 45, and the middle band falls through automatically.
  • Mention hysteresis — at exactly 60 °C sensor noise would toggle the relay rapidly; switching on at 60 and off at 57 prevents relay chatter and mechanical wear. This is the "optimal" the question asks for.
  • Justify the relay — a cooling fan or pump draws far more than the 40 mA per-pin limit.
  • Suggest the resolution improvement — at 60 °C the LM35 outputs 600 mV, using only 12 % of the ADC range. Using analogReference(INTERNAL) at 1.1 V would improve resolution from 0.488 °C to 0.107 °C per step.
Q4.1   Type P  ·  single threshold

Automatic street light

An LDR on A1 senses ambient light. Below a threshold the street lamp on pin 7 must switch on. Display the ADC value, the equivalent voltage and the lamp status every 500 ms. Add hysteresis to stop dusk flicker.

Solution Q4.1

Working

  1. The LDR forms a potential divider with a fixed resistor; the junction feeds A1.
  2. In bright light the LDR resistance falls, so the voltage at A1 rises and the count is high.
  3. The count is converted to voltage using V = (ADC × 5.0)/1023.
  4. Two thresholds are used rather than one: the lamp switches ON below 380 and OFF only above 420.
  5. This 40-count gap is the hysteresis band; it prevents rapid switching at dusk when the light hovers at the setpoint.
  6. Status, count and voltage are printed every 500 ms.
const int ldrPin  = A1;
const int lampPin = 7;
const int ON_BELOW  = 380;      // switch ON  below this
const int OFF_ABOVE = 420;      // switch OFF above this  (hysteresis band)

bool lampOn = false;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(lampPin, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  int   light   = analogRead(ldrPin);
  float voltage = (light * 5.0) / 1023.0;

  if (!lampOn && light < ON_BELOW)  lampOn = true;    // getting dark
  if ( lampOn && light > OFF_ABOVE) lampOn = false;   // getting bright

  digitalWrite(lampPin, lampOn ? HIGH : LOW);

  Serial.print(lampOn ? "DARK   - Lamp ON    " : "BRIGHT - Lamp OFF   ");
  Serial.print("LDR = ");  Serial.print(light);
  Serial.print("   V = "); Serial.print(voltage, 2);
  Serial.println(" V");

  delay(500);
}

Result: the lamp switches on automatically in darkness and off in daylight, without flickering at the transition.

Extra-mark line: an LDR is non-linear, so a calibrated formula is inappropriate — a threshold is the correct engineering approach.

Q4.2   Type D  ·  four bands

Air quality monitor with four alert levels

An MQ-135 gas sensor on A0 monitors air quality. Classify readings into Good (<200), Moderate (200–400), Poor (400–700) and Hazardous (>700), each with its own LED and message. Sound a buzzer only in the Hazardous band.

Solution Q4.2
const int gasPin    = A0;
const int greenPin  = 5;
const int yellowPin = 6;
const int orangePin = 7;
const int redPin    = 8;
const int buzzerPin = 9;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(greenPin,  OUTPUT); pinMode(yellowPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(orangePin, OUTPUT); pinMode(redPin,    OUTPUT);
  pinMode(buzzerPin, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  int ppm = analogRead(gasPin);

  digitalWrite(greenPin, LOW); digitalWrite(yellowPin, LOW);
  digitalWrite(orangePin,LOW); digitalWrite(redPin,    LOW);
  noTone(buzzerPin);

  if (ppm > 700) {                        // ordered highest first
    digitalWrite(redPin, HIGH);
    tone(buzzerPin, 2000);                // continuous alarm
    Serial.print("HAZARDOUS  ");
  }
  else if (ppm > 400) {
    digitalWrite(orangePin, HIGH);
    Serial.print("POOR       ");
  }
  else if (ppm > 200) {
    digitalWrite(yellowPin, HIGH);
    Serial.print("MODERATE   ");
  }
  else {
    digitalWrite(greenPin, HIGH);
    Serial.print("GOOD       ");
  }

  Serial.print("Level = "); Serial.println(ppm);
  delay(1000);
}
Two points examiners look for

Ladder ordering: test from the highest band downward. Each later branch then needs only one comparison, because everything above it has already been caught. Testing lowest-first would require compound conditions and is where students lose marks.

tone() uses Timer2, which disables PWM on pins 3 and 11. The buzzer is deliberately on pin 9 and the LEDs on 5–8, so nothing conflicts. Stating this conflict shows real understanding.

Q4.3   Type D  ·  two sensors

Greenhouse controller — temperature and soil moisture

Design a greenhouse controller. An LM35 on A0 controls a fan relay above 35 °C; a soil moisture sensor on A1 controls a water pump relay below 30 % moisture. Display both readings and both actuator states.

Solution Q4.3
const int tempPin  = A0;
const int soilPin  = A1;
const int fanPin   = 6;      // fan relay
const int pumpPin  = 7;      // pump relay

const int SOIL_DRY = 850;    // raw count when dry (calibrate on the bench)
const int SOIL_WET = 350;    // raw count when fully wet

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(fanPin,  OUTPUT);
  pinMode(pumpPin, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  // --- Temperature branch ---
  int   tAdc  = analogRead(tempPin);
  float tempC = (tAdc * 4.88) / 10.0;          // LM35: 10 mV per degree C
  bool  fanOn = (tempC > 35);
  digitalWrite(fanPin, fanOn ? HIGH : LOW);

  // --- Moisture branch ---
  int sAdc     = analogRead(soilPin);
  int moisture = map(sAdc, SOIL_DRY, SOIL_WET, 0, 100);   // note reversed range
  moisture     = constrain(moisture, 0, 100);
  bool pumpOn  = (moisture < 30);
  digitalWrite(pumpPin, pumpOn ? HIGH : LOW);

  Serial.print("T = ");        Serial.print(tempC, 1);
  Serial.print(" C  Fan:");    Serial.print(fanOn ? "ON " : "OFF");
  Serial.print("   Soil = ");  Serial.print(moisture);
  Serial.print(" %  Pump:");   Serial.println(pumpOn ? "ON" : "OFF");

  delay(2000);
}

Why map() has a reversed input range: a resistive soil probe gives a high count when dry and a low count when wet. Writing map(sAdc, 850, 350, 0, 100) handles the inversion cleanly — map() accepts descending ranges.

Why constrain(): readings outside the calibration points would otherwise produce percentages below 0 or above 100.

Why relays: both a fan and a pump draw far more than 40 mA. This is the point where the 40 mA rule from Unit 1 decides the whole hardware design.

Q4.4   Type P  ·  unit conversion

Temperature in three scales with min/max tracking

Read an LM35 and display the temperature in Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin, while tracking and reporting the minimum and maximum seen since power-on.

Solution Q4.4
const int lm35Pin = A0;

float minC =  999.0;
float maxC = -999.0;

void setup() { Serial.begin(9600); }

void loop() {
  int   adc   = analogRead(lm35Pin);
  float tempC = (adc * 4.88) / 10.0;           // LM35: 10 mV per degree C

  float tempF = tempC * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0;      // Celsius -> Fahrenheit
  float tempK = tempC + 273.15;                // Celsius -> Kelvin

  if (tempC < minC) minC = tempC;
  if (tempC > maxC) maxC = tempC;

  Serial.print(tempC, 1); Serial.print(" C   ");
  Serial.print(tempF, 1); Serial.print(" F   ");
  Serial.print(tempK, 1); Serial.print(" K   |  min ");
  Serial.print(minC, 1);  Serial.print("  max ");
  Serial.println(maxC, 1);

  delay(1000);
}

Why this variation appears: the deck's CAT-style question on the sanitiser dispenser specifies limits in Fahrenheit (97 °F to 99 °F). If a sensor gives Celsius and the specification is in Fahrenheit, you must convert — and showing the formula is a mark.

Initialisation trap: minC starts high and maxC starts low, so the very first reading replaces both. Initialising both to 0 would break the minimum tracking for any positive temperature.

Q4.5   Type D  ·  proportional output

Water level indicator with proportional alarm

An analog water-level sensor on A0 reads 0–100 %. Drive a 5-LED bar graph proportionally, and make a buzzer beep faster as the level rises above 80 %.

Solution Q4.5
const int levelPin  = A0;
const int buzzerPin = 12;
const int bar[5]    = {5, 6, 7, 8, 9};

unsigned long lastBeep = 0;
bool beepState = false;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) pinMode(bar[i], OUTPUT);
  pinMode(buzzerPin, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  int adc     = analogRead(levelPin);
  int percent = map(adc, 0, 1023, 0, 100);

  int lit = map(percent, 0, 100, 0, 5);          // how many LEDs to light
  for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
    digitalWrite(bar[i], i < lit ? HIGH : LOW);

  if (percent > 80) {
    // beep interval shrinks from 500 ms at 80 % to 50 ms at 100 %
    int interval = map(percent, 80, 100, 500, 50);
    if (millis() - lastBeep >= (unsigned long)interval) {
      lastBeep  = millis();
      beepState = !beepState;
      digitalWrite(buzzerPin, beepState);
    }
  } else {
    digitalWrite(buzzerPin, LOW);
  }

  Serial.print("Level = "); Serial.print(percent); Serial.println(" %");
}

Two map() calls doing different jobs: the first converts the ADC count to a percentage (unit conversion); the second converts the percentage to a beep interval (behaviour scaling). Note the second maps to a descending output range, so a higher level gives a shorter interval.

Why millis() and not delay(): the LED bar must keep updating while the buzzer beeps. A delay() would freeze the display between beeps. This is Unit 8 arriving early.

Q4.6   Type D  ·  PYQ-style

Contactless sanitiser dispenser with fever screening

Design a contactless hand sanitiser dispenser and temperature screening system for a supermarket. The system must be contactless. The door opens only if the temperature is within the normal limit of 97 °F to 99 °F; otherwise an alarm sounds. Choose appropriate sensors and actuators.

This is the deck's slide-147 question, adapted. It combines Units 4, 10 and 11.

Solution Q4.6

Component selection with justification

ElementChoiceJustification
Hand detectionIR proximity sensorContactless requirement; digital output, LOW on detection
TemperatureMLX90614 IR thermometer (or LM35 for the exam model)Non-contact measurement is mandatory for screening
SanitiserSmall pump / solenoid via relayExceeds 40 mA — must be switched, not driven
DoorServo motorTwo defined positions, 0° closed and 90° open
AlarmBuzzer + red LEDAudible and visual fever indication

Working

  1. The IR proximity sensor detects a hand placed beneath the nozzle without contact.
  2. On detection the pump relay is energised for one second, dispensing sanitiser.
  3. The temperature sensor reads body temperature in Celsius.
  4. The reading is converted to Fahrenheit using F = C × 9/5 + 32, because the specification is given in Fahrenheit.
  5. If the temperature lies between 97 °F and 99 °F inclusive, the green LED glows and the servo opens the door to 90°.
  6. The door remains open for three seconds and then closes to 0°.
  7. If the temperature falls outside the limits, the red LED glows and the buzzer sounds; the door remains closed.
#include <Servo.h>

Servo doorServo;

const int irPin     = 2;      // hand detection, LOW when hand present
const int tempPin   = A0;     // temperature sensor
const int pumpPin   = 7;      // sanitiser pump relay
const int greenPin  = 8;
const int redPin    = 9;
const int buzzerPin = 12;
const int servoPin  = 10;

const float LOW_F  = 97.0;
const float HIGH_F = 99.0;

void setup() {
  pinMode(irPin, INPUT_PULLUP);
  pinMode(pumpPin,  OUTPUT);
  pinMode(greenPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(redPin,   OUTPUT);
  pinMode(buzzerPin,OUTPUT);

  doorServo.attach(servoPin);
  doorServo.write(0);                 // door closed
  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
  if (digitalRead(irPin) == LOW) {                 // hand detected, contactless
    Serial.println("Hand detected - dispensing");
    digitalWrite(pumpPin, HIGH);
    delay(1000);                                   // one second of sanitiser
    digitalWrite(pumpPin, LOW);

    int   adc   = analogRead(tempPin);
    float tempC = (adc * 4.88) / 10.0;             // LM35: 10 mV per degree C
    float tempF = tempC * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0;        // specification is in Fahrenheit

    Serial.print("Temperature = "); Serial.print(tempF, 1); Serial.println(" F");

    if (tempF >= LOW_F && tempF <= HIGH_F) {       // within normal limits
      digitalWrite(greenPin, HIGH);
      doorServo.write(90);                         // open the door
      Serial.println("Normal temperature - ACCESS GRANTED");
      delay(3000);
      doorServo.write(0);                          // close
      digitalWrite(greenPin, LOW);
    }
    else {                                         // fever detected
      digitalWrite(redPin, HIGH);
      tone(buzzerPin, 2000, 2000);                 // 2 second alarm
      Serial.println("ABNORMAL TEMPERATURE - ACCESS DENIED");
      delay(2000);
      digitalWrite(redPin, LOW);
    }
  }
  delay(100);
}

Result: the system dispenses sanitiser without contact, screens body temperature, opens the door only for readings between 97 °F and 99 °F, and raises an audible and visual alarm otherwise.

Marks-earning notes
  • Address "contactless" explicitly — the IR proximity sensor is what satisfies that requirement, and it should be named as such.
  • Show the F conversion — the specification is in Fahrenheit but the sensor gives Celsius.
  • Justify the relay for the pump and note the servo's current draw.
  • Mention the ideal sensor — a contact LM35 would defeat the purpose; a real design uses a non-contact IR thermometer such as the MLX90614.
  • tone() occupies Timer2, disabling PWM on pins 3 and 11 — the servo is on pin 10 and unaffected, but the servo library itself takes Timer1 and disables PWM on 9 and 10.
UNIT 05

DAC — Digital to Analog Conversion

Slides 28–31  ·  Question types: T, N  ·  Weight: low-medium

The exact mirror of Unit 3

A digital-to-analog converter is a circuit which converts a binary input number into an analog output. It has a digital input D, a reference Vr, control lines, and an analog output Vo.

Vo = ( D / 2n ) × Vr Number of output values = 2n · Step size (resolution) = Vr / 2n
The three facts from slide 29 — and the one examiners target
  1. For each input digital value there is a corresponding analog output.
  2. The number of possible output values is 2n; the step size Vr/2n is called the resolution.
  3. The maximum output occurs at D = (2n−1), so the value of Vr as an output is never quite reached. An 8-bit DAC on 5 V maxes at (255/256) × 5 = 4.98 V, not 5 V. You always fall one step short.

ADC and DAC side by side

ADCDAC
DirectionAnalog → digitalDigital → analog
FormulaD = (Vi/Vr) × 2nVo = (D/2n) × Vr
ResolutionVr/2nVr/2n — same
Output range0 to 2n−1 (integer)0 to ((2n−1)/2n)×Vr
On the Uno6 channels, 10-bitNone — see below

They are algebraically inverse. Know one formula and rearrange for the other.

DAC circuits

Binary-weighted resistor DAC — each bit switches a resistor of value R, 2R, 4R, 8R… into a summing amplifier. Simple in principle, but needs a very wide range of precisely matched resistors, impractical beyond a few bits.

R-2R ladder DAC — uses only two resistor values in a repeating ladder. Preferred in practice: it scales easily to many bits.

The point the deck never states out loud

The Arduino Uno has no real DAC. There is no pin that can output 2.5 V. analogWrite fakes it — switching a digital pin between 0 V and 5 V very fast and varying the proportion of on-time, so the load responds to the average.

That is the entire reason Unit 6 exists. DAC is the theory; PWM is what you actually have.

Numericals

N5.1 — An 8-bit DAC with Vr = 5 V receives D = 128. Find Vo, the step size and the maximum output.

Vo = (128/256) × 5 = 2.5 V Step = 5/256 = 19.53 mV Vmax = (255/256) × 5 = 4.98 V → Vr is never reached

N5.2 — A 10-bit DAC with Vr = 3.3 V must output 1.5 V. Find the required input code.

D = (Vo/Vr) × 2^n = (1.5/3.3) × 1024 = 465.45 → D = 465 Check: (465/1024) × 3.3 = 1.4985 V ≈ 1.5 V ✓

N5.3 — Compare the resolution of an 8-bit and a 12-bit DAC on the same 5 V reference.

8-bit : 5/256 = 19.53 mV 12-bit: 5/4096 = 1.22 mV 16× finer, because 4 extra bits give 2^4 = 16 times as many levels

N5.4 — Complete the transfer table for an 8-bit DAC at Vr = 5 V.

D = 0 → 0.00 V D = 128 → 2.50 V D = 1 → 19.53 mV D = 192 → 3.75 V D = 64 → 1.25 V D = 255 → 4.98 V (not 5 V)

N5.5 — A PWM output on the Uno is filtered by an RC low-pass network to make a true DAC. What is the effective resolution?

analogWrite is 8-bit → 256 levels Effective resolution = 5/256 = 19.53 mV So a filtered Uno PWM output behaves as an 8-bit DAC, which is 4× coarser than its own 10-bit ADC input

Coding scenarios

Q5.1   Type P  ·  DAC simulation

Print the DAC transfer characteristic

Write a program that computes and prints the output voltage of an 8-bit DAC with a 5 V reference for input codes 0, 1, 64, 128, 192 and 255, and reports the step size and maximum output.

Solution Q5.1
const int   N_BITS = 8;
const float VREF   = 5.0;

float dacOutput(int D) {
  return ((float)D / (1L << N_BITS)) * VREF;   // Vo = (D / 2^n) x Vref
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  long levels = 1L << N_BITS;                  // 2^n = 256

  Serial.print("Levels     = "); Serial.println(levels);
  Serial.print("Step size  = "); Serial.print(VREF / levels * 1000, 2);
  Serial.println(" mV");
  Serial.print("Max output = "); Serial.print(dacOutput(levels - 1), 3);
  Serial.println(" V  (Vref is never reached)");
  Serial.println();

  int codes[] = {0, 1, 64, 128, 192, 255};
  Serial.println("D\tVo (V)");
  for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) {
    Serial.print(codes[i]); Serial.print('\t');
    Serial.println(dacOutput(codes[i]), 4);
  }
}

void loop() {}

1L << N_BITS computes 2n by bit-shifting — faster than pow() and exact, since pow() returns a float and can give 255.9999.

The observation to state: D = 255 gives 4.980 V, not 5.000 V. The reference is approached but never reached.

Q5.2   Type D  ·  PWM as a DAC

Build a real DAC from PWM with an RC filter

The Uno has no DAC. Design a circuit and program that produces a genuine adjustable DC voltage on an output pin, and verify it by reading the result back on an analog input.

Solution Q5.2

Circuit: pin 9 → 10 kΩ resistor → node → 10 µF capacitor → GND. The node is the smoothed DC output; wire it also to A0 for verification.

const int pwmPin  = 9;        // PWM out
const int sensePin = A0;      // reads the filtered voltage back

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(pwmPin, OUTPUT);
  Serial.println("target\tPWM\tmeasured");
}

void loop() {
  for (float target = 0.0; target <= 5.0; target += 0.5) {

    int value = (int)((target / 5.0) * 255.0);   // Vo = (D/256) x Vref, rearranged
    analogWrite(pwmPin, value);

    delay(500);                                  // let the RC filter settle

    float measured = (analogRead(sensePin) * 5.0) / 1023.0;

    Serial.print(target, 2);   Serial.print('\t');
    Serial.print(value);       Serial.print('\t');
    Serial.println(measured, 3);
  }
}
Why the filter is required, quantitatively

PWM on pin 9 runs at about 490 Hz. The RC time constant is τ = 10 kΩ × 10 µF = 100 ms, roughly 49 PWM periods. The capacitor therefore averages many pulses and the ripple is small.

The trade-off: a larger RC gives smoother DC but a slower response — 5τ = 500 ms to settle. A smaller RC responds faster but leaves visible ripple. This is the classic filter design compromise.

Effective resolution: 8-bit, so 19.53 mV steps — coarser than the Uno's own 10-bit ADC, which is why the measured values will not land exactly on the targets.

Q5.3   Type P  ·  waveform generation

Generate a staircase waveform

Produce a rising staircase voltage with 8 discrete steps on a filtered PWM output, printing the code and voltage at each step. This demonstrates the DAC transfer characteristic physically.

Solution Q5.3
const int dacPin = 9;
const int STEPS  = 8;                 // an effective 3-bit DAC

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(dacPin, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  for (int step = 0; step < STEPS; step++) {

    int   value = (step * 255) / (STEPS - 1);       // spread 0..255 over 8 steps
    float volts = (value / 255.0) * 5.0;

    analogWrite(dacPin, value);

    Serial.print("step "); Serial.print(step);
    Serial.print("  code "); Serial.print(value);
    Serial.print("  = ");   Serial.print(volts, 3);
    Serial.println(" V");

    delay(300);
  }
  Serial.println("--- repeat ---");
}

Why this is worth building: the staircase is the DAC's transfer characteristic made visible. Each step is Vr/2n tall. Reducing STEPS to 4 makes the quantization coarser and the staircase more obvious — that is exactly what "fewer bits" means physically.

Q5.4   Type P  ·  round trip

ADC and DAC round-trip error measurement

Write a program that sends a code to a filtered PWM output, reads it back with the ADC, and reports the round-trip error in millivolts and in ADC counts. Explain where the error comes from.

Solution Q5.4
const int dacPin  = 9;
const int adcPin  = A0;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(dacPin, OUTPUT);
  Serial.println("code\tsent(mV)\tread(mV)\terror(mV)\terror(counts)");
}

void loop() {
  for (int code = 0; code <= 255; code += 32) {
    analogWrite(dacPin, code);
    delay(600);                                  // settle the RC filter

    float sentMv = (code / 255.0) * 5000.0;      // DAC formula
    int   adc    = analogRead(adcPin);
    float readMv = adc * 4.88;                   // ADC formula

    Serial.print(code);                Serial.print('\t');
    Serial.print(sentMv, 1);           Serial.print("\t\t");
    Serial.print(readMv, 1);           Serial.print("\t\t");
    Serial.print(readMv - sentMv, 1);  Serial.print("\t\t");
    Serial.println((readMv - sentMv) / 4.88, 1);
  }
  Serial.println("--- sweep complete ---");
}
The four error sources — a complete exam answer
  1. DAC quantization: 8-bit output, ±½ × 19.53 mV = ±9.8 mV
  2. ADC quantization: 10-bit input, ±½ × 4.88 mV = ±2.44 mV
  3. Filter ripple: the RC network never fully smooths the 490 Hz square wave
  4. Reference tolerance: the 5 V rail from USB is typically 4.75–5.25 V, a ±5 % systematic error

The output resolution (19.53 mV) is four times coarser than the input resolution (4.88 mV), so the DAC side dominates the total error. That asymmetry is the whole reason analogRead/4 exists.

Q5.5   Type T+P  ·  comparison

Demonstrate why a DAC cannot drive a motor

Write a program that drives a motor two ways — a filtered "DAC" output and a direct PWM output — and explain, with reference to slide 30, why the PWM route is preferred.

Solution Q5.5
const int dacRoute = 9;    // filtered output -> would need a power amplifier
const int pwmRoute = 6;    // direct PWM      -> drives a transistor

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(dacRoute, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(pwmRoute, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  for (int duty = 0; duty <= 255; duty += 51) {

    analogWrite(dacRoute, duty);      // smooth DC after filtering, but micro-amps
    analogWrite(pwmRoute, duty);      // switching signal, drives a power transistor

    float vavg = (duty / 255.0) * 5.0;
    Serial.print("duty = "); Serial.print((duty / 255.0) * 100, 0);
    Serial.print(" %   Vavg = "); Serial.print(vavg, 2); Serial.println(" V");

    delay(1500);
  }
}
Slide 30's argument in three steps — memorise this
  1. DC motor speed is proportional to the applied DC voltage.
  2. The DAC route: a DAC produces a genuine analog voltage but at milliamps at most. It must be driven through an expensive and bulky power amplifier, whose output then drives the motor. The amplifier operates linearly and dissipates the difference as heat.
  3. The PWM route: the signal is digital, so it can drive a power transistor directly. A transistor fully on or fully off dissipates almost no power.

Conclusion: PWM is cheaper, smaller and far more efficient — which is why every motor drive, LED dimmer and switching power supply uses it.

Q5.6   Type P  ·  resolution scaling

Configurable-resolution DAC emulator

Write a program that emulates a DAC of configurable bit width (4, 6, 8 bits) on the same PWM pin, and reports the step size for each. Show that resolution doubles with every added bit.

Solution Q5.6
const int dacPin = 9;
const float VREF = 5.0;

void sweepAtResolution(int bits) {
  int levels = 1 << bits;                   // 2^bits
  float step = VREF / levels;

  Serial.print("=== "); Serial.print(bits); Serial.print("-bit : ");
  Serial.print(levels); Serial.print(" levels, step = ");
  Serial.print(step * 1000, 2); Serial.println(" mV ===");

  for (int code = 0; code < levels; code++) {
    float volts = (code / (float)levels) * VREF;
    int   pwm   = (int)((volts / VREF) * 255.0);   // map onto the 8-bit hardware
    analogWrite(dacPin, pwm);
    Serial.print("  code "); Serial.print(code);
    Serial.print(" -> ");    Serial.print(volts, 3); Serial.println(" V");
    delay(150);
  }
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(dacPin, OUTPUT);
  sweepAtResolution(4);
  sweepAtResolution(6);
  sweepAtResolution(8);
}

void loop() {}
BitsLevelsStep at 5 V
416312.5 mV
66478.1 mV
825619.5 mV

The rule to state: each additional bit halves the step size and doubles the number of levels. Four extra bits give a 16× improvement — which is exactly the 8-bit versus 12-bit comparison in N5.3.

UNIT 06

PWM — Pulse Width Modulation

Slides 32, 51–59  ·  Question types: P, D, N, T  ·  Weight: highest

Slide 53 is the key image of this unit. Mark t_on and T on it by hand and write the duty-cycle formula beside it.

The core idea (slide 51)

PWM creates a simple square wave by varying the duty cycle, and is used to control an analog variable — usually voltage or current — in applications ranging from telecommunications to robotic control. The Arduino has six PWM outputs on pins 11, 10, 9, 6, 5 and 3.

The definitions and formula (slide 52)

  • Pulse width, also called the period — a short duration of time in which the duty cycle will operate.
  • Duty cycle — the proportion of time the pulse is "on" or "high", expressed as a percentage. 100 % = continuously on, 0 % = continuously off.
Duty cycle = ( ton / T ) × 100 % Vavg = duty cycle × Vsupply duty % = ( analogWrite value / 255 ) × 100 %
analogWrite valueDutyVavg at 5 V
00 %0 V
6425.1 %1.25 V
12850.2 %2.51 V
19174.9 %3.75 V
255100 %5.00 V

PWM frequency on the Uno

PinsTimerFrequencyPeriod
5, 6Timer0~977 Hz1.02 ms
9, 10Timer1~490 Hz2.04 ms
3, 11Timer2~490 Hz2.04 ms
Key points
  • analogWrite changes the duty cycle, never the frequency. A guaranteed one-mark question.
  • analogWrite on a non-PWM pin does not error — it degrades silently into digitalWrite, LOW below 128 and HIGH at 128 and above.
  • PWM is not true analog. An LED or motor averages it because it is slow; feeding another analog input requires an RC low-pass filter.
  • tone() uses Timer2 → PWM on pins 3 and 11 stops working. The Servo library uses Timer1 → PWM on pins 9 and 10 stops working. Never reconfigure Timer0 — it runs millis() and delay().
  • Input is 10-bit, output is 8-bit — hence the /4.
  • A DC motor has a minimum starting duty cycle; below roughly 30–40 % it stalls and hums. Proportional designs need a floor value.

Why PWM beats a DAC for motors (slide 54)

  1. DC motor speed is proportional to the applied DC voltage.
  2. DAC route: analog voltage at milliamps → needs an expensive and bulky power amplifier → the amplifier dissipates heat.
  3. PWM route: digital signal → drives a power transistor directly → fully on or fully off dissipates almost nothing.

The two deck programs

Example 1 — LED fade (slides 56–57)

int brilho = 0;     // "brilho" = brightness (Portuguese) - just a variable name

void setup() { pinMode(3, OUTPUT); }

void loop() {
  for (brilho = 0; brilho <= 255; brilho += 5) {    // ramp up
    analogWrite(3, brilho);
    delay(30);
  }
  for (brilho = 255; brilho >= 0; brilho -= 5) {    // ramp down
    analogWrite(3, brilho);
    delay(30);
  }
}

Compute its timing — that is the exam skill: a step of 5 over 255 gives 51 steps, each 30 ms → ≈1.5 s per direction, ≈3 s per full "breathing" cycle.

Example 2 — motor speed by potentiometer (slides 32, 59)

int potvalue;

void setup() {
  pinMode(A0, INPUT);
  pinMode(6, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  potvalue = analogRead(A0)/4;      // 0..1023 -> 0..255
  analogWrite (6, potvalue);
}

The whole program is the /4 — the bridge from a 10-bit input to an 8-bit output.

Numericals

N6.1 — A PWM signal has a period of 2 ms and an on-time of 0.5 ms. Find the duty cycle, frequency and average voltage from a 5 V supply.

Duty = (0.5/2) × 100 = 25 % Freq = 1/T = 1/(2 × 10^-3) = 500 Hz Vavg = 0.25 × 5 = 1.25 V

N6.2 — What analogWrite value gives 60 % duty, and what average voltage results?

value = 0.60 × 255 = 153 Vavg = 0.60 × 5 = 3.0 V

N6.3 — A servo signal has a 20 ms period and a 1.5 ms on-time. Find the duty cycle. Can analogWrite produce it?

Duty = (1.5/20) × 100 = 7.5 % Nearest value = 0.075 × 255 ≈ 19 But analogWrite CANNOT drive a servo. Its PWM runs at ~490 Hz (period ~2 ms) whereas a servo needs a 20 ms period. That mismatch is why the Servo library exists and takes Timer1.

N6.4 — A potentiometer reads 768. It is divided by 4 and written to a PWM pin. Find the PWM value, duty cycle and average voltage.

PWM = 768/4 = 192 Duty = (192/255) × 100 = 75.3 % Vavg = 0.753 × 5 = 3.76 V

N6.5 — Derive the PWM frequency on pin 6 and on pin 9 from the timer settings.

f = f_clk / (N × counter range) Pin 6 : Timer0, Fast PWM, 8-bit, prescaler 64 f = 16×10^6 / (64 × 256) = 976.56 Hz Pin 9 : Timer1, Phase-correct PWM counts up AND down, range 510 f = 16×10^6 / (64 × 510) = 490.20 Hz

N6.6 — The LED fade program uses a step of 5 and delay(30). Find the time for one full breathing cycle. What if the step is changed to 15?

Steps per direction = 255/5 = 51 One direction = 51 × 30 ms = 1.53 s Full cycle = 2 × 1.53 = 3.06 s With step 15: 255/15 = 17 steps → 17 × 30 = 0.51 s per direction Full cycle = 1.02 s, but the fade is visibly coarser

N6.7 — A heater is driven at 40 % duty from a 12 V supply. Find the average voltage and the average power in a 6 Ω element.

Vavg = 0.40 × 12 = 4.8 V For a resistive load, average POWER follows the duty cycle directly: Pfull = V²/R = 144/6 = 24 W Pavg = 0.40 × 24 = 9.6 W (Note: do NOT compute Vavg²/R = 3.84 W — that is a common error, because the heater sees full 12 V during the on-time.)

Coding scenarios

Q6.1   Type P  ·  the integration program

Potentiometer dimmer with duty cycle readout

Read a potentiometer on A0 and set an LED's brightness on pin 9. Print the raw ADC value, the PWM value, the duty cycle percentage and the equivalent average voltage on one line, updating the display only every 250 ms while brightness updates continuously.

Solution Q6.1
const int potPin = A0;
const int ledPin = 9;
const unsigned long PRINT_INTERVAL = 250;
const float VSUPPLY = 5.0;

unsigned long lastPrint = 0;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(ledPin, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  // runs continuously - brightness is always responsive
  int adcVal = analogRead(potPin);        // 0..1023
  int pwmVal = adcVal / 4;                // 10-bit -> 8-bit
  analogWrite(ledPin, pwmVal);

  // runs every 250 ms - the display
  unsigned long now = millis();
  if (now - lastPrint >= PRINT_INTERVAL) {
    lastPrint = now;

    float duty = (pwmVal / 255.0) * 100.0;   // duty cycle formula
    float vavg = (duty / 100.0) * VSUPPLY;   // average output voltage

    Serial.print("ADC = ");    Serial.print(adcVal);
    Serial.print("  PWM = ");  Serial.print(pwmVal);
    Serial.print("  Duty = "); Serial.print(duty, 1); Serial.print("%");
    Serial.print("  Vavg = "); Serial.print(vavg, 2); Serial.println(" V");
  }
}
The sanity check to memorise

Turn the pot to the middle: ADC ≈ 512 → PWM ≈ 128 → duty ≈ 50 % → Vavg ≈ 2.5 V. If those four numbers do not line up, you have a bug.

This single program contains every formula from Units 3, 5 and 6. If you can write it from a blank file, you own slides 14–60.

Write 255.0, not 255 — the same integer-division trap. pwmVal / 255 is 0 for every input except exactly 255.

Q6.2   Type D  ·  proportional control

Temperature-controlled fan for a server room

An LM35 on A0 senses temperature. A fan driven through a transistor from PWM pin 6 must be off below 30 °C, at full speed at or above 50 °C, and proportional between. Display temperature, PWM value and duty cycle.

Solution Q6.2

Working

  1. The LM35 outputs 10 mV per °C into A0.
  2. analogRead gives a 10-bit count; multiplying by 4.88 converts it to millivolts.
  3. Dividing the millivolts by 10 gives the temperature in °C.
  4. Below 30 °C the PWM value is 0 and the fan is off.
  5. At or above 50 °C the PWM value is 255 and the fan runs at full speed.
  6. Between, map() scales the temperature linearly onto a PWM range of 100–255. The floor of 100 exists because a DC motor will not start from rest at very low duty.
  7. analogWrite generates the PWM signal that sets the average voltage across the fan.
  8. Temperature, PWM value and duty cycle are printed every second.
const int tempPin  = A0;
const int motorPin = 6;      // must be a PWM pin
const int ledPin   = 13;     // indicator: fan running

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(motorPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(ledPin,   OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  int   adc   = analogRead(tempPin);
  float mv    = adc * 4.88;          // count -> millivolts
  float tempC = mv / 10.0;           // LM35: 10 mV per degree C

  int speed;
  if (tempC < 30) {
    speed = 0;                                     // fan off
    digitalWrite(ledPin, LOW);
  } else if (tempC >= 50) {
    speed = 255;                                   // full speed
    digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH);
  } else {
    speed = map((int)tempC, 30, 50, 100, 255);     // proportional
    digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH);
  }

  analogWrite(motorPin, speed);

  Serial.print("T = ");        Serial.print(tempC, 1);
  Serial.print(" C   PWM = "); Serial.print(speed);
  Serial.print("   Duty = ");  Serial.print((speed / 255.0) * 100.0, 0);
  Serial.println(" %");

  delay(1000);
}
Marks-earning notes
  • The transistor is not optional — a fan draws far more than 40 mA, so the PWM signal switches a power transistor. This is slide 54's argument applied.
  • Explain map() in words: it linearly rescales the 30–50 input band onto the 100–255 output band.
