  • Justify the floor of 100: a DC motor has a minimum starting duty; below it the motor stalls and only hums.
  • Add a flyback diode across the motor to absorb the inductive spike when the transistor switches off.
  • Duty ≠ frequency: analogWrite varies only duty; the frequency stays at ~977 Hz on pin 6.
Q6.3   Type P  ·  RGB colour mixing

RGB LED colour fader

Drive an RGB LED on PWM pins 9, 10 and 11 to fade smoothly through the colour spectrum. Print the current RGB values and each channel's duty cycle.

Solution Q6.3
const int redPin   = 9;
const int greenPin = 10;
const int bluePin  = 11;

void setColour(int r, int g, int b) {
  analogWrite(redPin,   r);
  analogWrite(greenPin, g);
  analogWrite(bluePin,  b);

  Serial.print("R="); Serial.print(r);
  Serial.print(" G="); Serial.print(g);
  Serial.print(" B="); Serial.print(b);
  Serial.print("   duties: ");
  Serial.print((r/255.0)*100, 0); Serial.print("% ");
  Serial.print((g/255.0)*100, 0); Serial.print("% ");
  Serial.print((b/255.0)*100, 0); Serial.println("%");
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(redPin, OUTPUT); pinMode(greenPin, OUTPUT); pinMode(bluePin, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  int i;
  for (i = 0; i < 255; i++) setColour(255 - i, i, 0);   // red   -> green
  for (i = 0; i < 255; i++) setColour(0, 255 - i, i);   // green -> blue
  for (i = 0; i < 255; i++) setColour(i, 0, 255 - i);   // blue  -> red
}
The timer conflict to point out

Pins 9 and 10 are on Timer1; pin 11 is on Timer2. This program therefore occupies both. Adding tone() would break the blue channel (Timer2), and adding a Servo would break red and green (Timer1).

Choosing 9, 10, 11 rather than 3, 5, 6 is deliberate: pins 5 and 6 sit on Timer0, and although PWM works there, reconfiguring Timer0 would break millis().

Colour mixing is three independent duty cycles. Each channel's average voltage sets that colour's brightness, and the eye integrates the three into one perceived colour.

Q6.4   Type D  ·  bidirectional motor

Motor speed and direction with an H-bridge

Control a DC motor's speed and direction from a centre-detented potentiometer: centre = stopped, turning one way runs forward with increasing speed, the other way runs reverse. Use an L293D H-bridge.

Solution Q6.4
const int potPin  = A0;
const int enPin   = 6;     // L293D enable - PWM controls SPEED
const int in1Pin  = 4;     // direction bit 1
const int in2Pin  = 5;     // direction bit 2

const int DEADBAND = 40;   // counts either side of centre where the motor is off

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(enPin,  OUTPUT);
  pinMode(in1Pin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(in2Pin, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  int adc = analogRead(potPin);          // 0..1023, centre = 512
  int offset = adc - 512;                // -512 .. +511

  int speed;
  if (abs(offset) < DEADBAND) {          // centre: stop
    digitalWrite(in1Pin, LOW);
    digitalWrite(in2Pin, LOW);
    speed = 0;
    Serial.print("STOP    ");
  }
  else if (offset > 0) {                 // forward
    digitalWrite(in1Pin, HIGH);
    digitalWrite(in2Pin, LOW);
    speed = map(offset, DEADBAND, 511, 60, 255);
    Serial.print("FORWARD ");
  }
  else {                                 // reverse
    digitalWrite(in1Pin, LOW);
    digitalWrite(in2Pin, HIGH);
    speed = map(-offset, DEADBAND, 512, 60, 255);
    Serial.print("REVERSE ");
  }

  speed = constrain(speed, 0, 255);
  analogWrite(enPin, speed);

  Serial.print("speed = "); Serial.print(speed);
  Serial.print("  duty = "); Serial.print((speed/255.0)*100, 0);
  Serial.println(" %");

  delay(100);
}
Three design points worth marks
  • Speed and direction are separate concerns. PWM on the enable pin sets speed; two digital pins set direction. Trying to encode both in one PWM signal is a common wrong answer.
  • Why a deadband: a potentiometer never sits exactly at 512, and noise would make the motor twitch and reverse near centre. A ±40-count dead zone makes "off" reliable.
  • Why an H-bridge and not a transistor: a single transistor can only switch current one way. Reversing a DC motor requires reversing the polarity across it, which needs four switching elements — an H-bridge.
Q6.5   Type P  ·  buzzer and tone

LED brightness with an audible tone indicator

Reproduce the deck's slide-56 requirement: fade an LED and interface a buzzer that plays a different tone at each brightness level. Then state which PWM pins become unusable and why.

Solution Q6.5
const int ledPin    = 9;      // Timer1
const int buzzerPin = 8;      // plain digital pin - tone() drives it

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(ledPin, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  for (int b = 0; b <= 255; b += 15) {
    analogWrite(ledPin, b);                       // brightness = duty cycle

    int freq = map(b, 0, 255, 200, 2000);         // brightness -> pitch
    tone(buzzerPin, freq);

    Serial.print("PWM = ");   Serial.print(b);
    Serial.print("  duty = ");Serial.print((b/255.0)*100, 0);
    Serial.print("%  tone = ");Serial.print(freq); Serial.println(" Hz");

    delay(120);
  }
  noTone(buzzerPin);
  delay(400);
}
The conflict this question is really testing

tone() uses Timer2. While a tone is playing, analogWrite on pins 3 and 11 stops working.

That is why the LED is deliberately on pin 9 (Timer1) and not on pin 3 or 11. If the question had specified pin 3 for the LED, the correct answer would be to point out the conflict and move either the LED or the buzzer.

The full conflict table:

FeatureTimer usedPWM pins disabled
tone()Timer23 and 11
Servo libraryTimer19 and 10
millis(), delay()Timer05 and 6 if reconfigured

Also note: tone() controls frequency, not duty cycle. It is a different use of the same timer hardware.

Q6.6   Type D  ·  soft start

Motor soft-start with overload protection

Design a conveyor motor drive that ramps the motor from stopped to full speed over three seconds rather than starting abruptly, monitors current on A1, and shuts down if the current exceeds a limit.

Solution Q6.6
const int motorPin   = 6;
const int currentPin = A1;     // current-sense amplifier output
const int alarmPin   = 8;
const int startBtn   = 2;

const int   RAMP_MS   = 3000;  // soft-start duration
const float I_LIMIT_A = 2.0;   // amps
const float SENSE_V_PER_A = 0.185;   // ACS712-05B: 185 mV per amp

bool running = false;
unsigned long rampStart = 0;

float readCurrent() {
  int   adc = analogRead(currentPin);
  float v   = (adc * 5.0) / 1023.0;
  return (v - 2.5) / SENSE_V_PER_A;    // sensor idles at Vcc/2
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(motorPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(alarmPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(startBtn, INPUT_PULLUP);
  analogWrite(motorPin, 0);
}

void loop() {
  if (!running && digitalRead(startBtn) == LOW) {
    running = true;
    rampStart = millis();
    Serial.println("Soft start begins");
  }

  if (running) {
    unsigned long elapsed = millis() - rampStart;

    int speed;
    if (elapsed >= RAMP_MS) speed = 255;                    // fully ramped
    else speed = map(elapsed, 0, RAMP_MS, 60, 255);         // linear ramp

    analogWrite(motorPin, speed);

    float amps = readCurrent();
    if (amps > I_LIMIT_A) {                                 // overload
      analogWrite(motorPin, 0);
      digitalWrite(alarmPin, HIGH);
      running = false;
      Serial.print("OVERLOAD - shut down at ");
      Serial.print(amps, 2); Serial.println(" A");
    } else {
      Serial.print("speed = "); Serial.print(speed);
      Serial.print("  duty = "); Serial.print((speed/255.0)*100, 0);
      Serial.print("%  I = ");  Serial.print(amps, 2); Serial.println(" A");
    }
  }
  delay(50);
}
Why soft start matters — the engineering justification

A DC motor at rest has no back-EMF, so applying full voltage draws the stall current, often five to eight times the running current. That surge stresses the transistor, sags the supply and can reset the microcontroller through brownout.

Ramping the duty cycle limits the average voltage while the motor accelerates and back-EMF builds. The ramp uses millis() rather than a blocking loop, so the current sensor is checked throughout — a blocking ramp could not detect an overload during the ramp itself.

Why the ramp starts at 60, not 0: below the minimum starting duty the motor would sit stalled, drawing high current without turning — the exact condition the design is trying to avoid.

UNIT 07

Timers and Counters — Hardware

Slides 35–42  ·  Question types: T, N  ·  Weight: high

Why timers exist (slide 35)

Digital timer/counters provide a series of time- or count-related events within the system with the minimum of processor and software overhead. That phrase is the whole justification: you could count clock cycles in software, but the CPU would do nothing else. A hardware timer counts in the background while your code runs.

The deck's list of uses, worth quoting: timing references for control sequences · system ticks for operating systems · generation of waveforms · serial port baud rate generation · audible tones.

Timer vs counter (slide 36)

They are distinguished largely by their use, not their logic.

TimerCounter
Input signalPeriodic — a clockAperiodic — external events
Each tick meansA known durationOne event
The count tells youHow longHow many
ExampleGenerating a 1-second delayItems on a conveyor

Same silicon. Only the clock source and your interpretation differ. On the Uno, an external counting signal is fed to pin 4 (T0 input) or pin 5 (T1 input).

The internal structure (slides 37–38)

  1. Clock source — internal to the timer/counter, or external via a separate pin.
  2. Prescaler — divides the clock by the value written into the prescaler register. Values: 1, 8, 64, 256, 1024.
  3. Counter — count-up or count-down operation.
  4. Event — when a zero count is reached, an event occurs: an interrupt, or an external line changing state.
  5. I/O control block — generates the interrupts and can control the counter from external signals.

The prescaler table — memorise the ÷1024 row

PrescalerTick period8-bit max (256)16-bit max (65536)
162.5 ns16 µs4.096 ms
8500 ns128 µs32.8 ms
644 µs1.024 ms262 ms
25616 µs4.096 ms1.048 s
102464 µs16.4 ms4.194 s
Why a prescaler is necessary

At 16 MHz even a 16-bit counter overflows in 4.096 ms. With ÷1024 that stretches to 4.19 seconds. The prescaler trades resolution for range — that sentence is the answer to "why is a prescaler needed?"

The three timers on the Uno (slide 39)

TimerWidthMax countOwnsPWM pins
Timer08-bit255delay(), millis()5, 6
Timer116-bit65535Servo library9, 10
Timer28-bit255tone()3, 11

The Uno has a 16 MHz internal clock, so a single count takes 62 ns (62.5 ns exactly).

Control registers (slides 40, 42)

RegisterFull namePurpose
TCCRnATimer/Counter Control Register ASets the mode
TCCRnBTimer/Counter Control Register BMode + prescaler bits
TCNTnTimer/Counter RegisterThe count; write it to preload
OCRnAOutput Compare Register ACompare value
OCRnBOutput Compare Register BSecond compare value

Recognise the Unit 2 pattern: TCCR is the control register, TCNT and OCR are data registers, TIFR is the status register. One model, every device.

The four timer modes (slide 41)

ModeBehaviourUsed for
NormalCounts up to maximum, resets to 0Simple overflow interrupts
CTC (Clear Timer on Compare)Counts up to OCRnA, clears immediatelyInterrupt generation
Fast PWMAs fast as the clock allows, not synchronised with the timing clockMaximum PWM frequency
Phase-correct PWMSymmetric with respect to the system clockMotor control

How to distinguish the PWM modes: Fast PWM counts up and snaps back to zero — a sawtooth, single-slope, double the frequency. Phase-correct counts up then back down — a triangle, dual-slope, so the pulse stays centred as duty changes, avoiding glitches in motor drive.

The preload calculation (slide 42) — guaranteed exam question

An AVR timer always counts up and fires on overflow. To get an interval shorter than a full overflow, preload TCNT so fewer counts remain.

TCNT1 = 65535 − ( 16 × 106 × time(s) / prescaler ) ticks = fclk × time / prescaler For an 8-bit timer, TCNT0 = 255 − ticks

The deck's worked example — 2 s on Timer1, prescaler 1024: ticks = (16×106 × 2)/1024 = 31250; TCNT1 = 65535 − 31250 = 34285.

The trap that catches most students

If ticks exceeds 65535, the preload goes negative — meaning that delay is impossible with that prescaler. Increase the prescaler and recheck. Always verify before writing your answer.

The payoff — where Unit 6's PWM frequencies came from

fPWM = fclk / ( N × counter range )
  • Pins 5, 6 (Timer0) — Fast PWM, 8-bit, prescaler 64: 16×106/(64 × 256) = 976.56 Hz ✓
  • Pins 9, 10, 3, 11 — Phase-correct counts up and down, range 510: 16×106/(64 × 510) = 490.2 Hz ✓

PWM is not a separate feature — it is what a timer does when placed in a PWM mode.

Numericals — every variation

N7.1 — Deck example. Timer1 preload for a 2-second delay at prescaler 1024.

ticks = (16 × 10^6 × 2)/1024 = 32 × 10^6 / 1024 = 31250 TCNT1 = 65535 − 31250 = 34285

N7.2 — Timer1 preload for a 0.2 s delay at prescaler 64.

ticks = (16 × 10^6 × 0.2)/64 = 3.2 × 10^6/64 = 50000 50000 < 65535 ✓ achievable TCNT1 = 65535 − 50000 = 15535

N7.3 — Timer1 preload for 0.5 s at prescaler 256.

ticks = (16 × 10^6 × 0.5)/256 = 8 × 10^6/256 = 31250 TCNT1 = 65535 − 31250 = 34285 Same answer as N7.1 — both need 31250 ticks. Good method check.

N7.4 — Can Timer1 give a 1-second delay at prescaler 8? Find the smallest workable prescaler.

ticks = (16 × 10^6 × 1)/8 = 2,000,000 >> 65535 NO — preload would be 65535 − 2,000,000 = −1,934,465, meaningless Testing each: /64 → 250,000 ✗ /256 → 62,500 ✓ Smallest workable prescaler = 256, TCNT1 = 65535 − 62500 = 3035 (/1024 also works: ticks = 15625, but coarser resolution)

N7.5 — Find the longest interval Timer1 can measure at prescaler 1024, and Timer0 at prescaler 64.

Timer1: 65536 × (1024/16×10^6) = 65536 × 64 µs = 4.194 s Timer0: 256 × ( 64/16×10^6) = 256 × 4 µs = 1.024 ms

N7.6 — Compute the 8-bit Timer0 preload for a 1 ms delay at prescaler 64.

tick period = 64/16×10^6 = 4 µs ticks = 1 ms / 4 µs = 250 250 < 255 ✓ TCNT0 = 255 − 250 = 5

N7.7 — Derive OCR1A for a 1 Hz CTC interrupt at prescaler 1024.

ticks per second = 16 × 10^6 / 1024 = 15625 OCR1A counts from 0, so load one less: OCR1A = 15625 − 1 = 15624

N7.8 — A conveyor counter must count up to 5000 items. Which timer can hold that count, and why not the others?

Timer0 max = 255 ✗ Timer2 max = 255 ✗ Timer1 max = 65535 ✓ → use Timer1, the only 16-bit timer External counting input for Timer1 is Arduino pin 5 (T1)

N7.9 — Derive the PWM frequency on pins 5/6 and on pins 9/10.

f = f_clk / (N × range) Pins 5,6 : Timer0, Fast PWM, range 256, N = 64 16×10^6/(64 × 256) = 976.56 Hz Pins 9,10 : Timer1, Phase-correct, range 510, N = 64 16×10^6/(64 × 510) = 490.20 Hz

Coding scenarios

Q7.1   Type P  ·  register-level timer

Precise 1 Hz LED using Timer1 in CTC mode

Toggle an LED at exactly 1 Hz using Timer1 configured in CTC mode with a compare-match interrupt. Do not use delay() or millis(). Derive the OCR1A value.

Solution Q7.1
const int LED = 13;

void setup() {
  pinMode(LED, OUTPUT);

  cli();                                 // disable interrupts while configuring

  TCCR1A = 0;                            // clear both control registers
  TCCR1B = 0;
  TCNT1  = 0;                            // start the count at zero

  OCR1A  = 15624;                        // 16e6/1024 = 15625 ticks per second, minus 1
  TCCR1B |= (1 << WGM12);                // CTC mode: clear timer on compare match
  TCCR1B |= (1 << CS12) | (1 << CS10);   // prescaler = 1024
  TIMSK1 |= (1 << OCIE1A);               // enable compare-match A interrupt

  sei();                                 // re-enable interrupts
}

ISR(TIMER1_COMPA_vect) {                 // fires exactly once per second
  digitalWrite(LED, !digitalRead(LED));
}

void loop() {
  // completely free for other work - the timer runs in hardware
}
The derivation to show in an exam

At prescaler 1024 one tick is 1024/16×106 = 64 µs. One second needs 1/64 µs = 15,625 ticks. The register counts from 0, so load 15,625 − 1 = 15,624.

Why CTC and not preload: in CTC mode the hardware clears the counter automatically on every match, so no software reload is needed and there is no cumulative drift. Preloading requires the ISR to rewrite TCNT each time, and the few cycles of interrupt latency accumulate as error.

Why cli() and sei(): the 16-bit registers are written as two 8-bit halves. An interrupt between the two writes would corrupt the value.

Q7.2   Type P  ·  preload method

Timer1 overflow interrupt using the deck's preload formula

Generate a 2-second interval using Timer1 in Normal mode with an overflow interrupt and the preload value from slide 42. Show that the preload must be rewritten in the ISR.

Solution Q7.2
const int LED = 13;
const unsigned int PRELOAD = 34285;    // 65535 - (16e6 x 2 / 1024)

void setup() {
  pinMode(LED, OUTPUT);
  Serial.begin(9600);

  cli();
  TCCR1A = 0;
  TCCR1B = 0;
  TCNT1  = PRELOAD;                      // start 31250 counts short of overflow
  TCCR1B |= (1 << CS12) | (1 << CS10);   // prescaler 1024, Normal mode
  TIMSK1 |= (1 << TOIE1);                // enable OVERFLOW interrupt
  sei();
}

ISR(TIMER1_OVF_vect) {
  TCNT1 = PRELOAD;                       // MUST reload - Normal mode restarts at 0
  digitalWrite(LED, !digitalRead(LED));
}

void loop() {
  Serial.print("millis = "); Serial.println(millis());
  delay(500);
}

The calculation, written out: ticks = (16 × 106 × 2)/1024 = 31,250. TCNT1 = 65535 − 31250 = 34,285.

Why the reload line is essential

In Normal mode the counter overflows to 0, not back to the preload. Without TCNT1 = PRELOAD; in the ISR, the first interval is 2 s and every one after it is a full 4.19 s overflow. Forgetting this line is the single most common error in timer questions.

Contrast with Q7.1: CTC mode reloads in hardware; Normal mode requires software. That is the practical difference between the two modes.

Q7.3   Type P  ·  counter mode

Hardware event counter using the T1 external input

Count pulses from a sensor using Timer1 as a true counter clocked from its external pin, rather than counting in software. Report the count every second and explain the advantage.

Solution Q7.3
// Timer1 external clock input T1 = Arduino pin 5
const int T1_PIN = 5;

unsigned long lastReport = 0;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(T1_PIN, INPUT_PULLUP);

  cli();
  TCCR1A = 0;
  TCCR1B = 0;
  TCNT1  = 0;
  // CS12:CS11:CS10 = 110 -> external clock on T1, falling edge
  TCCR1B |= (1 << CS12) | (1 << CS11);
  sei();

  Serial.println("Hardware counter running on pin 5");
}

void loop() {
  if (millis() - lastReport >= 1000) {
    lastReport = millis();

    unsigned int count = TCNT1;      // read the hardware count
    TCNT1 = 0;                       // reset for the next window

    Serial.print("Pulses in last second = "); Serial.print(count);
    Serial.print("   frequency = ");          Serial.print(count);
    Serial.println(" Hz");
  }
}
Timer versus counter, demonstrated

This is the deck's distinction made real: the same Timer1 hardware, but clocked from an aperiodic external signal instead of the internal periodic clock. The count now means how many events, not how long.

The advantage over software counting: the hardware counts every edge with zero CPU involvement, even at frequencies far above what an interrupt could service. An attachInterrupt approach costs several microseconds per pulse and saturates above roughly 50 kHz; the hardware counter works to several MHz.

The pins: T0 = Arduino pin 4, T1 = Arduino pin 5. These are the only two external counting inputs.

Q7.4   Type P  ·  custom PWM frequency

Change the PWM frequency on pins 9 and 10

The default 490 Hz PWM causes audible whine in a motor. Reconfigure Timer1 to produce roughly 31 kHz PWM on pins 9 and 10, and explain the trade-off.

Solution Q7.4
const int motorPin = 9;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(motorPin, OUTPUT);

  // Timer1: phase-correct PWM, 8-bit, prescaler 1  -> 16e6/(1 x 510) = 31372 Hz
  TCCR1B = (TCCR1B & 0b11111000) | 0x01;   // set prescaler bits to 1

  Serial.println("PWM on pins 9/10 now ~31 kHz - above hearing");
}

void loop() {
  for (int d = 0; d <= 255; d += 5) {
    analogWrite(motorPin, d);
    delay(40);
  }
}

The derivation: f = fclk/(N × 510) = 16×106/(1 × 510) = 31,372 Hz, comfortably above the ~20 kHz limit of human hearing.

The trade-offs to state
  • Benefit: the motor no longer whines, because the switching frequency is ultrasonic.
  • Cost: switching losses in the transistor rise with frequency, so the driver runs hotter.
  • Critical: this is safe on Timer1 (pins 9, 10). Doing the same to Timer0 (pins 5, 6) would break millis() and delay(), because they are derived from Timer0's overflow rate. All timing in your program would be wrong by the same factor.
  • It also disables the Servo library, which needs Timer1 at its own settings.
Q7.5   Type P  ·  multi-rate

Two independent timer interrupts at different rates

Use Timer1 to flash an LED at 1 Hz and Timer2 to sample a sensor at 100 Hz, both by interrupt, while loop() stays free for serial output.

Solution Q7.5
const int LED = 13;
const int SENSOR = A0;

volatile int  latestSample = 0;
volatile bool ledState = false;
volatile unsigned int sampleCount = 0;

void setup() {
  pinMode(LED, OUTPUT);
  Serial.begin(9600);

  cli();
  // --- Timer1: CTC at 1 Hz ---
  TCCR1A = 0; TCCR1B = 0; TCNT1 = 0;
  OCR1A  = 15624;                              // 16e6/1024 - 1
  TCCR1B |= (1 << WGM12) | (1 << CS12) | (1 << CS10);
  TIMSK1 |= (1 << OCIE1A);

  // --- Timer2: CTC at 100 Hz ---
  TCCR2A = 0; TCCR2B = 0; TCNT2 = 0;
  OCR2A  = 155;                                // 16e6/(1024 x 100) - 1 = 155.25
  TCCR2A |= (1 << WGM21);                      // CTC
  TCCR2B |= (1 << CS22) | (1 << CS21) | (1 << CS20);   // prescaler 1024
  TIMSK2 |= (1 << OCIE2A);
  sei();
}

ISR(TIMER1_COMPA_vect) {          // 1 Hz
  ledState = !ledState;
  digitalWrite(LED, ledState);
}

ISR(TIMER2_COMPA_vect) {          // 100 Hz
  latestSample = analogRead(SENSOR);
  sampleCount++;
}

void loop() {
  Serial.print("sample = ");  Serial.print(latestSample);
  Serial.print("   count = ");Serial.println(sampleCount);
  delay(1000);
}

OCR2A derivation: 16×106/(1024 × 100) = 156.25, minus 1 = 155.25 → 155, giving an actual rate of 16×106/(1024 × 156) = 100.16 Hz — a 0.16 % error.

Two consequences to state

PWM lost: Timer1 is reconfigured so pins 9 and 10 lose PWM; Timer2 is reconfigured so pins 3 and 11 lose PWM and tone() stops working. Only pins 5 and 6 remain usable for analogWrite.

Why 8-bit Timer2 needs a big prescaler: its maximum count is 255, so at prescaler 64 the longest interval is 1.024 ms — far short of the 10 ms needed for 100 Hz. Only ÷1024 makes 100 Hz reachable.

Q7.6   Type P  ·  verification

Measure and verify prescaler tick periods

Write a program that empirically verifies the prescaler table by timing a known number of timer ticks against micros(), for prescalers 64, 256 and 1024.

Solution Q7.6
void measurePrescaler(byte csBits, const char *label, unsigned long divisor) {
  cli();
  TCCR1A = 0;
  TCCR1B = 0;
  TCNT1  = 0;
  TCCR1B |= csBits;                     // start the timer with this prescaler
  sei();

  unsigned long t0 = micros();
  while (TCNT1 < 10000) { }             // wait for exactly 10000 ticks
  unsigned long t1 = micros();

  TCCR1B = 0;                           // stop the timer

  float measuredTick = (t1 - t0) / 10000.0;      // microseconds per tick
  float expectedTick = divisor / 16.0;           // N / 16 MHz, in microseconds

  Serial.print(label);
  Serial.print(": expected "); Serial.print(expectedTick, 3);
  Serial.print(" us   measured "); Serial.print(measuredTick, 3);
  Serial.println(" us");
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  delay(200);
  measurePrescaler((1<<CS11)|(1<<CS10), "prescaler   64", 64);
  measurePrescaler((1<<CS12),            "prescaler  256", 256);
  measurePrescaler((1<<CS12)|(1<<CS10),  "prescaler 1024", 1024);
}

void loop() {}
PrescalerCS12:CS11:CS10Expected tick
10010.0625 µs
80100.5 µs
640114 µs
25610016 µs
102410164 µs
External T1, falling110—
External T1, rising111—

This table is the content of TCCRnB's lower three bits, and reproducing it is worth marks in a register question.

UNIT 08

Timer Software and Non-Blocking Code

Slides 43–48  ·  Question types: P  ·  Weight: high  ·  The most transferable skill in the module

The four functions (slides 43–46)

FunctionReturnsNotes
delay(ms)nothingPauses the program, in milliseconds. 1000 ms = 1 s. Argument unsigned long. Blocking.
delayMicroseconds(us)nothingMuch shorter delays. 1000 µs = 1 ms. Argument unsigned int.
millis()unsigned longMilliseconds since power-on or reset. Non-blocking.
micros()unsigned longMicroseconds since the program started.
Key points
  • delay() stops your program; millis() merely reports the time and returns instantly. Everything responsive is built on millis().
  • delay() is busy-wait — literally the same technique as AGAIN: JNB TF0, AGAIN from Unit 2.
  • Rollover: millis() overflows after 232 ms ≈ 49.7 days; micros() after about 70 minutes.
  • delayMicroseconds is accurate from about 3 µs to 16,383 µs.
  • Always unsigned long for time variables — a 16-bit int overflows after 32.7 seconds.
  • Subtract, never compare to an absolute target. now - previous >= interval survives rollover because unsigned arithmetic wraps cleanly.
Deck contradiction — answer with Timer0

Slide 39 says Timer0 handles millis(). Slide 45 says millis() uses "internal timer1". Slide 39 is correct — millis() runs on Timer0.

The deck's example (slides 47–48)

#define LED 13
int buttonState = 0;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(LED, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(7, INPUT);
}

void loop() {
  digitalWrite(LED, HIGH);
  delay(500);
  digitalWrite(LED, LOW);
  delay(500);

  buttonState = digitalRead(7);
  if(buttonState==LOW) {
    Serial.write("micros()=");
    Serial.println(micros());
  } else {
    Serial.write("millis()=");
    Serial.println(millis());
  }
}

Two things to notice. First, LOW means pressed — with a pull-up the pin idles HIGH and the button pulls it to ground. Second, and more important: the button is checked only once per second, because the two delay(500) calls block everything between. Press and release quickly and the program never notices.

The millis() pattern — the most important technique in Module 2

unsigned long previousMillis = 0;
const unsigned long INTERVAL = 500;

void loop() {
  unsigned long currentMillis = millis();

  if (currentMillis - previousMillis >= INTERVAL) {
    previousMillis = currentMillis;    // remember when we last acted
    // ... the periodic thing ...
  }
  // ... everything else runs on EVERY pass ...
}

Edge detection — the companion technique

int buttonState = digitalRead(BUTTON);
if (buttonState == LOW && lastButtonState == HIGH) {   // falling edge
  // fires exactly once per press
}
lastButtonState = buttonState;

Without this, holding a button for one second counts as thousands of presses. Every counter, toggle and "press to start" needs it.

Numericals

N8.1 — After how long does millis() roll over? And micros()?

millis(): 2^32 ms = 4,294,967,296 ms = 4,294,967 s = 49.71 days → ≈ 49.7 days micros(): 2^32 µs = 4294.97 s = ≈ 71.6 minutes

N8.2 — A variable storing millis() is declared int. After how long does it break?

A signed 16-bit int holds up to 32,767 32,767 ms = 32.77 seconds After that it goes negative and all timing logic fails

N8.3 — The deck's LED fade uses step 5 and delay(30). How many times per second is a button polled in that loop?

Steps per direction = 255/5 = 51 Full cycle = 2 × 51 × 30 ms = 3060 ms Button polled once per full cycle → 0.33 times per second i.e. a press shorter than 3 seconds can be missed entirely

N8.4 — A non-blocking loop runs 20,000 times per second. How many times is a button sampled during a 30 ms press?

Loop period = 1/20000 = 50 µs Samples in 30 ms = 30,000 µs / 50 µs = 600 samples Compare with the blocking version above: 600 vs possibly 0

Coding scenarios

PYQ   Deck slide 47  ·  Type P  ·  10 marks

Pushbutton with millis() and micros()

Code an Arduino board to read a pushbutton connected to a digital input to display millis() when ON and display micros() when OFF. Blink an LED connected to a digital output with 500 ms delay.

Model answer — full exam format

Aim

To demonstrate the Arduino timing functions by blinking an LED at 500 ms intervals while reporting elapsed time in milliseconds or microseconds according to the state of a pushbutton.

Components

Arduino Uno, pushbutton, LED with 220 Ω resistor, pull-up resistor (or the internal pull-up), connecting wires.

Circuit connections

Arduino pinConnected to
D7Pushbutton, other side to GND, pull-up enabled
D13LED through 220 Ω

Timing functions used

FunctionPurpose
delay(ms)Pauses the program for the given milliseconds; 1000 ms = 1 s
delayMicroseconds(us)Delays for a much shorter time; 1000 µs = 1 ms
millis()Milliseconds since the microcontroller was turned on or reset
micros()Microseconds since the program started

Working

  1. Serial communication is initialised at 9600 baud; pin 13 is set as output and pin 7 as input.
  2. The LED is switched HIGH, held 500 ms, switched LOW and held 500 ms, giving a 1 Hz blink.
  3. The pushbutton on pin 7 is read with digitalRead.
  4. With a pull-up arrangement the pin idles HIGH and reads LOW when pressed.
  5. If pressed, micros() is printed with the label micros()=.
  6. If not pressed, millis() is printed with the label millis()=.
  7. Both functions are maintained by a hardware timer running continuously in the background.
  8. The cycle repeats indefinitely.

Flowchart

Program

#define LED 13
int buttonState = 0;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(LED, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(7, INPUT);
}

void loop() {
  digitalWrite(LED, HIGH);
  delay(500);
  digitalWrite(LED, LOW);
  delay(500);

  buttonState = digitalRead(7);

  if (buttonState == LOW) {           // pressed
    Serial.write("micros()=");
    Serial.println(micros());
  } else {                            // not pressed
    Serial.write("millis()=");
    Serial.println(millis());
  }
}

Result

The LED blinks at 500 ms intervals, and the serial monitor displays elapsed microseconds while the button is pressed and elapsed milliseconds while it is released.

The paragraph that lifts the mark

Limitation and improvement: because both delay(500) calls are blocking, the button is sampled only once per second, so any press shorter than that is missed entirely. delay() is a busy-wait — the CPU spins uselessly and cannot execute digitalRead during the pause. The correct solution is the millis() pattern: record a timestamp and test millis() - previousMillis >= 500 on every pass of the loop, leaving the processor free to read the button continuously.

Q8.1   Type P  ·  the core technique

Non-blocking blink with press counting

Blink an LED every 500 ms and simultaneously count button presses on pin 2, printing the running count. The program must not use delay() and must not miss any press.

Solution Q8.1

Working

  1. millis() returns elapsed time since reset and, unlike delay(), does not block execution.
  2. previousMillis stores the instant the LED last changed state.
  3. Elapsed time is tested as currentMillis - previousMillis >= 500. Subtraction is used rather than comparison against an absolute target so the test survives the 49.7-day rollover.
  4. When the interval elapses, the timestamp is updated and the LED toggled with ledState = !ledState.
  5. The button is read on every pass, because nothing blocks the loop.
  6. A HIGH-to-LOW transition is detected by comparing with the previous reading — edge detection ensures one press gives one count.
  7. All timing variables are unsigned long, since millis() would overflow a 16-bit int in 32.7 seconds.
const int LED    = 13;
const int BUTTON = 2;
const unsigned long BLINK_INTERVAL = 500;

unsigned long previousMillis = 0;
int ledState = LOW;
int lastButtonState = HIGH;      // idles HIGH with pull-up
unsigned int count = 0;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(LED, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(BUTTON, INPUT_PULLUP);
}

void loop() {
  unsigned long currentMillis = millis();

  // --- Task 1: blink without blocking ---
  if (currentMillis - previousMillis >= BLINK_INTERVAL) {
    previousMillis = currentMillis;
    ledState = !ledState;
    digitalWrite(LED, ledState);
  }

  // --- Task 2: count presses, checked every pass ---
  int buttonState = digitalRead(BUTTON);

  if (buttonState == LOW && lastButtonState == HIGH) {   // falling edge
    count++;
    Serial.print("Press count = ");
    Serial.println(count);
  }
  lastButtonState = buttonState;
}

Result: the LED blinks continuously while every press is counted, because no blocking delay prevents the button from being read.

Name the technique in your answer

This structure — loop() runs freely while each task checks whether it is due — is cooperative multitasking, and it is how multiple tasks run on a microcontroller without an RTOS.

Q8.2   Type P  ·  multi-task

Three independent tasks at three different rates

Run three tasks concurrently in one loop with no delay(): an LED blinking every 200 ms, a sensor sampled every 500 ms, and a serial report every 2 seconds.

Solution Q8.2
const int LED    = 13;
const int SENSOR = A0;

const unsigned long T_BLINK  = 200;
const unsigned long T_SAMPLE = 500;
const unsigned long T_REPORT = 2000;

unsigned long lastBlink = 0, lastSample = 0, lastReport = 0;

int  ledState = LOW;
long sum = 0;
int  n = 0;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(LED, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  unsigned long now = millis();

  // Task 1 - blink at 200 ms
  if (now - lastBlink >= T_BLINK) {
    lastBlink = now;
    ledState = !ledState;
    digitalWrite(LED, ledState);
  }

  // Task 2 - sample at 500 ms and accumulate
  if (now - lastSample >= T_SAMPLE) {
    lastSample = now;
    sum += analogRead(SENSOR);
    n++;
  }

  // Task 3 - report the average every 2 s
  if (now - lastReport >= T_REPORT) {
    lastReport = now;
    if (n > 0) {
      float avgV = ((sum / (float)n) * 5.0) / 1023.0;
      Serial.print("avg of "); Serial.print(n);
      Serial.print(" samples = "); Serial.print(avgV, 3);
      Serial.println(" V");
      sum = 0; n = 0;
    }
  }
}
Why this is impossible with delay()

The three intervals — 200, 500 and 2000 ms — are not multiples of one another in a way any single delay() could satisfy. Each task owns its own lastXxx timestamp, and each independently decides whether it is due. Adding a fourth task costs one more variable and one more if.

The scaling rule: the loop must complete faster than the shortest interval. Here it runs in microseconds against a 200 ms shortest task, so there is enormous margin.

Q8.3   Type P  ·  timeout

Vending machine coin timeout

A vending machine waits up to 30 seconds for enough coins. Each coin pulse on pin 2 adds ₹5. If the total reaches ₹20 the product is dispensed; if the timeout expires, all coins are refunded. Display the countdown continuously.

Solution Q8.3
const int coinPin    = 2;
const int dispensePin= 7;
const int refundPin  = 8;

const int PRICE       = 20;
const int COIN_VALUE  = 5;
const unsigned long TIMEOUT = 30000;   // 30 seconds

int  credit = 0;
unsigned long firstCoinTime = 0;
bool waiting = false;
int  lastCoinState = HIGH;
unsigned long lastDisplay = 0;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(coinPin, INPUT_PULLUP);
  pinMode(dispensePin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(refundPin,   OUTPUT);
  Serial.println("Insert coins - price Rs.20");
}

void loop() {
  unsigned long now = millis();

  // --- coin detection by edge, checked every pass ---
  int coinState = digitalRead(coinPin);
  if (coinState == LOW && lastCoinState == HIGH) {
    credit += COIN_VALUE;
    if (!waiting) { waiting = true; firstCoinTime = now; }
    Serial.print("Credit = Rs."); Serial.println(credit);
  }
  lastCoinState = coinState;

  // --- enough money: dispense ---
  if (credit >= PRICE) {
    Serial.println("Dispensing product");
    digitalWrite(dispensePin, HIGH);
    delay(500);                                  // brief actuator pulse
    digitalWrite(dispensePin, LOW);
    if (credit > PRICE) {
      Serial.print("Change Rs."); Serial.println(credit - PRICE);
    }
    credit = 0; waiting = false;
  }

  // --- timeout: refund ---
  if (waiting && (now - firstCoinTime >= TIMEOUT)) {
    Serial.print("TIMEOUT - refunding Rs."); Serial.println(credit);
    digitalWrite(refundPin, HIGH);
    delay(500);
    digitalWrite(refundPin, LOW);
    credit = 0; waiting = false;
  }

  // --- countdown display, twice per second ---
  if (waiting && now - lastDisplay >= 500) {
    lastDisplay = now;
    Serial.print("Time left = ");
    Serial.print((TIMEOUT - (now - firstCoinTime)) / 1000);
    Serial.println(" s");
  }
}

The timeout pattern: record the start instant, then test now - startTime >= TIMEOUT. This is the same subtraction pattern as the blink, used for a deadline instead of a repeat.

Why the countdown needs non-blocking code: a delay(30000) would make the machine deaf to coins for the whole waiting period — exactly the opposite of what is required.

Design link: this is the deck's Automatic Chocolate Vending Machine case study, whose specification says the machine waits a maximum of 30 s for coins and delivers within 60 s.

Q8.4   Type P  ·  measurement

Reaction-time tester

Build a reaction timer. After a random delay the LED lights; the user presses a button as fast as possible. Measure and report the reaction time in milliseconds, and keep the best score.

Solution Q8.4
const int LED    = 13;
const int BUTTON = 2;

unsigned long bestTime = 999999;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(LED, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(BUTTON, INPUT_PULLUP);
  randomSeed(analogRead(A0));         // seed from a floating analog pin
  Serial.println("Reaction tester - press when the LED lights");
}

void loop() {
  digitalWrite(LED, LOW);
  delay(random(2000, 6000));          // unpredictable wait

  // false-start check
  if (digitalRead(BUTTON) == LOW) {
    Serial.println("FALSE START - wait for the light");
    delay(2000);
    return;
  }

  digitalWrite(LED, HIGH);
  unsigned long startTime = millis();       // the instant the light appears

  while (digitalRead(BUTTON) == HIGH) {     // wait for the press
    if (millis() - startTime > 5000) {      // give up after 5 s
      Serial.println("Too slow - no response");
      digitalWrite(LED, LOW);
      return;
    }
  }

  unsigned long reaction = millis() - startTime;
  digitalWrite(LED, LOW);

  Serial.print("Reaction time = "); Serial.print(reaction); Serial.println(" ms");
  if (reaction < bestTime) {
    bestTime = reaction;
    Serial.println("NEW BEST!");
  }
  Serial.print("Best so far   = "); Serial.print(bestTime); Serial.println(" ms");

  delay(3000);
}
Two techniques worth naming

Interval measurement: capture millis() at the start, capture it again at the end, subtract. The same pattern used to time analogRead in Unit 3.

Why randomSeed(analogRead(A0)): a floating analog pin picks up electrical noise, giving a genuinely different seed on each power-up. Without it, random() produces the identical sequence every time and the delay becomes predictable.

Why micros() would be better here: human reaction is 150–300 ms, so millisecond resolution is adequate — but for anything under about 10 ms you would need micros().

Q8.5   Type P  ·  frequency measurement

Tachometer using micros()

Measure the rotational speed of a motor from a slotted-disc sensor on pin 2, using micros() to time between pulses. Display RPM, updating twice per second.

Solution Q8.5
const int sensorPin = 2;
const int SLOTS = 1;               // pulses per revolution

volatile unsigned long lastPulse = 0;
volatile unsigned long period    = 0;   // microseconds between pulses
volatile bool haveReading = false;

unsigned long lastDisplay = 0;

void pulseISR() {
  unsigned long now = micros();
  if (now - lastPulse > 1000) {        // reject bounce shorter than 1 ms
    period    = now - lastPulse;
    lastPulse = now;
    haveReading = true;
  }
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(sensorPin, INPUT_PULLUP);
  attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(sensorPin), pulseISR, FALLING);
}

void loop() {
  if (millis() - lastDisplay >= 500) {
    lastDisplay = millis();

    noInterrupts();                       // atomic copy of a multi-byte volatile
    unsigned long p = period;
    bool ok = haveReading;
    interrupts();

    if (ok && p > 0 && micros() - lastPulse < 1000000UL) {
      float rpm = 60000000.0 / (p * SLOTS);   // 60e6 us per minute
      Serial.print("Period = "); Serial.print(p);
      Serial.print(" us   RPM = "); Serial.println(rpm, 0);
    } else {
      Serial.println("Stopped");
    }
  }
}
The derivation and the two subtleties

RPM formula: one revolution takes period microseconds. There are 60 × 106 µs in a minute, so RPM = 60,000,000 / (period × slots).

Why noInterrupts() around the copy: period is a 32-bit variable read in four 8-bit operations. If the ISR fires midway, you get half the old value and half the new one — a torn read. Disabling interrupts briefly makes the copy atomic.

Why the stopped check: if no pulse has arrived for a second, the last measured period is stale and would report a false RPM forever.

Q8.6   Type D  ·  traffic control

Four-way traffic light controller

Design a traffic light controller for two directions with green 8 s, yellow 2 s and red accordingly, plus a pedestrian request button that shortens the current green to a minimum of 3 s. No delay() may be used.

Solution Q8.6
// Direction A
const int A_RED = 2, A_YEL = 3, A_GRN = 4;
// Direction B
const int B_RED = 5, B_YEL = 6, B_GRN = 7;
const int PED_BTN = 8, PED_LED = 9;

enum State { A_GREEN, A_YELLOW, B_GREEN, B_YELLOW };
State state = A_GREEN;

const unsigned long T_GREEN = 8000, T_YELLOW = 2000, T_MIN_GREEN = 3000;

unsigned long stateStart = 0;
bool pedRequest = false;
int  lastBtn = HIGH;

void applyLights() {
  digitalWrite(A_RED, state == B_GREEN || state == B_YELLOW);
  digitalWrite(A_YEL, state == A_YELLOW);
  digitalWrite(A_GRN, state == A_GREEN);
  digitalWrite(B_RED, state == A_GREEN || state == A_YELLOW);
  digitalWrite(B_YEL, state == B_YELLOW);
  digitalWrite(B_GRN, state == B_GREEN);
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  int pins[] = {A_RED,A_YEL,A_GRN,B_RED,B_YEL,B_GRN,PED_LED};
  for (int i = 0; i < 7; i++) pinMode(pins[i], OUTPUT);
  pinMode(PED_BTN, INPUT_PULLUP);
  stateStart = millis();
  applyLights();
}

void loop() {
  unsigned long now = millis();
  unsigned long elapsed = now - stateStart;

  // pedestrian request, edge detected, sampled every pass
  int btn = digitalRead(PED_BTN);
  if (btn == LOW && lastBtn == HIGH) {
    pedRequest = true;
    digitalWrite(PED_LED, HIGH);
    Serial.println("Pedestrian request registered");
  }
  lastBtn = btn;

  unsigned long limit;
  switch (state) {
    case A_GREEN:
    case B_GREEN:
      // a request shortens green, but never below the safety minimum
      limit = pedRequest ? T_MIN_GREEN : T_GREEN;
      if (elapsed >= limit) {
        state = (state == A_GREEN) ? A_YELLOW : B_YELLOW;
        stateStart = now; applyLights();
      }
      break;

    case A_YELLOW:
    case B_YELLOW:
      if (elapsed >= T_YELLOW) {
        state = (state == A_YELLOW) ? B_GREEN : A_GREEN;
        stateStart = now; applyLights();
        pedRequest = false;
        digitalWrite(PED_LED, LOW);
      }
      break;
  }
}
Why this needs a state machine, not delays

A delay()-based traffic controller cannot respond to a pedestrian button, because it is asleep during every phase. Here the loop runs thousands of times per second, so the button is sampled continuously while the phase timing still runs from millis().

The pattern to name: a finite state machine with state, stateStart and a per-state duration. Every phase transition sets stateStart = now, which is the millis() pattern applied to a sequence rather than a repeat.

The safety constraint: the minimum green of 3 s prevents a pedestrian request from cutting traffic off dangerously fast — a real requirement in signal design, and worth stating.

UNIT 09

UART — Serial Communication

Slides 62–76  ·  Question types: T, P  ·  Weight: high

What UART is (slide 62)

UART stands for Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter. It transmits and receives serially, requiring two wires — the Tx and Rx pins.

Asynchronous — the defining property (slide 63)

UARTs have no clock signal and follow asynchronous data communication. Start and stop bits are added to the data packet for identifying the beginning and end of the packet, and are used instead of a clock signal.

In a synchronous link (SPI, I²C) a separate clock wire tells the receiver when to sample. UART has no such wire, so it embeds timing in the data itself and both ends must already agree on the speed. That agreement is the baud rate.

Baud rate (slide 64)

After detecting the start bit the UART begins reading the packet. A specific frequency called the baud rate, expressed in bits per second, measures the speed of transfer. Both the transmitting and receiving UART must work at the same baud rate — otherwise the receiver samples at the wrong instants and reads garbage.

tbit = 1 / baud rate   →   at 9600 baud, tbit = 104.17 µs

The parameters table (slide 65) — memorise it

ParameterSpecification
Wires used2
Maximum speed115200 baud
Synchronous?No
Serial?Yes
Max number of master1
Max number of slave1

The last pair matters: UART is strictly point-to-point.

How UART works (slide 66)

  1. Data is transmitted in serial from the data bus to the transmitting UART.
  2. The transmitting UART adds a start bit, a stop bit and a parity bit to the parallel data.
  3. The packet is transmitted serially from Tx to Rx.
  4. The Rx pin reads the data and converts it back to parallel by removing the other bits.

So a UART is a parallel-to-serial converter at the transmitter and serial-to-parallel at the receiver. Wiring note: Tx connects to Rx and Rx to Tx — the connection is crossed.

The frame format (slide 67) — draw this from memory

FieldLength
Start bit1
Data bits5 to 9
Parity bit0 or 1
Stop bits1 to 2

The line idles HIGH. The start bit is a transition to LOW — that falling edge wakes the receiver. Stop bits return the line HIGH, guaranteeing an edge is available for the next start bit.

Why "8N1 = 10 bits" is the number to remember

8N1 — 8 data bits, No parity, 1 stop bit — totals 10 bits per byte. Only 8 of those 10 are data, so UART carries 20 % framing overhead. At 9600 baud you get 9600/10 = 960 bytes per second, not 1200.

Parity — what it can and cannot do: the parity bit makes the total number of 1s even or odd, and the receiver recounts. It detects single-bit errors but cannot correct them, and fails entirely on a two-bit error because two flips restore the original parity.

UART in the Arduino (slide 70)

UART allows the ATmega chip to do serial communication while working on other tasks, through a 64-byte serial buffer. It communicates on digital pins 0 (RX) and 1 (TX) as well as with the computer via USB. If you use these functions you cannot also use pins 0 and 1 for digital input or output.

The Serial functions (slide 71)

FunctionWhat it does
if (Serial)Indicates whether the USB serial connection is open
Serial.available()Gets the number of bytes available for reading
Serial.begin()Sets the data rate in bits per second (baud)
Serial.end()Disables serial communication, freeing RX and TX for I/O
Serial.find()Reads from the buffer until the target is found
Serial.println()Prints as ASCII text followed by carriage return and newline
Serial.read()Reads incoming serial data
Serial.readString()Reads characters from the buffer into a String
Serial.write()Writes binary data — sent as a byte or series of bytes
Key points
  • print vs write: Serial.print(65) sends the text "65" (two characters); Serial.write(65) sends the raw byte 'A'. That is why the deck echoes with Serial.write(Serial.read()).
  • Serial.read() returns an int, not a char, and returns −1 when the buffer is empty. Always guard with Serial.available().
  • Serial.available() returns a count. if (Serial.available() >= 4) waits for four bytes — exactly what the CAT password question needs.
  • The 64-byte buffer is why UART does not block; overflow silently loses bytes.
  • The Serial Monitor appends a newline or carriage return — a leftover '\n' corrupts the next comparison. Flush it.
  • Baud rate generation is a timer function — slide 35 listed it. See N9.4.

SoftwareSerial (slides 74–76)

The SoftwareSerial library allows serial communication on other digital pins, using software to replicate the hardwired RX and TX lines. Multiple software ports are possible up to 115200 bps, useful when communicating with two or more serial-enabled devices.

Limitations (slide 74): maximum RX speed is 57600 bps · RX does not work on pin 13 · with multiple software ports, only one can receive at a time.

Why these limits exist: the CPU must sample every bit in software, so it cannot keep up at high speeds or watch two ports at once. Hardware UART has dedicated silicon and none of these problems.

Functions (slide 75): SoftwareSerial(), available(), begin(), overflow(), peek(), read(), print(), listen(), write(). listen() selects which software port is currently active for receiving.

UART vs SPI vs I²C — bridges to Unit 12

UARTSPII²C
Wires2 (Tx, Rx)4 (MOSI, MISO, SCK, SS)2 (SDA, SCL)
ClockNone — asynchronousSynchronousSynchronous
Max speed115200 baud10+ MHz100/400 kHz
Masters11Multiple
Slaves1Many (one SS each)Up to 127 (addressed)
DuplexFullFullHalf

Numericals — every variation

N9.1 — A UART at 9600 baud, 8N1. Find bit time, frame time and throughput.

Bit time = 1/9600 = 104.17 µs Frame = 1 start + 8 data + 0 parity + 1 stop = 10 bits Frame time= 10 × 104.17 µs = 1.0417 ms per byte Throughput= 9600/10 = 960 bytes per second (20 % overhead)

N9.2 — How long to transmit "EMBEDDED" at 9600 baud, 8N1?

"EMBEDDED" = 8 characters = 8 bytes Time = 8 × 1.0417 ms = 8.33 ms

N9.3 — A frame has 7 data bits, even parity, 2 stop bits at 4800 baud. Find frame length and throughput.

Frame = 1 + 7 + 1 + 2 = 11 bits Bit time = 1/4800 = 208.33 µs Frame time = 11 × 208.33 = 2.29 ms Throughput = 4800/11 = 436 bytes per second

N9.4 — The ATmega328 sets baud via UBRR = (f_osc/(16 × baud)) − 1. Find the value for 9600 at 16 MHz and the resulting error.

UBRR = (16 × 10^6 /(16 × 9600)) − 1 = 104.17 − 1 = 103.17 → UBRR = 103 Actual baud = 16 × 10^6 /(16 × 104) = 9615.4 bps Error = (9615.4 − 9600)/9600 × 100 = 0.16 % Well within the ~2 % a UART tolerates, which is why 9600 works reliably.

N9.5 — At 115200 baud 8N1, find bit time, frame time and throughput.

Bit time = 1/115200 = 8.68 µs Frame time = 10 × 8.68 = 86.8 µs Throughput = 115200/10 = 11,520 bytes per second (12× faster than 9600)

N9.6 — A program prints a 30-character line every loop at 9600 baud. What is the maximum loop rate?

30 bytes × 1.0417 ms = 31.25 ms per line Max loop rate = 1/0.03125 = 32 Hz The serial link, not the ADC, is the bottleneck. At 115200 baud: 30 × 86.8 µs = 2.6 ms → 384 Hz

N9.7 — How long can the 64-byte buffer hold incoming data at 9600 baud before overflowing?

64 bytes × 1.0417 ms = 66.7 ms If your loop takes longer than 67 ms between Serial.read() calls, bytes are lost silently. This is why long delay() calls break serial reception.

Coding scenarios

Q9.1   Deck slide 72  ·  Type P

Serial echo

Print data received through serial communication back onto the serial monitor of the Arduino.

Solution Q9.1
void setup() {
   Serial.begin(9600);   //set up serial library baud rate to 9600
}

void loop() {
   if(Serial.available())   //if bytes are available for reading
   {
      Serial.print("I received:");     //print I received
      Serial.write(Serial.read());     //send what you read
   }
}

Why write and not print: Serial.write() sends the raw byte, so typing a echoes a. Using Serial.print(Serial.read()) would echo 97, the ASCII code, because print converts numbers to text.

Q9.2   Deck slide 73  ·  Type P  ·  10 marks

Serial-controlled LED

Write an Arduino program for a serial interface that switches an LED on when the character 'a' is received on the serial port, and off otherwise, printing the status on the serial monitor.

Model answer — full exam format

Aim

To control a digital output remotely through UART serial communication, using characters received from the serial monitor as commands.

Components

Arduino Uno, LED with 220 Ω resistor, USB cable, serial monitor set to 9600 baud.

Circuit connections

Arduino pinConnected to
D13LED anode through 220 Ω
GNDLED cathode
D0 / D1RX / TX — used internally by Serial via USB

Working

  1. Serial.begin(9600) initialises the UART at 9600 baud. The monitor must match, since UART is asynchronous with no shared clock.
  2. Pin 13 is configured as an output for the LED.
  3. "Ready" is printed to indicate the system can receive commands.
  4. Serial.available() returns the number of bytes waiting in the 64-byte receive buffer.
  5. When a byte is present, Serial.read() retrieves it into inByte.
  6. The byte is compared with the character literal 'a', ASCII 97.
  7. On a match the LED is switched HIGH and "LED - On" is printed.
  8. Otherwise the LED is switched LOW and "LED - off" is printed.
  9. The hardware buffer captures characters even while the processor executes other instructions.

Flowchart

Program

int inByte;                    // stores the incoming command

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);          // UART at 9600 baud
  pinMode(13, OUTPUT);         // LED pin
  Serial.println("Ready");     // ready to receive commands
}

void loop() {
  if (Serial.available() > 0) {        // a byte is ready to receive
    inByte = Serial.read();

    if (inByte == 'a') {               // byte is 'a'
      digitalWrite(13, HIGH);
      Serial.println("LED - On");
    }
    else {                             // byte isn't 'a'
      digitalWrite(13, LOW);
      Serial.println("LED - off");
    }
  }
}

Result

The LED switches on when 'a' is sent from the serial monitor and off for any other character, with the status reported back over the same serial link.

Points that earn the extra marks
  • Serial.available() returns the count of bytes in the 64-byte hardware buffer, which is what lets the UART receive while the CPU does other work.
  • 'a' versus "a" — single quotes give a one-byte character literal (ASCII 97); double quotes give a two-byte string. Serial.read() returns an int, so it must be compared against a character literal.
  • Baud must match at both ends — no clock wire exists, so a mismatch produces garbage.
  • Line-ending caveat — the monitor may append \n, which reads as a non-'a' character and immediately switches the LED off. The deck's alternative if(Serial.find("a")) avoids this.
  • Pins 0 and 1 are unavailable for digital I/O while Serial is in use.
Q9.3   Type P  ·  command parser

Multi-command serial terminal

Build a serial command interface: a = LED on, b = LED off, s = report status, t = report temperature. Ignore line endings and report unknown commands.

Solution Q9.3
const int ledPin  = 13;
const int tempPin = A0;
int inByte;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(ledPin, OUTPUT);
  Serial.println("Ready. Commands: a=ON  b=OFF  s=STATUS  t=TEMP");
}

void loop() {
  if (Serial.available() > 0) {
    inByte = Serial.read();

    switch (inByte) {
      case 'a':
        digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH);
        Serial.println("LED - On");
        break;

      case 'b':
        digitalWrite(ledPin, LOW);
        Serial.println("LED - off");
        break;

      case 's':
        Serial.print("LED status = ");
        Serial.println(digitalRead(ledPin) ? "ON" : "OFF");
        break;

      case 't': {
        int   adc = analogRead(tempPin);
        float t   = (adc * 4.88) / 10.0;      // LM35
        Serial.print("Temperature = "); Serial.print(t, 1);
        Serial.println(" C");
        break;
      }

      case '\n':
      case '\r':
        break;                                 // ignore line endings

      default:
        Serial.print("Unknown command: ");
        Serial.println((char)inByte);
        break;
    }
  }
}
The line-ending trap — this exact problem appears in CAT Q3

The Serial Monitor appends \n (Newline), \r\n (Both NL & CR), or nothing, depending on its dropdown. Without the '\n' and '\r' cases, every command produces a bonus "Unknown command".

Two fixes exist: handle the cases as here, or flush the buffer after reading — while (Serial.available()) Serial.read(); — which is what the CAT password answer does.

Q9.4   Type P  ·  multi-byte parsing

Set a PWM value from a typed number

Accept a multi-digit number typed on the serial monitor (0–255) and use it to set an LED's brightness, validating the range and reporting the resulting duty cycle.

Solution Q9.4
const int ledPin = 9;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(ledPin, OUTPUT);
  Serial.println("Enter a PWM value 0-255 then press Enter");
}

void loop() {
  if (Serial.available() > 0) {

    int value = Serial.parseInt();      // reads digits until a non-digit or timeout

    while (Serial.available()) Serial.read();    // flush the line ending

    if (value >= 0 && value <= 255) {
      analogWrite(ledPin, value);

      float duty = (value / 255.0) * 100.0;
      float vavg = (duty / 100.0) * 5.0;

      Serial.print("PWM set to ");  Serial.print(value);
      Serial.print("   duty = ");   Serial.print(duty, 1);
      Serial.print(" %   Vavg = "); Serial.print(vavg, 2);
      Serial.println(" V");
    } else {
      Serial.print("Out of range: "); Serial.println(value);
    }
  }
}

Why parseInt() and not read(): Serial.read() returns one character. Typing 128 sends three separate bytes '1', '2', '8'. parseInt() collects consecutive digit characters and converts them to a single integer.

The timeout: parseInt() waits up to 1 second (settable with Serial.setTimeout()) for more digits, which is why a slow typist can get a truncated value.

Manual alternative for an exam where libraries feel risky:

value = 0;
while (Serial.available()) {
  char c = Serial.read();
  if (c >= '0' && c <= '9') value = value * 10 + (c - '0');
}

The expression c - '0' converts the ASCII digit character to its numeric value — worth knowing.

Q9.5   Deck slide 76  ·  Type P

SoftwareSerial bridge between two ports

Write a program that receives from the hardware serial and sends to a software serial port, and receives from the software serial and sends to the hardware serial, running the two at different baud rates.

Solution Q9.5
#include <SoftwareSerial.h>

SoftwareSerial mySerial(10, 11); // RX, TX

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(57600);           // hardware serial to the PC
  while (!Serial) {
    ;   // wait for serial port to connect. Needed for native USB port only
  }
  mySerial.begin(4800);          // set the data rate for the SoftwareSerial port
  mySerial.println("Hello, world?");
}

void loop() {                    // run over and over
  if (mySerial.available()) {
    Serial.write(mySerial.read());     // software -> hardware
  }
  if (Serial.available()) {
    mySerial.write(Serial.read());     // hardware -> software
  }
}
Why a bridge is needed, and its limits

The Uno has only one hardware UART, already used by the USB link. A GPS module plus a Bluetooth module needs three ports, so SoftwareSerial bit-bangs the extras.

The different baud rates are deliberate: 57600 to the fast PC link, 4800 to a slow peripheral such as a GPS. The bridge translates between them.

Limits to state: maximum software RX speed is 57600 bps; RX does not work on pin 13; with multiple software ports only one can receive at a time, selected by listen(). These exist because the CPU samples every bit in software.

Q9.6   Type D  ·  telemetry

CSV data logger over serial

Design a three-channel data logger that streams timestamped comma-separated readings over UART at the highest sustainable rate, and reports the achieved sample rate once per second.

Solution Q9.6
const int CH[3] = {A0, A1, A2};

unsigned long lastRate = 0;
unsigned int  samples  = 0;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);                 // fastest standard rate
  Serial.println("time_ms,ch0,ch1,ch2");   // CSV header
}

void loop() {
  unsigned long t = millis();

  Serial.print(t);
  for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    Serial.print(',');
    Serial.print(analogRead(CH[i]));
  }
  Serial.println();
  samples++;

  if (t - lastRate >= 1000) {
    lastRate = t;
    Serial.print("# rate = "); Serial.print(samples);
    Serial.println(" samples/s");
    samples = 0;
  }
}
Working out the bottleneck — the analysis is the answer

Each line is roughly 22 characters (timestamp + three values + commas + CRLF).

BaudTime per lineMax rate
960022 × 1.042 ms = 22.9 ms~43 Hz
11520022 × 86.8 µs = 1.91 ms~523 Hz

Three analogRead calls cost only 3 × 100 µs = 300 µs. So at 9600 baud the serial link is 76× slower than the ADC — the transmission, not the measurement, limits the system. Raising the baud rate is the single most effective optimisation.

Why CSV: the output pastes directly into a spreadsheet, which is what makes this a practical data acquisition system.

UNIT 10

Sensors, Actuators and the Servo Motor

Slides 77–103  ·  Question types: P, D  ·  Weight: highest  ·  Contains CAT Q4

Slides 77–96 are an image gallery of sensor and actuator types. As you page through them, ask one question of each image: is this an input (sensor) or an output (actuator), and is its signal analog or digital? That is the only classification the exam needs.

The vocabulary

A transducer converts one form of energy into another. A sensor is an input transducer — physical quantity to electrical signal. An actuator is an output transducer — electrical signal to physical action.

Every embedded system is sensor → processor → actuator. That is the block diagram of every design answer.

Classifying sensors — three ways

Analog sensorDigital sensor
OutputContinuous voltageHIGH/LOW or a coded pulse
Read withanalogRead()digitalRead() or pulseIn()
PinsA0–A5 onlyAny digital pin
ExamplesLM35, LDR, potentiometer, soil moistureIR obstacle, PIR, limit switch, ultrasonic

By power requirement: active sensors need external excitation (LDR, strain gauge, LVDT, thermistor); passive or self-generating sensors produce their own output (thermocouple, piezoelectric, photovoltaic).

By measured quantity: temperature, light, distance, pressure, humidity, gas, motion, force, position.

The sensor interfacing table

SensorOutputRead withConversion
LM35Analog, 10 mV/°CanalogRead(adc×4.88)/10
TMP36Analog, 10 mV/°C + 500 mV offsetanalogRead(adc×4.88−500)/10
LDRAnalog, non-linearanalogReadThreshold
PotentiometerAnalog 0–5 V linearanalogReadmap()
IR obstacleDigital, LOW on detectdigitalReadDirect
PIR motionDigital, HIGH on motiondigitalReadDirect
UltrasonicPulse widthpulseInduration/29/2
DHT11 / DHT22Coded digital protocolLibraryLibrary returns values
The polarity trap

IR obstacle sensors go LOW when they detect. PIR motion sensors go HIGH. Getting this backwards inverts your entire program. CAT Q4 uses IR — so LOW means vehicle present.

The actuator interfacing table

ActuatorDrive methodCritical note
LEDdigitalWrite / analogWriteAlways through a 220 Ω resistor
BuzzerdigitalWrite / tone()tone() uses Timer2 → kills PWM on pins 3, 11
Servo motorServo libraryNot analogWrite — see below
DC motorPWM + transistor or H-bridgeNever direct — exceeds 40 mA
Stepper motorStepper library + driverNeeds a driver IC
RelaydigitalWrite + driver transistorFor mains or high-current loads
LCD 16×2LiquidCrystal libraryConsumes 6 digital pins

The 40 mA rule from Unit 1 governs this entire table. Any actuator drawing more than ~20 mA must be switched, not driven. That single sentence justifies every transistor, relay and H-bridge in every design answer.

The servo motor

A servo is not a plain motor. It is a closed-loop position control system in one package.

Pulse widthAngleDuty cycle
1.0 ms0°5 %
1.5 ms90°7.5 %
2.0 ms180°10 %

The servo expects a pulse every 20 ms (50 Hz), with the angle encoded in the pulse width.

Why you cannot use analogWrite for a servo

analogWrite runs at ~490 Hz, a period of about 2 ms. A servo needs a period of 20 ms — ten times longer. The frequencies do not match, so analogWrite can never produce a valid servo signal.

That is exactly why the Servo library exists, and why it takes over the 16-bit Timer1 — which disables PWM on pins 9 and 10.

Power warning: an SG90 draws 100–250 mA moving and can stall at 700 mA, far above the 40 mA per-pin limit. Power it from the 5 V rail with a common ground and only signal it from the Arduino pin.

The Knob circuit (slides 97–99)

A potentiometer (a knob) is used as an input device to control a parameter such as the angle of a servo motor. The potentiometer acts as a variable resistor, changing its resistance with position and providing an analog voltage output.

How it works, per the deck: (1) the potentiometer's analog output is read via an analog pin; (2) the Arduino converts this value (0–1023) to a meaningful output, such as an angle for the servo (0–180°); (3) the servo moves to the corresponding angle. Commonly used in robotic applications and controls where manual adjustment is needed.

#include <Servo.h>

Servo myServo;
const int potPin = A0;

void setup() {
  myServo.attach(9);
}

void loop() {
  int val   = analogRead(potPin);            // 0..1023
  int angle = map(val, 0, 1023, 0, 180);     // scale to 0..180 degrees
  myServo.write(angle);
  delay(15);                                 // let the servo reach position
}

The Sweep circuit (slides 100–101)

The Arduino sends a signal making the servo continuously move back and forth (sweep) between two angular positions, simulating continuous motion — useful for testing, demonstrating, or applications like oscillating fans or robotic arms. The servo starts at 0° and gradually moves to 180°, pausing slightly after each step to ensure smooth movement, then reverses.

#include <Servo.h>

Servo myservo;      // create servo object to control a servo
int pos = 0;        // variable to store the servo position

void setup() {
  myservo.attach(9);          // attaches the servo on pin 9
}

void loop() {
  for (pos = 0; pos <= 180; pos += 1) {   // 0 to 180 degrees, 1 degree steps
    myservo.write(pos);                   // tell servo to go to position
    delay(15);                            // wait 15ms for the servo to reach it
  }
  for (pos = 180; pos >= 0; pos -= 1) {   // 180 back to 0 degrees
    myservo.write(pos);
    delay(15);
  }
}

Note the structural identity with Unit 6's LED fade — two for loops, up and down, with a per-step delay. Compute its timing: 180 steps × 15 ms = 2.7 s per direction, 5.4 s per full sweep.

The Servo library

CallPurpose
myServo.attach(pin)Attach to a pin (any digital pin)
myServo.write(angle)0 to 180 degrees
myServo.writeMicroseconds(us)Fine control, 1000–2000 µs
myServo.read()Returns the last commanded angle
myServo.detach()Release the pin

Numericals

N10.1 — A servo signal has 20 ms period, 1.5 ms on-time. Find duty cycle and frequency.

Duty = (1.5/20) × 100 = 7.5 % Freq = 1/0.020 = 50 Hz

N10.2 — Find the pulse width for 45° and for 135°.

Range: 1.0 ms at 0° to 2.0 ms at 180° → 1 ms spread over 180° Per degree = 1000 µs/180 = 5.56 µs 45° : 1000 + 45 × 5.56 = 1250 µs = 1.25 ms 135° : 1000 + 135 × 5.56 = 1750 µs = 1.75 ms

N10.3 — A potentiometer reads 768. What servo angle results from map(val,0,1023,0,180)?

angle = (768/1023) × 180 = 135° Corresponding pulse width = 1.75 ms (from N10.2)

N10.4 — Compute the total time for one full sweep cycle at delay(15) and 1° steps.

One direction = 181 steps × 15 ms = 2715 ms ≈ 2.7 s Full cycle = 2 × 2.7 = 5.4 s With 2° steps: 91 steps × 15 = 1.37 s per direction → 2.7 s per cycle

N10.5 — An SG90 draws 250 mA while moving. Can two be powered from the Arduino's 5 V pin?

Two servos = 500 mA Per-pin limit = 40 mA → signal only, never power ✓ (correct approach) Uno 5V pin from USB ≈ 500 mA total, shared with the board itself Marginal — use an external 5 V supply with a common ground. Stall current of 700 mA each would certainly brown out the board.

Coding scenarios

PYQ   CAT-1 Q4  ·  Type D  ·  10 marks

Automatic parking gate control system

Design an automatic parking gate control system using servo motor and IR sensor. If no vehicle is detected the parking gate should be closed (servo = 0°), else the gate should open (servo = 90°). The IR sensor should provide input to the servo motor. The gate should be open for 3 seconds and close automatically if the vehicle is not entering the gate, and simultaneously blink an LED when the gate is open.

Model answer — full exam format

Aim

To design a contactless automatic parking gate that opens a servo-actuated barrier when an IR sensor detects a vehicle, holds it open for three seconds with a blinking warning indicator, and closes it automatically once the vehicle has passed.

Components required

ComponentPurpose
Arduino Uno (ATmega328P)Control unit
IR obstacle sensorDetects vehicle presence; output LOW when detected
SG90 micro servoActuates the gate barrier — 0° closed, 90° open
LED + 220 Ω resistorVisual warning while the gate is open
5 V supplyPowers the servo and sensor

Circuit connections

Arduino pinConnected to
D2IR sensor output
D8LED anode through 220 Ω
D9Servo signal line
5V, GNDServo and sensor supply (common ground)

Working

  1. The servo is initialised to 0°, so the gate starts closed, and the LED is switched off.
  2. The IR sensor output on D2 is read continuously. An IR obstacle module pulls its output LOW when a vehicle reflects its beam.
  3. On detection, the servo is driven to 90° and the gate opens.
  4. The gate is held open for 3000 ms, measured with millis(), while the LED blinks at 250 ms intervals as a warning.
  5. After three seconds the sensor is read again. If it now reads HIGH, the vehicle has entered, so the servo returns to 0° and the LED is switched off.
  6. If the sensor still reads LOW, the vehicle has not yet passed, so the gate is held open at 90° and the LED remains on.
  7. When no vehicle is present the gate remains closed at 0° with the LED off.

Flowchart

Arduino program

#include <Servo.h>

Servo gateServo;

const int irPin    = 2;
const int ledPin   = 8;
const int servoPin = 9;

void setup() {
  pinMode(irPin, INPUT);
  pinMode(ledPin, OUTPUT);

  gateServo.attach(servoPin);

  gateServo.write(0);            // gate initially closed
  digitalWrite(ledPin, LOW);

  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
  int vehicleDetected = digitalRead(irPin);   // LOW = vehicle present

  if (vehicleDetected == LOW) {
    Serial.println("Vehicle Detected");

    gateServo.write(90);                      // open the gate

    // hold open for 3 seconds, blinking the LED as a warning
    unsigned long startTime = millis();
    while (millis() - startTime < 3000UL) {
      digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH);
      delay(250);
      digitalWrite(ledPin, LOW);
      delay(250);
    }

    if (digitalRead(irPin) == HIGH) {         // vehicle has entered
      gateServo.write(0);
      digitalWrite(ledPin, LOW);
      Serial.println("Gate Closed");
    } else {                                  // vehicle still waiting
      gateServo.write(90);
      digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH);
      Serial.println("Gate Remains Open");
    }
  }
  else {                                      // no vehicle
    gateServo.write(0);
    digitalWrite(ledPin, LOW);
  }

  delay(100);
}

Result

The gate opens to 90° when a vehicle is detected, blinks the warning LED for three seconds, and closes automatically to 0° once the vehicle has passed. It remains open while the vehicle is still present, and stays closed at 0° when no vehicle is detected.

The five points that lift this from a 7 to a 10
  1. State the sensor polarity and why — an IR obstacle module pulls its output LOW when its beam reflects off an object, so LOW means a vehicle is present. The question does not tell you this; showing you know it is a mark.
  2. Justify millis() for the 3-second hold — a single delay(3000) would freeze the LED; the millis() window lets the blink run inside the hold.
  3. Point at the re-check — the second digitalRead after three seconds is what implements "close automatically if the vehicle is not entering the gate", the question's exact wording.
  4. Servo current — an SG90 draws 100–250 mA, exceeding the 40 mA per-pin limit, so it is powered from the 5 V rail with a common ground and only signalled from D9.
  5. Why the Servo library and not analogWrite — a servo needs a 20 ms period; analogWrite gives ~490 Hz, a 2 ms period. The library uses Timer1, which is why PWM on pins 9 and 10 becomes unavailable.
Honest note on this code

The official key uses delay(250) inside the millis() window, reproduced here so it matches what you are marked against. It is a hybrid — the outer 3-second window is non-blocking in style while the inner blink still blocks in 250 ms chunks. Write it this way in the exam. If asked to improve the design, the improvement is to track the blink with its own previousMillis.

Common mistakes on this question
MistakeConsequence
analogWrite(9, 90) for the servoWrong frequency — servo will not move correctly
HIGH means vehicle detectedEntire logic inverted
delay(3000) for the holdLED cannot blink — fails the requirement
No gateServo.write(0) in setup()Gate starts at an undefined angle
No re-check after 3 secondsFails "close automatically if not entering"
Powering the servo from the signal pinExceeds 40 mA; brownouts and resets
Forgetting #include <Servo.h>Will not compile
Q10.1   Deck slides 97–99  ·  Type P

Knob — servo angle from a potentiometer

Use a potentiometer as a knob to set a servo's angle, and additionally display the ADC value, the resulting angle and the equivalent pulse width on the serial monitor.

Solution Q10.1
#include <Servo.h>

Servo myServo;
const int potPin   = A0;
const int servoPin = 9;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  myServo.attach(servoPin);
}

void loop() {
  int val   = analogRead(potPin);            // 0..1023
  int angle = map(val, 0, 1023, 0, 180);     // scale to 0..180 degrees
  myServo.write(angle);

  // 0 deg = 1000 us, 180 deg = 2000 us
  int pulseUs = map(angle, 0, 180, 1000, 2000);

  Serial.print("ADC = ");     Serial.print(val);
  Serial.print("  angle = "); Serial.print(angle);
  Serial.print(" deg  pulse = "); Serial.print(pulseUs);
  Serial.print(" us  duty = ");
  Serial.print((pulseUs / 20000.0) * 100.0, 2);   // 20 ms period
  Serial.println(" %");

  delay(15);                                 // let the servo reach position
}

The sanity check: pot at centre → ADC ≈ 512 → angle ≈ 90° → pulse ≈ 1500 µs → duty ≈ 7.5 %. All four numbers must agree.

Why delay(15): a servo takes time to move physically. Commanding a new angle before it arrives produces jerky motion — the deck calls this "pausing slightly after each step to ensure smooth movement."

Q10.2   Type D  ·  sensor to actuator

Temperature-controlled ventilation flap

A servo controls a ventilation flap. It must stay closed (0°) below 25 °C, fully open (90°) at or above 40 °C, and open proportionally between. Display temperature and flap angle.

Solution Q10.2
#include <Servo.h>

Servo flapServo;
const int tempPin  = A0;
const int servoPin = 9;

const float T_CLOSED = 25.0;
const float T_OPEN   = 40.0;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  flapServo.attach(servoPin);
  flapServo.write(0);
}

void loop() {
  int   adc   = analogRead(tempPin);
  float tempC = (adc * 4.88) / 10.0;         // LM35: 10 mV per degree C

  int angle;
  if (tempC <= T_CLOSED)      angle = 0;                       // shut
  else if (tempC >= T_OPEN)   angle = 90;                      // fully open
  else angle = map((int)tempC, (int)T_CLOSED, (int)T_OPEN, 0, 90);   // proportional

  flapServo.write(angle);

  Serial.print("T = ");      Serial.print(tempC, 1);
  Serial.print(" C   flap = "); Serial.print(angle);
  Serial.println(" deg");

  delay(1000);
}

The chain in one program: Unit 3's ADC conversion → Unit 4's decision → Unit 10's actuator, joined by map(). This structure answers almost any "sensor controls actuator proportionally" question.

Why no floor value here, unlike the fan in Q6.2: a servo is a position device with gearing and holds any commanded angle, so there is no minimum-duty stall problem. A DC motor needs a floor; a servo does not. Knowing which actuator needs a floor is a real design distinction.

Q10.3   Type D  ·  automatic door

Automatic door with PIR and safety hold

Design an automatic sliding door using a PIR motion sensor. The door opens on motion, stays open at least 5 seconds, and re-triggers the hold if motion continues. Include a manual override button.

Solution Q10.3
#include <Servo.h>

Servo doorServo;
const int pirPin      = 2;     // PIR: HIGH on motion  (opposite of IR obstacle)
const int overridePin = 3;
const int servoPin    = 9;
const int ledPin      = 8;

const unsigned long HOLD_MS = 5000;

bool doorOpen = false;
unsigned long openedAt = 0;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(pirPin, INPUT);
  pinMode(overridePin, INPUT_PULLUP);
  pinMode(ledPin, OUTPUT);
  doorServo.attach(servoPin);
  doorServo.write(0);                       // closed
}

void loop() {
  unsigned long now = millis();

  bool motion   = (digitalRead(pirPin) == HIGH);      // PIR is HIGH on detect
  bool override = (digitalRead(overridePin) == LOW);

  if (motion || override) {
    if (!doorOpen) {
      doorServo.write(90);
      doorOpen = true;
      Serial.println("Door OPEN");
    }
    openedAt = now;                          // re-trigger the hold on every detection
    digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH);
  }

  if (doorOpen && (now - openedAt >= HOLD_MS)) {
    doorServo.write(0);
    doorOpen = false;
    digitalWrite(ledPin, LOW);
    Serial.println("Door CLOSED");
  }
}
The polarity difference from CAT Q4 — state it

A PIR motion sensor outputs HIGH on detection, whereas the IR obstacle sensor in CAT Q4 outputs LOW. This program therefore tests == HIGH where the parking gate tests == LOW. Using the wrong polarity leaves the door permanently open.

The re-trigger pattern: openedAt = now executes on every detection, not just the first. This resets the 5-second countdown whenever someone is still present, so the door never closes on a person — a genuine safety requirement.

Why millis() rather than delay(5000): during a blocking delay the PIR could not re-trigger, and the door would close on anyone still in the doorway.

Q10.4   Type D  ·  multiple servos

Two-axis robotic arm with joystick control

Control a two-axis robotic arm using a two-axis joystick. Add software limits so neither servo can be driven beyond a safe mechanical range, and report both angles.

Solution Q10.4
#include <Servo.h>

Servo baseServo, armServo;

const int joyX = A0;
const int joyY = A1;

// mechanical safety limits
const int BASE_MIN = 10,  BASE_MAX = 170;
const int ARM_MIN  = 30,  ARM_MAX  = 150;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  baseServo.attach(9);       // Timer1
  armServo.attach(10);       // Timer1 - same timer, both fine
  baseServo.write(90);
