  armServo.write(90);
}

void loop() {
  int xRaw = analogRead(joyX);
  int yRaw = analogRead(joyY);

  int baseAngle = map(xRaw, 0, 1023, BASE_MIN, BASE_MAX);
  int armAngle  = map(yRaw, 0, 1023, ARM_MIN,  ARM_MAX);

  baseAngle = constrain(baseAngle, BASE_MIN, BASE_MAX);   // belt and braces
  armAngle  = constrain(armAngle,  ARM_MIN,  ARM_MAX);

  baseServo.write(baseAngle);
  armServo.write(armAngle);

  Serial.print("base = "); Serial.print(baseAngle);
  Serial.print(" deg   arm = "); Serial.print(armAngle);
  Serial.println(" deg");

  delay(20);
}
Three design points
  • Why software limits: a servo commanded past its mechanical stop stalls, drawing several hundred milliamps continuously and overheating. map() to a restricted range plus constrain() makes that impossible.
  • Both servos share Timer1 — the library multiplexes up to 12 servos on one timer, so this costs no extra timer. But PWM on pins 9 and 10 is now unavailable for analogWrite.
  • Power: two SG90s can draw 500 mA together, more on stall. An external 5 V supply with a common ground is required — the Uno's regulator cannot supply this.
Q10.5   Type D  ·  sorting system

Colour-based object sorter

An LDR-based sensor on A0 distinguishes dark from light objects on a conveyor. A servo diverts each object into one of two bins. Count objects of each type and report totals.

Solution Q10.5
#include <Servo.h>

Servo sorterServo;
const int ldrPin     = A0;
const int presencePin= 2;      // IR obstacle: LOW when an object is present
const int servoPin   = 9;

const int DARK_THRESHOLD = 400;
const int BIN_A = 30, BIN_B = 150, NEUTRAL = 90;

int darkCount = 0, lightCount = 0;
int lastPresence = HIGH;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(presencePin, INPUT_PULLUP);
  sorterServo.attach(servoPin);
  sorterServo.write(NEUTRAL);
  Serial.println("Sorter ready");
}

void loop() {
  int presence = digitalRead(presencePin);

  // falling edge = a new object has arrived
  if (presence == LOW && lastPresence == HIGH) {

    delay(50);                            // let the object settle under the sensor
    int light = analogRead(ldrPin);

    if (light < DARK_THRESHOLD) {
      sorterServo.write(BIN_A);
      darkCount++;
      Serial.print("DARK  object -> bin A   reading = ");
    } else {
      sorterServo.write(BIN_B);
      lightCount++;
      Serial.print("LIGHT object -> bin B   reading = ");
    }
    Serial.print(light);
    Serial.print("   totals: dark = "); Serial.print(darkCount);
    Serial.print("  light = ");         Serial.println(lightCount);

    delay(400);                           // allow the object to fall through
    sorterServo.write(NEUTRAL);           // return to centre
  }
  lastPresence = presence;
}

Two sensors, two roles: the IR obstacle sensor answers when (a digital event, detected by edge), and the LDR answers what (an analog classification, decided by threshold). Recognising that split is the design insight.

Why edge detection is essential: without it, one slowly-passing object would be counted hundreds of times per second and the servo would chatter.

Why the settle delay: the object must be fully under the LDR before it is read, otherwise the reading is taken mid-transit and is unreliable.

UNIT 11

Ultrasonic Distance Measurement

Slides 102–103  ·  Question types: P, D  ·  Weight: medium-high

How it works — time of flight

An ultrasonic sensor measures distance by timing an echo. It is a digital sensor whose information lives in a pulse width, not a voltage — so it is read with pulseIn(), never analogRead().

  1. The Trigger pin is pulsed HIGH for 10 µs, which makes the sensor emit an ultrasonic burst.
  2. The waves travel out, strike an object and reflect back to the sensor.
  3. The Echo pin goes HIGH for exactly as long as the round trip takes.
  4. pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH) measures that duration in microseconds.
  5. Helper functions convert the time into distance.

The conversion — derive it, do not memorise it

cm = duration / 29 / 2      inches = duration / 74 / 2 Divide by 2 because the sound travels out and back

Where 29 comes from: sound travels at about 340 m/s = 0.034 cm/µs. The time to cover one centimetre is therefore 1/0.034 = 29.4 µs per cm. Quoting the derivation rather than the number is worth a mark.

Key points
  • pulseIn() is blocking. It waits for the pulse to start and finish. With no echo it blocks for its full timeout — one second by default. Always pass an explicit timeout: pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH, 30000).
  • A timeout returns 0, which naively converts to a distance of 0 cm — reading as "object touching the sensor" when in fact nothing is there. Always test for 0.
  • Practical range is roughly 2 cm to 400 cm. Below 2 cm the echo returns before the receiver is listening.
  • Maximum useful timeout: 400 cm round trip = 800 cm × 29 µs = 23,200 µs. A 30 ms timeout covers the full range with margin.
  • Do not sample faster than ~20 Hz. Echoes from the previous burst are still bouncing around the room and will be mistaken for the new one.
  • Soft, angled or fabric surfaces absorb or deflect the burst and give no echo — a real limitation to state in a design answer.
  • The deck's slide-103 code uses a 3-pin variant where one pin is switched between OUTPUT and INPUT. The common HC-SR04 is 4-pin with separate Trig and Echo.

The deck's program (slide 103)

void loop() {
    long duration, inches, cm;

    pinMode(pingPin, OUTPUT);       // Configure the pingPin as an output
    digitalWrite(pingPin, LOW);     // Ensure it's LOW initially
    delayMicroseconds(2);           // Wait for 2 microseconds
    digitalWrite(pingPin, HIGH);    // Trigger the ultrasonic burst
    delayMicroseconds(10);          // Duration of the pulse (10 us)
    digitalWrite(pingPin, LOW);     // End the pulse

    pinMode(echoPin, INPUT);        // Set echoPin as input
    duration = pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH);   // Measure the time for echo

    inches = microsecondsToInches(duration);
    cm     = microsecondsToCentimeters(duration);

    Serial.print(inches); Serial.print("in, ");
    Serial.print(cm);     Serial.println("cm");
    delay(100);
}

long microsecondsToInches(long microseconds) { return microseconds / 74 / 2; }
long microsecondsToCentimeters(long microseconds) { return microseconds / 29 / 2; }

Numericals

N11.1 — pulseIn returns 1740 µs. Find the distance in cm and inches.

cm = 1740 / 29 / 2 = 30 cm inches = 1740 / 74 / 2 = 11.75 in Check: 30 cm = 11.8 in ✓

N11.2 — An object is at 150 cm. What duration does the echo pin report?

Round-trip path = 2 × 150 = 300 cm duration = 300 × 29 = 8700 µs

N11.3 — Derive the 29 µs/cm constant from the speed of sound.

Speed of sound = 340 m/s = 34000 cm/s = 0.034 cm/µs Time per cm = 1 / 0.034 = 29.4 µs/cm → rounded to 29 For inches: 1 inch = 2.54 cm → 29.4 × 2.54 = 74.7 µs/inch → 74

N11.4 — What timeout should be used to cover a 400 cm maximum range?

Round trip = 800 cm duration = 800 × 29 = 23,200 µs Use 30,000 µs (30 ms) for margin. Default pulseIn timeout is 1,000,000 µs — 33× longer than needed, which is why a missing echo stalls the loop for a full second.

N11.5 — What is the maximum safe sampling rate, and why?

Worst-case measurement = 23.2 ms, plus echo settling time Recommended minimum gap ≈ 50 ms → ≤ 20 Hz Faster sampling lets residual echoes from the previous burst be mistaken for the current one, giving false short readings.

Coding scenarios

Q11.1   Type P  ·  robust base version

Distance meter with error handling

Write a distance meter using a 4-pin HC-SR04 that prints distance in centimetres and inches, and correctly reports "out of range" rather than 0 cm when no echo returns.

Solution Q11.1
const int trigPin = 9;
const int echoPin = 10;
const unsigned long TIMEOUT_US = 30000;   // ~5 m of round trip

long readDurationUs() {
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);
  delayMicroseconds(2);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, HIGH);            // 10 us trigger burst
  delayMicroseconds(10);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);

  return pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH, TIMEOUT_US);   // 0 if it times out
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(trigPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(echoPin, INPUT);
}

void loop() {
  long duration = readDurationUs();

  if (duration == 0) {                    // no echo received
    Serial.println("Out of range / no echo");
  } else {
    long cm     = duration / 29 / 2;      // 29 us per cm, halved for round trip
    long inches = duration / 74 / 2;

    if (cm < 2 || cm > 400) {
      Serial.print("Unreliable reading: "); Serial.print(cm); Serial.println(" cm");
    } else {
      Serial.print(duration); Serial.print(" us  =  ");
      Serial.print(cm);       Serial.print(" cm, ");
      Serial.print(inches);   Serial.println(" in");
    }
  }
  delay(100);
}
Why the zero check is not optional

With no timeout argument, pulseIn blocks for a full second when nothing echoes, and then returns 0 — which the formula converts to 0 cm, i.e. "object touching the sensor". In a reverse parking aid that would trigger a maximum-danger alarm for empty space. Both the timeout and the zero test are required for a correct answer.

Q11.2   Type D  ·  banded alarm

Reverse parking sensor

Design a reverse parking aid: green LED beyond 50 cm, yellow between 20 and 50 cm, red below 20 cm, with a buzzer that beeps faster as the obstacle approaches. Print the distance.

Solution Q11.2

Working

  1. The trigger pin is pulsed HIGH for 10 µs, emitting an ultrasonic burst.
  2. The burst reflects off the obstacle and returns to the receiver.
  3. pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH) measures the round-trip time of flight in microseconds.
  4. Sound travels 1 cm every 29 µs, so distance = duration / 29 / 2; the division by 2 accounts for the out-and-back path.
  5. The distance is classified into three bands and the corresponding LED is lit.
  6. The buzzer interval is set from the band: 100 ms when critical, 400 ms when close, silent when clear.
  7. The beep is produced non-blockingly with millis() so distance measurement continues between beeps.
const int trigPin   = 9;
const int echoPin   = 10;
const int buzzerPin = 8;
const int redPin    = 5;
const int yellowPin = 6;
const int greenPin  = 7;

unsigned long lastBeep = 0;
bool beepOn = false;

long readCm() {
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);  delayMicroseconds(2);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, HIGH); delayMicroseconds(10);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);
  long d = pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH, 30000);
  return (d == 0) ? 999 : d / 29 / 2;      // 999 = nothing in range
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(trigPin, OUTPUT);   pinMode(echoPin, INPUT);
  pinMode(buzzerPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(redPin, OUTPUT); pinMode(yellowPin, OUTPUT); pinMode(greenPin, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  long cm = readCm();

  digitalWrite(redPin, LOW); digitalWrite(yellowPin, LOW); digitalWrite(greenPin, LOW);

  int beepGap;
  if (cm < 20)      { digitalWrite(redPin, HIGH);    beepGap = 100; }   // critical
  else if (cm < 50) { digitalWrite(yellowPin, HIGH); beepGap = 400; }   // close
  else              { digitalWrite(greenPin, HIGH);  beepGap = 0;   }   // clear

  Serial.print("Distance = "); Serial.print(cm); Serial.println(" cm");

  // non-blocking beeping so measurement continues
  if (beepGap > 0) {
    if (millis() - lastBeep >= (unsigned long)beepGap) {
      lastBeep = millis();
      beepOn = !beepOn;
      if (beepOn) tone(buzzerPin, 2000); else noTone(buzzerPin);
    }
  } else {
    noTone(buzzerPin);
  }

  delay(60);                                 // stay under 20 Hz
}

Extra-mark note: tone() uses Timer2, so PWM on pins 3 and 11 stops working while the buzzer sounds. The LEDs here are deliberately on pins 5, 6 and 7 and driven with digitalWrite, so nothing conflicts.

Q11.3   Type D  ·  tank level

Water tank level monitor with pump control

An ultrasonic sensor mounted at the top of a 100 cm tank measures the air gap to the water surface. Convert to a fill percentage, run a pump below 25 % and stop it above 90 %, and display a bar graph.

Solution Q11.3
const int trigPin = 9, echoPin = 10, pumpPin = 7;

const int TANK_DEPTH_CM = 100;    // sensor face to tank bottom
const int SENSOR_OFFSET =   5;    // sensor sits 5 cm above the full level

bool pumping = false;

long readCm() {
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);  delayMicroseconds(2);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, HIGH); delayMicroseconds(10);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);
  long d = pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH, 30000);
  return (d == 0) ? -1 : d / 29 / 2;
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(trigPin, OUTPUT); pinMode(echoPin, INPUT);
  pinMode(pumpPin, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  long gap = readCm();                       // distance to the water surface

  if (gap < 0) { Serial.println("Sensor error"); delay(500); return; }

  int waterDepth = TANK_DEPTH_CM - gap;                       // invert the reading
  int percent    = map(waterDepth, 0, TANK_DEPTH_CM - SENSOR_OFFSET, 0, 100);
  percent        = constrain(percent, 0, 100);

  if (!pumping && percent < 25) { pumping = true;  Serial.println("PUMP ON"); }
  if ( pumping && percent > 90) { pumping = false; Serial.println("PUMP OFF"); }
  digitalWrite(pumpPin, pumping ? HIGH : LOW);

  Serial.print("gap ");  Serial.print(gap);
  Serial.print(" cm  level "); Serial.print(percent); Serial.print(" %  [");
  for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) Serial.print(i < percent / 5 ? '#' : '.');
  Serial.print("]  pump ");    Serial.println(pumping ? "ON" : "OFF");

  delay(500);
}
Two design points that earn marks

The reading is inverted. The sensor measures the air gap, so a large distance means an empty tank. Subtracting from the tank depth converts gap to level — forgetting this inversion is the classic error in this question.

Hysteresis is essential here. Pumping on below 25 % and off above 90 % gives a wide band, so the pump runs in long cycles instead of switching on and off every few seconds at a single setpoint. Rapid cycling destroys pump motors and relay contacts.

Q11.4   Type P  ·  filtering

Median-filtered distance for a noisy environment

Ultrasonic readings occasionally return wild outliers from stray reflections. Take five readings and use the median rather than the mean, and explain why the median is the correct choice here.

Solution Q11.4
const int trigPin = 9, echoPin = 10;
const int N = 5;

long singleReadCm() {
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);  delayMicroseconds(2);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, HIGH); delayMicroseconds(10);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);
  long d = pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH, 30000);
  return (d == 0) ? 999 : d / 29 / 2;
}

long medianCm() {
  long v[N];
  for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) { v[i] = singleReadCm(); delay(50); }

  for (int i = 0; i < N - 1; i++)              // simple insertion sort
    for (int j = i + 1; j < N; j++)
      if (v[j] < v[i]) { long t = v[i]; v[i] = v[j]; v[j] = t; }

  return v[N / 2];                             // the middle value
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(trigPin, OUTPUT); pinMode(echoPin, INPUT);
}

void loop() {
  long raw = singleReadCm();
  long med = medianCm();

  Serial.print("raw = ");    Serial.print(raw);
  Serial.print(" cm   median(5) = "); Serial.print(med);
  Serial.println(" cm");
}
Why median and not mean — the answer the question wants

A mean is dragged by outliers. One spurious 400 cm reading among four correct 30 cm readings gives a mean of 104 cm — badly wrong. The median discards it entirely and still returns 30 cm.

The rule: use averaging against random, symmetric noise (as in Unit 3's ADC jitter); use the median against occasional wild outliers, which is exactly what stray ultrasonic reflections produce.

Cost: five readings at 50 ms apart means the measurement takes 250 ms, so the update rate drops to 4 Hz. Robustness is traded for speed.

Q11.5   Type D  ·  combined units

Obstacle-avoiding robot with servo scanning

Mount an ultrasonic sensor on a servo. Scan left, centre and right, choose the clearest direction, and drive two motors accordingly. Combine Units 6, 10 and 11.

Solution Q11.5
#include <Servo.h>

Servo scanServo;
const int trigPin = 9, echoPin = 10, servoPin = 11;
const int leftEn  = 5, rightEn = 6;            // motor PWM (Timer0 pins)
const int leftDir = 4, rightDir = 7;

const int CLEAR_CM = 30;

long readCm() {
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);  delayMicroseconds(2);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, HIGH); delayMicroseconds(10);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);
  long d = pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH, 30000);
  return (d == 0) ? 999 : d / 29 / 2;
}

long lookAt(int angle) {
  scanServo.write(angle);
  delay(300);                                   // let the servo settle
  return readCm();
}

void drive(int l, int r) {
  digitalWrite(leftDir, HIGH); digitalWrite(rightDir, HIGH);
  analogWrite(leftEn,  l);     analogWrite(rightEn, r);
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(trigPin, OUTPUT); pinMode(echoPin, INPUT);
  pinMode(leftEn, OUTPUT);  pinMode(rightEn, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(leftDir, OUTPUT); pinMode(rightDir, OUTPUT);
  scanServo.attach(servoPin);
  scanServo.write(90);
  delay(500);
}

void loop() {
  long ahead = lookAt(90);
  Serial.print("ahead = "); Serial.print(ahead); Serial.println(" cm");

  if (ahead > CLEAR_CM) {
    drive(180, 180);                            // clear: go straight
  } else {
    drive(0, 0);                                // stop and scan
    long left  = lookAt(150);
    long right = lookAt(30);
    scanServo.write(90);

    Serial.print("left = ");  Serial.print(left);
    Serial.print("  right = ");Serial.println(right);

    if (left > right) { drive(0, 160); delay(400); }   // pivot left
    else              { drive(160, 0); delay(400); }   // pivot right
  }
  delay(50);
}
Pin allocation is the hidden exam point

The servo is on pin 11 and the motors on pins 5 and 6. That is deliberate:

ResourceTimerConsequence
Servo libraryTimer1PWM on pins 9 and 10 unavailable
Motor analogWriteTimer0 (pins 5, 6)Unaffected — still works

Putting the motors on pins 9 and 10 would have produced a robot whose motors silently refused to vary speed. Naming this conflict is worth a mark in any design answer that combines a servo with PWM.

Why the servo settles for 300 ms: reading the sensor while the servo is still swinging measures the wrong direction.

Q11.6   Type D  ·  PYQ-adjacent

Contactless queue-distance monitor

Design a social-distancing monitor for a queue. Two ultrasonic sensors measure the gap between consecutive people. If the gap falls below 1 metre, sound an alarm and light a red LED; otherwise show green. Track how many violations occur.

Solution Q11.6
const int trigA = 9,  echoA = 10;
const int trigB = 11, echoB = 12;
const int redPin = 5, greenPin = 6, buzzerPin = 8;

const int MIN_GAP_CM = 100;              // 1 metre

int violations = 0;
bool inViolation = false;

long readCm(int trig, int echo) {
  digitalWrite(trig, LOW);  delayMicroseconds(2);
  digitalWrite(trig, HIGH); delayMicroseconds(10);
  digitalWrite(trig, LOW);
  long d = pulseIn(echo, HIGH, 30000);
  return (d == 0) ? 999 : d / 29 / 2;
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(trigA, OUTPUT); pinMode(echoA, INPUT);
  pinMode(trigB, OUTPUT); pinMode(echoB, INPUT);
  pinMode(redPin, OUTPUT); pinMode(greenPin, OUTPUT); pinMode(buzzerPin, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  long a = readCm(trigA, echoA);
  delay(60);                               // avoid cross-talk between sensors
  long b = readCm(trigB, echoB);

  bool bothPresent = (a < 300 && b < 300);
  long gap = a + b;                        // separation across the two stations

  if (bothPresent && gap < MIN_GAP_CM) {
    digitalWrite(redPin, HIGH); digitalWrite(greenPin, LOW);
    tone(buzzerPin, 1500);
    if (!inViolation) { violations++; inViolation = true;
      Serial.print("VIOLATION #"); Serial.println(violations); }
    Serial.print("Too close: "); Serial.print(gap); Serial.println(" cm");
  } else {
    digitalWrite(redPin, LOW); digitalWrite(greenPin, HIGH);
    noTone(buzzerPin);
    inViolation = false;
    Serial.print("OK  gap = "); Serial.print(gap); Serial.println(" cm");
  }
  delay(200);
}

The 60 ms gap between sensors is required. Firing two ultrasonic sensors simultaneously means sensor A can hear sensor B's burst — cross-talk — giving nonsense readings. Staggering the triggers eliminates it.

Why inViolation: this is edge detection again (Unit 8). Without it, a single person standing too close would increment the violation counter five times a second.

UNIT 12

SPI and EEPROM Memory Interfacing

Slides 104–124  ·  Question types: T, P  ·  Weight: high  ·  Contains CAT Q3

Read this before anything else — the taught/examined mismatch

The deck teaches external EEPROM over the SPI protocol (an AT25HP512 chip). Your CAT-1 Q3 asks about the internal EEPROM using the EEPROM.h library. These are different things, and both are examinable. This unit covers SPI theory first (the deck's content, likely as a Type T question), then the internal EEPROM (the Type P question you actually got).

Part A — SPI (slides 105–108)

Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI) is a synchronous serial data protocol used by microcontrollers to communicate with one or more peripheral devices quickly over short distances. There is always one master device (usually the microcontroller) which controls the peripherals.

LineFull namePurposeUno pin
MISOMaster In Slave OutSlave line for sending data to the master12
MOSIMaster Out Slave InMaster line for sending data to the peripherals11
SCKSerial ClockClock pulses that synchronise transmission, generated by the master13
SSSlave SelectOne per device; the master enables and disables specific devices, avoiding false transmissions due to line noise10

The first three lines are common to all devices; only SS is per-device. That is what lets one master drive many slaves on four wires plus one extra line each.

The three SPI registers (slide 107)

All SPI settings are determined by the Arduino SPI Control Register (SPCR).

RegisterTypeRole
SPCRControlEach bit sets a particular setting such as speed or polarity
SPDRDataHolds the byte about to be shifted out MOSI, and the data just shifted in on MISO
SPSRStatusChanges state on microcontroller conditions; bit 7 (SPIF) is set when a value has been shifted in or out
This is Unit 2's register model, exactly

Control / Data / read-only Status. SPCR is written by you; SPDR carries the bytes; SPSR is set by the hardware and polled by you. The while (!(SPSR & (1<<SPIF))); loop is busy-wait — the same technique as AGAIN: JNB TF0, AGAIN.

The SPCR bit map (slide 108) — reproduce this in a theory answer

BitNameMeaning
7SPIESPI Interrupt Enable — enables the SPI interrupt when 1
6SPESPI Enable — must be set to enable any SPI operation
5DORDData Order — LSB first when 1, MSB first when 0
4MSTRMaster/Slave Select — master when 1, slave when 0
3CPOLClock Polarity — SCK high when idle if 1, low when idle if 0
2CPHAClock Phase — sample on falling edge when 1, rising edge when 0
1,0SPR1, SPR0SPI Clock Rate — 00 fastest (4 MHz), 11 slowest (250 kHz)
Decoding SPCR = 01010000 — the deck's own example, and a guaranteed exam question

Slide 116 sets SPCR to binary 0101 0000. Read it bit by bit:

BitValueEffect
SPIE (7)0SPI interrupt disabled
SPE (6)1SPI enabled
DORD (5)0Most significant bit first
MSTR (4)1Arduino in Master mode
CPOL (3)0Data clock idle when low
CPHA (2)0Sample on the rising edge
SPR1,0 (1,0)00System speed / 4 — the fastest, 4 MHz

After setting SPCR, the deck reads SPSR and SPDR into a junk variable clr to clear out any spurious data from past runs.

The AT25HP512 EEPROM (slides 109–112)

  • A 65,536 byte serial EEPROM — note this is exactly 216, matching the 16-bit address bus.
  • Supports SPI modes 0 and 3, runs up to 10 MHz at 5 V and down to 1.8 V at slower speeds.
  • Memory organised as 512 pages of 128 bytes each.
  • Can only be written 128 bytes at a time, but can be read 1–128 bytes at a time.
  • Offers various degrees of write protection and a hold pin.
  • The device is enabled by pulling Chip Select (CS) low.
  • Instructions are sent as 8-bit opcodes, shifted in on the rising edge of the data clock.
  • It takes about 10 ms to write a page, so a 10 ms pause must follow each write routine.

Wiring (slide 112): EEPROM pins 3, 7 and 8 to 5 V, pin 4 to ground. EEPROM pin 1 → Arduino 10 (SS), pin 2 → Arduino 12 (MISO), pin 5 → Arduino 11 (MOSI), pin 6 → Arduino 13 (SCK).

The write sequence (slides 118–119)

  1. The EEPROM MUST be write enabled before every write instruction. Pull SLAVESELECT low, send the WREN opcode, pull SLAVESELECT high again.
  2. Pull SLAVESELECT low again after a brief delay.
  3. Send the WRITE instruction.
  4. Send the 16-bit address in two bytes, most significant byte first.
  5. Send the 128 bytes of data from the buffer, one after another without pause.
  6. Set SLAVESELECT high to release the device and pause 10 ms to allow the write to complete.

The read sequence (slide 123): set SLAVESELECT low → transmit the READ instruction → send the 16-bit address MSB first → send a dummy byte to shift the data out → pull SLAVESELECT high and return the data.

The spi_transfer function (slide 122): loads the output data into the data transmission register, which starts the transmission; polls the SPIF bit in SPSR to detect completion using a bit mask; then returns whatever data has been shifted in.

Part B — the internal EEPROM (what CAT Q3 actually needs)

The deck notes on slide 105 that "the chip on the Arduino board contains an internal EEPROM". That is the 1 KB of on-chip EEPROM from Unit 1, addresses 0 to 1023, reached through the EEPROM.h library — no SPI, no wiring.

CallBehaviour
EEPROM.read(addr)Returns one byte
EEPROM.write(addr, val)Always writes
EEPROM.update(addr, val)Writes only if the value differs — preferred
EEPROM.put(addr, var)Writes a multi-byte variable (int, float, struct)
EEPROM.get(addr, var)Reads a multi-byte variable back
EEPROM.length()1024 on the Uno
Key points — these are the marks in CAT Q3
  • A fresh or erased EEPROM cell reads 0xFF (255). That is what makes the marker-byte technique work: any value other than 255 means "someone has been here before".
  • Endurance is about 100,000 write cycles per cell. This is why the question says "check whether it is already available… if not write". Without the check, setup() rewrites on every reset and wears the cell out.
  • EEPROM.update() reads before writing and skips unchanged bytes — always prefer it where an address is written repeatedly.
  • An EEPROM write takes about 3.3 ms and blocks. Writing 100 bytes takes a third of a second.
  • SRAM vs EEPROM is the justification to state: SRAM loses its contents on power-off, EEPROM does not.
  • One byte holds 0–255. For larger values use EEPROM.put(), which spans multiple bytes.

Numericals

N12.1 — The AT25HP512 holds 65,536 bytes in 128-byte pages. How many pages, and why is 65,536 significant?

Pages = 65536 / 128 = 512 pages 65,536 = 2^16 — exactly what a 16-bit address bus can address, which is why the address is sent as two bytes, MSB first.

N12.2 — Writing a page takes 10 ms. How long to fill the whole chip?

512 pages × 10 ms = 5120 ms = 5.12 seconds Reading is far faster — no write cycle is involved.

N12.3 — SPI runs at system speed / 4. Find the clock rate and the time to transfer one byte.

SPI clock = 16 MHz / 4 = 4 MHz One byte = 8 bits → 8 / (4 × 10^6) = 2 µs per byte Compare UART at 9600 baud: 1.04 ms per byte — SPI is 520× faster.

N12.4 — A sensor logs one calibration byte every hour to the same EEPROM address. How long until the cell wears out with write(), and with update() if the value rarely changes?

With write(): 100,000 cycles / 24 per day = 4166 days ≈ 11.4 years With update(): only actual changes count. If the value changes once a month, that is 12 writes/year → over 8000 years. This is the practical argument for update().

N12.5 — How many 4-character passwords plus a marker fit in the Uno's internal EEPROM?

Each record = 1 marker + 4 characters = 5 bytes EEPROM = 1024 bytes Records = 1024 / 5 = 204 records (CAT Q3 uses just one, at addresses 0 to 4.)

N12.6 — Compare SPI, I²C and UART speed for moving 1 KB of data.

SPI at 4 MHz : 1024 × 8 / 4×10^6 = 2.05 ms I2C at 400 kHz : 1024 × 9 / 400×10^3 = 23 ms (9 bits incl. ACK) UART at 9600 8N1 : 1024 × 10 / 9600 = 1067 ms SPI is fastest because it is synchronous with no framing overhead.

Coding scenarios

PYQ   CAT-1 Q3  ·  Type P  ·  10 marks

EEPROM password storage and verification

Write an Arduino program for storing a password in EEPROM and verifying using input from serial monitor. Define a password and check whether it is already available in EEPROM; if not, write the password. If the entered password matches the stored password display "Access Granted", else display "Access Denied" in serial monitor.

Model answer — full exam format

Aim

To store a predefined password in the internal EEPROM of the ATmega328P exactly once, and to verify a password entered through the Serial Monitor against it, granting or denying access accordingly.

Components required

Arduino Uno (ATmega328P with 1 KB internal EEPROM), USB cable, Serial Monitor set to 9600 baud. No external hardware is required — the EEPROM is on-chip.

EEPROM memory map

AddressContentsValue
0Marker / signature0xA5
1Password character 1'1' = 49
2Password character 2'2' = 50
3Password character 3'3' = 51
4Password character 4'4' = 52

The password is stored as ASCII bytes, not as the number 1234.

Working

  1. The predefined password is 1234.
  2. EEPROM address 0 is used as a marker.
  3. If the marker value is not present, the password is written into EEPROM starting at address 1, and the marker is then written to address 0.
  4. If the marker is already available, the EEPROM password is not written again, preserving the EEPROM's write endurance of approximately 100,000 cycles.
  5. The stored password is read back from EEPROM into a buffer.
  6. The user enters a password through the Serial Monitor. Serial.available() returns the number of bytes waiting in the 64-byte UART receive buffer.
  7. The stored password is compared with the entered password using strcmp.
  8. If both match, Access Granted is displayed; otherwise Access Denied.

Flowchart

Arduino program

#include <EEPROM.h>

const int  MARKER_ADDR = 0;      // marker byte address
const int  PASS_ADDR   = 1;      // password stored from here
const byte MARKER_VAL  = 0xA5;   // signature meaning "already written"
const int  PASS_LEN    = 4;

char defaultPassword[PASS_LEN + 1] = "1234";
char storedPassword[PASS_LEN + 1];
char enteredPassword[PASS_LEN + 1];

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);

  // Step 1: write the password only if it is not already stored
  if (EEPROM.read(MARKER_ADDR) != MARKER_VAL) {
    for (int i = 0; i < PASS_LEN; i++)
      EEPROM.write(PASS_ADDR + i, defaultPassword[i]);
    EEPROM.write(MARKER_ADDR, MARKER_VAL);
    Serial.println("Default password written to EEPROM");
  } else {
    Serial.println("Password already present in EEPROM");
  }

  // Step 2: read the stored password back from EEPROM
  for (int i = 0; i < PASS_LEN; i++)
    storedPassword[i] = EEPROM.read(PASS_ADDR + i);
  storedPassword[PASS_LEN] = '\0';      // null-terminate the string

  Serial.println("Enter password:");
}

void loop() {
  if (Serial.available() >= PASS_LEN) {          // wait for 4 characters

    for (int i = 0; i < PASS_LEN; i++)
      enteredPassword[i] = Serial.read();
    enteredPassword[PASS_LEN] = '\0';

    if (strcmp(enteredPassword, storedPassword) == 0)
      Serial.println("Access Granted");
    else
      Serial.println("Access Denied");

    while (Serial.available()) Serial.read();    // flush newline / CR
    Serial.println("Enter password:");
  }
}

Result

The program stores the password in EEPROM only once and subsequently verifies the password entered through the Serial Monitor, displaying Access Granted on a match and Access Denied otherwise. The stored password is retained across power-off and reset.

Shorter alternative for exam handwriting speed

#include <EEPROM.h>

String password = "1234";
String stored   = "";

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);

  if (EEPROM.read(0) != 1) {                       // marker check
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) EEPROM.write(i + 1, password[i]);
    EEPROM.write(0, 1);                            // set marker
    Serial.println("Password stored in EEPROM");
  } else {
    Serial.println("Password already in EEPROM");
  }

  for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) stored += char(EEPROM.read(i + 1));
  Serial.println("Enter password:");
}

void loop() {
  if (Serial.available()) {
    String entered = Serial.readString();
    entered.trim();                                // removes \n and \r

    if (entered == stored) Serial.println("Access Granted");
    else                   Serial.println("Access Denied");

    Serial.println("Enter password:");
  }
}
The five points that separate a 7 from a 10
  1. Explain why the marker exists. EEPROM contents survive power-off and reset, so setup() runs again on every reset. Without the marker the password would be rewritten every boot and consume the ~100,000 write-cycle endurance. This is the examiner's actual target.
  2. Note that fresh EEPROM reads 0xFF. An erased cell is all ones, which is why any marker value other than 255 works as a signature.
  3. Mention EEPROM.update() — it reads before writing and only writes if the byte differs.
  4. Explain the buffer flush. The Serial Monitor appends a newline or carriage return; without flushing, the leftover character stays in the 64-byte buffer and corrupts the next comparison.
  5. Null-terminate before strcmp. strcmp requires a terminating '\0'; omitting it makes the comparison read past the array.
Common mistakes
MistakeConsequence
No marker — writing unconditionally in setup()Fails the explicit requirement, wears EEPROM
if (Serial.available()) instead of >= PASS_LENReads one character, compares against four — always denies
Forgetting storedPassword[PASS_LEN] = '\0'strcmp reads garbage past the array
Comparing char arrays with ==Compares pointers, not contents — always false. Use strcmp
No buffer flushEvery second attempt fails on a leftover \n
Storing the password as an intIt is four ASCII characters, not the number 1234
Forgetting #include <EEPROM.h>Will not compile
Q12.1   Type P  ·  deck content

Register-level SPI transfer

Following the deck's method, configure SPI by writing SPCR directly and implement the spi_transfer function that polls SPIF. Explain each bit of the SPCR value.

Solution Q12.1
#define DATAOUT     11    // MOSI
#define DATAIN      12    // MISO
#define SPICLOCK    13    // SCK
#define SLAVESELECT 10    // SS

// AT25HP512 opcodes
#define WREN  6
#define WRITE 2
#define READ  3
#define RDSR  5

byte clr;

char spi_transfer(volatile char data) {
  SPDR = data;                          // start transmission by loading SPDR
  while (!(SPSR & (1 << SPIF))) {       // poll the status flag - busy wait
    ;
  }
  return SPDR;                          // return what was shifted in
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);

  pinMode(DATAOUT,     OUTPUT);
  pinMode(DATAIN,      INPUT);
  pinMode(SPICLOCK,    OUTPUT);
  pinMode(SLAVESELECT, OUTPUT);

  digitalWrite(SLAVESELECT, HIGH);      // deselect: avoids false transmissions

  SPCR = B01010000;                     // see the bit-by-bit table below
  clr = SPSR;                           // clear spurious data from past runs
  clr = SPDR;
  delay(10);
}

void loop() {}
BitValueEffect
SPIE0SPI interrupt disabled
SPE1SPI enabled — mandatory for any SPI operation
DORD0Most significant bit transmitted first
MSTR1Arduino is the Master
CPOL0Clock idles low
CPHA0Data sampled on the rising edge
SPR1:SPR000System speed / 4 = 4 MHz, the fastest

Why loading SPDR starts the transfer: in SPI the master generates the clock, so writing the data register is what makes the hardware begin shifting. There is no separate "go" bit.

Why SPI is inherently full-duplex: as each bit shifts out on MOSI, a bit shifts in on MISO. spi_transfer therefore always returns a byte, even when you only meant to send one — which is why the read routine sends a dummy byte to clock data out of the slave.

Q12.2   Type P  ·  deck content

Write and read a page of external SPI EEPROM

Implement the deck's write-enable, page-write and byte-read sequences for the AT25HP512, and explain why the write-enable must precede every write.

Solution Q12.2
char buffer[128];        // 128 byte array holding the page to write

void fill_buffer() {
  for (int i = 0; i < 128; i++) buffer[i] = i;
}

void write_page(unsigned int addr) {
  // --- Step 1: WRITE ENABLE - required before EVERY write ---
  digitalWrite(SLAVESELECT, LOW);
  spi_transfer(WREN);
  digitalWrite(SLAVESELECT, HIGH);
  delay(1);

  // --- Step 2: WRITE instruction, address, then the data ---
  digitalWrite(SLAVESELECT, LOW);
  spi_transfer(WRITE);
  spi_transfer((char)(addr >> 8));     // 16-bit address, MSB first
  spi_transfer((char)(addr));          // then LSB
  for (int i = 0; i < 128; i++)
    spi_transfer(buffer[i]);           // 128 bytes without pause
  digitalWrite(SLAVESELECT, HIGH);

  delay(10);                           // page write takes ~10 ms
}

byte read_eeprom(unsigned int addr) {
  digitalWrite(SLAVESELECT, LOW);
  spi_transfer(READ);
  spi_transfer((char)(addr >> 8));     // MSB first
  spi_transfer((char)(addr));
  byte data = spi_transfer(0xFF);      // dummy byte shifts the data OUT
  digitalWrite(SLAVESELECT, HIGH);
  return data;
}

unsigned int address = 0;

void loop() {
  Serial.print(address); Serial.print(" : ");
  Serial.println(read_eeprom(address), DEC);
  address++;
  if (address == 128) address = 0;     // only 128 addresses were filled
  delay(500);
}
Four points the examiner looks for
  • Why WREN before every write: the EEPROM clears its internal write-enable latch automatically after each completed write. This is a deliberate safety feature — a glitch or noise cannot corrupt memory unless a valid WREN opcode was received first.
  • Why the 10 ms delay: the write is performed by an internal charge pump and takes about 10 ms per 128-byte page. Sending the next command sooner is ignored or corrupts the write.
  • Why the address is two bytes, MSB first: 65,536 bytes needs 16 address bits, and SPI transfers 8 bits at a time. MSB first matches DORD = 0.
  • Why a dummy byte in the read: SPI is master-clocked. The slave cannot send anything unless the master generates clock pulses, and the only way to generate them is to transmit something.
Q12.3   Type P  ·  internal EEPROM

Power-cycle counter that survives reset

Count how many times the board has been powered on, storing the count in EEPROM so it survives power loss. Handle the case of a fresh chip and support counts above 255.

Solution Q12.3
#include <EEPROM.h>

const int  MARKER_ADDR = 0;
const int  COUNT_ADDR  = 1;      // an int occupies addresses 1 and 2
const byte MARKER_VAL  = 0x5A;

int bootCount = 0;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  delay(200);

  if (EEPROM.read(MARKER_ADDR) != MARKER_VAL) {   // fresh chip
    bootCount = 0;
    EEPROM.put(COUNT_ADDR, bootCount);
    EEPROM.write(MARKER_ADDR, MARKER_VAL);
    Serial.println("First run - counter initialised");
  } else {
    EEPROM.get(COUNT_ADDR, bootCount);            // restore the int
  }

  bootCount++;
  EEPROM.put(COUNT_ADDR, bootCount);              // store the new value

  Serial.print("Board has started ");
  Serial.print(bootCount);
  Serial.println(" times");
}

void loop() {}
Why put/get rather than write/read

EEPROM.write() stores one byte, so it can only count to 255. EEPROM.put() writes any variable byte by byte — an int spans two addresses, allowing counts to 32,767. This is exactly the "one-byte limit" caveat that applies to CAT Q3 variations.

put() internally uses update(), so unchanged bytes are not rewritten — endurance is preserved automatically.

Why the marker is still needed: a fresh chip reads 0xFF at every address, so EEPROM.get would return −1 as the starting count. The marker distinguishes "never initialised" from "legitimately stored".

Q12.4   Type D  ·  calibration storage

Sensor calibration stored in EEPROM

A weighing system needs a calibration factor and a tare offset that survive power-off, settable over serial. Store both as floats in EEPROM and apply them to live readings.

Solution Q12.4
#include <EEPROM.h>

const int  MARKER_ADDR = 0;
const int  SCALE_ADDR  = 1;      // float = 4 bytes -> addresses 1..4
const int  TARE_ADDR   = 5;      // float = 4 bytes -> addresses 5..8
const byte MARKER_VAL  = 0xC3;

const int sensorPin = A0;

float scaleFactor = 1.0;
float tareOffset  = 0.0;

void loadCalibration() {
  if (EEPROM.read(MARKER_ADDR) != MARKER_VAL) {
    scaleFactor = 1.0; tareOffset = 0.0;
    EEPROM.put(SCALE_ADDR, scaleFactor);
    EEPROM.put(TARE_ADDR,  tareOffset);
    EEPROM.write(MARKER_ADDR, MARKER_VAL);
    Serial.println("Defaults written");
  } else {
    EEPROM.get(SCALE_ADDR, scaleFactor);
    EEPROM.get(TARE_ADDR,  tareOffset);
  }
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  loadCalibration();
  Serial.print("scale = "); Serial.print(scaleFactor, 4);
  Serial.print("   tare = ");Serial.println(tareOffset, 2);
  Serial.println("Commands:  t = tare now   s<value> = set scale");
}

void loop() {
  int   adc  = analogRead(sensorPin);
  float mass = (adc - tareOffset) * scaleFactor;

  if (Serial.available()) {
    char c = Serial.read();

    if (c == 't') {                       // tare: current reading becomes zero
      tareOffset = adc;
      EEPROM.put(TARE_ADDR, tareOffset);
      Serial.print("Tared at ADC "); Serial.println(adc);
    }
    else if (c == 's') {
      float v = Serial.parseFloat();
      if (v > 0) {
        scaleFactor = v;
        EEPROM.put(SCALE_ADDR, scaleFactor);
        Serial.print("Scale set to "); Serial.println(scaleFactor, 4);
      }
    }
    while (Serial.available()) Serial.read();     // flush
  }

  Serial.print("ADC ");   Serial.print(adc);
  Serial.print("   mass = "); Serial.print(mass, 1);
  Serial.println(" g");
  delay(500);
}

The address map matters: a float is 4 bytes on AVR, so the scale factor occupies addresses 1–4 and the tare 5–8. Overlapping them would corrupt both — always plan the EEPROM address map before writing the code.

This is the CAT weighing-machine question in software form. The Module 1 answer says the ATmega328P's 1 KB EEPROM "stores the calibration factor and tare data" — this program is that sentence implemented.

Q12.5   Type D  ·  access control

Door lock with changeable password and lockout

Extend the CAT Q3 password system into a door lock: three wrong attempts trigger a 30-second lockout, the password can be changed over serial, and both the password and the failed-attempt count survive power loss.

Solution Q12.5
#include <EEPROM.h>
#include <Servo.h>

Servo lockServo;

const int  MARKER_ADDR   = 0;
const int  PASS_ADDR     = 1;      // 4 bytes: 1..4
const int  ATTEMPTS_ADDR = 5;
const byte MARKER_VAL    = 0xA5;
const int  PASS_LEN      = 4;
const int  MAX_ATTEMPTS  = 3;
const unsigned long LOCKOUT_MS = 30000;

const int servoPin = 9, greenPin = 6, redPin = 7;

char storedPassword[PASS_LEN + 1];
char entered[PASS_LEN + 1];
int  failedAttempts = 0;
unsigned long lockoutUntil = 0;

void readStored() {
  for (int i = 0; i < PASS_LEN; i++) storedPassword[i] = EEPROM.read(PASS_ADDR + i);
  storedPassword[PASS_LEN] = '\0';
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(greenPin, OUTPUT); pinMode(redPin, OUTPUT);
  lockServo.attach(servoPin);
  lockServo.write(0);                       // locked

  if (EEPROM.read(MARKER_ADDR) != MARKER_VAL) {
    const char def[] = "1234";
    for (int i = 0; i < PASS_LEN; i++) EEPROM.write(PASS_ADDR + i, def[i]);
    EEPROM.update(ATTEMPTS_ADDR, 0);
    EEPROM.write(MARKER_ADDR, MARKER_VAL);
    Serial.println("Default password written");
  }
  readStored();
  failedAttempts = EEPROM.read(ATTEMPTS_ADDR);      // survives a power cycle
  if (failedAttempts > MAX_ATTEMPTS) failedAttempts = 0;

  Serial.print("Failed attempts on record: "); Serial.println(failedAttempts);
  Serial.println("Enter password ( # followed by 4 chars changes it ):");
}

void loop() {
  if (millis() < lockoutUntil) {                    // locked out
    digitalWrite(redPin, HIGH);
    return;
  }

  if (Serial.available() > 0) {

    if (Serial.peek() == '#') {                     // change password
      Serial.read();
      while (Serial.available() < PASS_LEN) { }
      for (int i = 0; i < PASS_LEN; i++) {
        char c = Serial.read();
        EEPROM.update(PASS_ADDR + i, c);
      }
      readStored();
      Serial.println("Password changed");
      while (Serial.available()) Serial.read();
      return;
    }

    if (Serial.available() >= PASS_LEN) {
      for (int i = 0; i < PASS_LEN; i++) entered[i] = Serial.read();
      entered[PASS_LEN] = '\0';
      while (Serial.available()) Serial.read();     // flush line ending

      if (strcmp(entered, storedPassword) == 0) {
        Serial.println("Access Granted");
        digitalWrite(greenPin, HIGH); digitalWrite(redPin, LOW);
        lockServo.write(90);                        // unlock
        failedAttempts = 0;
        EEPROM.update(ATTEMPTS_ADDR, 0);
        delay(5000);
        lockServo.write(0);                         // relock
        digitalWrite(greenPin, LOW);
      } else {
        failedAttempts++;
        EEPROM.update(ATTEMPTS_ADDR, failedAttempts);
        Serial.print("Access Denied  (attempt ");
        Serial.print(failedAttempts); Serial.print(" of ");
        Serial.print(MAX_ATTEMPTS); Serial.println(")");
        digitalWrite(redPin, HIGH); delay(500); digitalWrite(redPin, LOW);

        if (failedAttempts >= MAX_ATTEMPTS) {
          lockoutUntil = millis() + LOCKOUT_MS;
          Serial.println("LOCKED OUT for 30 seconds");
          failedAttempts = 0;
          EEPROM.update(ATTEMPTS_ADDR, 0);
        }
      }
      Serial.println("Enter password:");
    }
  }
}
Why the attempt count goes in EEPROM — the security argument

If the failed-attempt counter lived only in SRAM, an attacker could defeat the lockout by cutting power after two wrong guesses and starting fresh. Storing it in EEPROM makes the count survive a power cycle, so the lockout cannot be bypassed.

update() not write() here matters: the attempt counter is written on every failure. With write() a persistent attacker could wear the cell out in a few days; update() skips writes where the value is unchanged.

This is the most likely escalation of CAT Q3 — the same core with lockout, password change, and an actuator added.

Q12.6   Type T+P  ·  comparison

Compare internal and external EEPROM, with a benchmark

Write a program that times writes to the internal EEPROM and reports the throughput, then explain when an external SPI EEPROM becomes necessary.

Solution Q12.6
#include <EEPROM.h>

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  delay(300);

  const int N = 50;

  unsigned long t0 = micros();
  for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) EEPROM.write(100 + i, i);
  unsigned long t1 = micros();

  unsigned long t2 = micros();
  for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) EEPROM.update(100 + i, i);   // same values - no write
  unsigned long t3 = micros();

  unsigned long t4 = micros();
  volatile byte v = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) v = EEPROM.read(100 + i);
  unsigned long t5 = micros();

  Serial.print("write  : "); Serial.print((t1-t0)/(float)N, 1); Serial.println(" us/byte");
  Serial.print("update : "); Serial.print((t3-t2)/(float)N, 1); Serial.println(" us/byte (no change)");
  Serial.print("read   : "); Serial.print((t5-t4)/(float)N, 1); Serial.println(" us/byte");
  Serial.print("Capacity: "); Serial.print(EEPROM.length()); Serial.println(" bytes");
}

void loop() {}

Expected results: write ≈ 3300 µs per byte, update on unchanged data ≈ a few µs (it only reads), read ≈ 1–2 µs. That 1000× write/read asymmetry is the defining characteristic of EEPROM.

Internal EEPROMExternal SPI EEPROM (AT25HP512)
Capacity1 KB64 KB
InterfaceEEPROM.h, no wiringSPI — 4 wires
Pins used04 (10, 11, 12, 13)
Write granularity1 byte128-byte page
Write time~3.3 ms per byte~10 ms per 128-byte page
Effective write speed~300 bytes/s~12,800 bytes/s
Endurance~100,000 cycles~1,000,000 cycles
When to choose which — the design answer

Use the internal EEPROM for small, infrequently-changed data: calibration factors, tare offsets, a password, configuration settings, a device serial number. It costs no pins and no components.

Move to an external SPI EEPROM when you need more than 1 KB, or when you must write quickly and in bulk — data logging is the classic case. Page writing makes external EEPROM roughly 40× faster in bytes per second, at the cost of four pins and a component.
